en: The Scripture on the Gradual Preparation for All-Wisdom and Virtue, Scroll One;
also titled *The Ten Abodes*, or alternatively *The Samādhi of Great Wisdom Light*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Joyful Abiding of the Initial Resolve. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the Palace of the Heavenly King of the Sixth Heavens of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, atop the Wondrous Jewel Hall of the Wish-Fulfilling Treasury, together with an incalculable assembly of great Bodhisattvas who had each come from various Buddha-fields in other directions and gathered here, including Vajragarbha Bodhisattva and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, entered the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of Great Wisdom Light.

As soon as his mind was thus composed, in each of the ten directions throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten quarters—extending across as many billions of lands as there are atoms in ten billion Buddha-fields—the Tathāgatas appeared, each accompanied by a Bodhisattva likewise named Vajragarbha;
it was the same in all ten directions, and they all bore this identical name.
Then all these Buddhas praised him together, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

By means of this Bodhisattva Samādhi of Great Wisdom Light, you have entered into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions—each as numerous as the atoms filling ten billion worlds—you have established all the identical names of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones; all these are illuminations brought about by the original vows of the Tathāgatas, and they are also the result of your own pure wisdom. Furthermore, through the inconceivable light of the Dharma and the noble intent of all Bodhisattvas, you abide on the stage of clear wisdom, liberating many beings, gathering the roots of all virtues, fully understanding the original practices accomplished by all Buddhas, and out of compassion for the ten directions, you master skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), expound the transformation of the Way, universally propagate the wisdom of the Dharma, and circulate throughout the ten directions.
The principles of the sutras they expound are all made firm; their wisdom is so brilliant that none can destroy it. According to the times, they establish [the Dharma] so that all may find peace.

Wandering through the various worlds, they do not cling to worldly customs; they transcend the world with purity, adorning themselves with the roots of goodness. Entering the realm of inconceivable wisdom and attaining omniscience, they follow the lofty and remote path of the sages, thereby able to summon all bodhisattvas to abide in the ten stages of practice.

Just as the assembly of bodhisattvas should establish themselves, proclaiming the teachings, moving to and fro in their activities, upholding the untainted Dharma, illuminating all with light, reflecting well, composing their minds in detachment, and understanding things according to the occasion.
With the great wisdom-light, those who have not yet skillfully crossed over are led to the gateway of the holy path so that they may attain liberation without attachment.

Abiding in internal practice, they single-mindedly and diligently cultivate the unsurpassed Mahāyāna; their eloquence and wisdom are beyond measure, and their majestic radiance shines everywhere to dispel the darkness. Having transcended all mundane practices, they proclaim the infinite; dwelling in the stage of a Buddha while attaining the intent of a Bodhisattva, they compassionately regard sentient beings, never forgetting or abandoning them. They enter into the ultimate, true, and skillful means of all Buddhas to sever the web of the fetters of the multitude.

Receiving the Buddha’s holy decree, you have freely expounded and elucidated this Dharma-gate so that all may understand it; it was for this purpose that the Tathāgata established it while in the world, and it is also the result of your own original virtuous vows.

With pure conduct, they truly adorn the entire dharma-realm and rescue sentient beings from their delusions and distractions, thereby attaining the dharma-body and the essence of supreme wisdom. Fully realizing the original vows of all Buddhas, their physical actions transcend the mundane and universally surpass worldly, unbeneficial activities; they are adorned with the pure Dharma that delivers the world.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, out of no stinginess toward the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, each manifested their own bodies and proclaimed the meaning of infinite eloquence. They analyzed and resolved matters with exceedingly pure wisdom, holding them in mind without forgetfulness, establishing and revealing them according to what was appropriate for the occasion, and dispelling the doubts of the multitude. They universally entered into that which all Buddhas keep in mind, the source of the ten powers of the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the four fearlessnesses attained by the Tathāgatas; remaining undaunted, they proclaimed the ultimate teachings, the deeds of omniscience, and various analytical eloquences. They transcended and attained entry into the realization of the Dharma, entering the bodily, verbal, and mental activities of all Tathāgatas.

Why is this so? It is because they have achieved perfection through this very concentration, and because their original vows are profound and far-reaching; their minds are pure and free from defilement.

Internally, their nature is lucid and they constantly maintain purity; with majestic brilliance shining far and wide, they enter the field of wisdom. There is no practice or deed that they do not fully possess;

all that they establish is entirely complete. Their capacity for the Way is immeasurable; their faith and resolve are pure, lofty, and universally pervasive. Having attained the gateway of *dhāraṇī*, they remain indestructible, and they always use the seal of the Dharma-realm’s gate of wisdom to skillfully seal all things.
These Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, each manifested themselves individually and extended their right arms, all together stroking the head of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha with their hands.

At that time, as his head was being stroked by these World-Honored Ones, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha’s virtue and realization became most exalted and fully perfected; his majestic brilliance shone forth so radiantly that he was no different from a Buddha.
At that time, he immediately arose from samādhi and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Most Victorious! I have already clearly realized the vows of all bodhisattvas;

having destroyed the net of doubt, there is nothing further to be destroyed. There is no birth in the world, nor is there any fault or transgression. The dharma-realm is vast and expansive, with neither distance nor proximity. Their dwelling and wandering are like empty space; by means of this salvation, they protect and sustain all sentient beings throughout the ten directions."

The reason for this is that you, son of noble family, know that the bodhisattvas of the past and the buddhas of antiquity attained transcendence by means of this ground of wisdom; those of the future and the present are likewise so.
"Sons of the Buddha, you should know that when I previously spoke of the stages of the bodhisattva, what was meant by this?

There are ten stages of the path for the training of bodhisattvas, through which they achieve unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; these are what the Buddhas of the past, future, and present have taught."

The first stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Pramuditā* (Joy); the second stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Vimalā* (Stainless); the third stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Prabhākārī* (Luminous); the fourth stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Arciṣmatī* (Radiant); the fifth stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Sudurjayā* (Difficult to Conquer); the sixth stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Abhimukhī* (Facing); the seventh stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Dūraṅgamā* (Far-reaching); the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Acalā* (Immovable); the ninth stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Sādhumatī* (Excellent Intelligence); and the tenth stage of the Bodhisattva is called *Dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma). These are the ten stages of the path of the Bodhisattvas.

I observe that among the Buddhas of the ten directions—those of the past, future, and present—all the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, have none who do not expound this practice of the Ten Abodes. Why is this so?

O sons of the Buddha, these ten abodes cause all bodhisattvas to now draw near to the gateways of the unconditioned dharmas of the pure path. Their names manifest and illuminate countless buddha-lands throughout the ten directions; all sentient beings within the triple world receive deliverance thereby. They illuminate the world like the brilliance of the sun, heal all ailments like a king of physicians, ferry across the masses like a maritime captain, shine upon the ten directions like the full moon, sustain all things like the earth, bring peace to sentient beings like timely rain, contain the dharma of the Way like space, and stand firm and upright like Mount Sumeru. By proclaiming this teaching, one attains steadfast establishment in the ten stages of the path. Furthermore, one understands the inconceivable dwellings of the bodhisattvas in these stages and enters universally into noble wisdom.

At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva briefly set forth the essentials, extolling the deeds of these ten stages of the bodhisattva dwellings; he then immediately fell silent and did not further elaborate upon them.

At that time, the great assembly was filled with a sense of longing and thirst for the Dharma. Having heard the names of this Bodhisattva’s ten stages of dwelling (*daśabhūmi*), they desired him to analyze and further expound their meaning so that all who hear might understand and resolve to enter the Way, thereby departing from all perversions. Each thought to themselves:

"For what reason does the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha now merely outline the essentials and proclaim the practices of the Bodhisattvas of the ten dwellings, praising their titles yet remaining silent, without further elaborating upon or explaining their origins and conclusions?"
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Candravimokṣa who had also come to the gathering.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candravimokṣa, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas in the assembly, praised them with verses and questioned Vajragarbha regarding the ultimate meaning of this matter:
"For what reason is Pure Mindfulness (Vimalaprajñā) Endowed with wisdom and renowned for its meritorious achievements?"
The Wise One proclaims the ten stages; why does he not further explain that which they enter?
The bodhisattvas are courageous, yet each harbors doubts in their hearts:
Why do you speak of the names of the meanings, while we do not hear of the locations of the stages of the Way?
All desire together to hear from the fearless Son of the Most Victorious:
the definitive meaning that enters into equality, and the stages of the path upon which he dwells.
The entire assembly is filled with joy; they are purified and rid of flattery and deceit.
Firmly abiding in the stage of clear understanding, their merit and wisdom are balanced and even.
All stand in reverence, looking toward one another with mutual expectation;
seeking the subtle and flawless, their resolve is set upon the unsurpassed nectar of immortality.
Having heard from Vajragarbha, who possesses fearless and great wisdom, the assembly has come with constant joy;
O Benevolent One, you should now discourse with the Buddha.
What has never before been reached by others is most difficult to attain; may you reveal the conduct of the Bodhisattvas.
Discriminating according to the stages of the path, that by which one proceeds is most supreme and excellent.
Abandoning perceptions, subtle and difficult to perceive, one dwells eternally with a mind detached from the world;
through the practice of gentleness and benevolence, wisdom is perfected, and one hears directly of the destination to which one returns.
Their dwelling is like a vajra; they possess the foremost understanding of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Establishing the mind to relinquish the self, one then hears this supreme knowledge.
The Tathāgata exhausts all that is void and non-existent; his freedom from desire is likewise like space.
Wisdom is like the earth, untainted; its arising in distinction is most difficult to perceive.
The Path is thus free from conceptualization, and those who have faith in it are exceedingly rare to encounter.
The Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable; therefore, he remains silent and does not speak of it again.
The Bodhisattva Candravimukti addressed the Vajragarbha: "O Son of the Buddha, you should observe!

Those who have gathered here are pure in nature and conduct, refined and free from defilement; their wills are benevolent and harmonious. They are all bodhisattvas whose practices are authentic, who have accumulated merit and virtue through successive lifetimes of self-discipline. Adorned by the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), they cultivate the four immeasurables and the four ways of winning over others, employing skillful means; their achievements are far-reaching and their fame and virtue are immeasurable."

Possessing great kindness and great compassion, he desires to promote the transformation of the Way and disseminate the teachings of the Dharma to rescue and deliver all beings in peril within the three realms. He dispels the darkness of the world like the brilliance of the sun; he produces the factors of enlightenment like a fertile field; he achieves perfect awakening like space; he long propagates the teachings like flowing water; he removes doubt like the light of the sun; he cures the three poisons like a king of physicians; and he ferries others across birth and death like a master mariner.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is well that you, O Benevolent One, should proclaim and disseminate these present practices and studies, so that this ground of the Way may become the destination for those who cultivate through conditions, and so that all those gathered here may each attain understanding—like one seeing light in the darkness—and receive medicine according to their ailments, leaving no further doubts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Moon-Liberation (Candravimukti), wishing to further elaborate upon the origins and details of this meaning and to reveal its ultimate destination,
spoke these verses to Vajragarbha: "May you, O Flourishing One, please expound upon the extraordinary and supreme Dharma—
The conduct of those foremost among men, the practice of all Bodhisattvas."
He expounds and proclaims his teaching, the stages of the path where he dwells;
his noble wisdom is exceedingly pure, and his deeds of benevolence and harmony are sublime.
Those gathered in the assembly are pure, beyond measure and foremost.
Firmly established upon the true path, their wills and natures embrace profound faith.
Having skillfully accumulated merit and built up virtue, they have served countless billions of Buddhas;
each desiring definitive understanding, they soon manifest the attainment of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied to Candravimokṣa:
"O Son of the Buddha, observe this!
This assembly has gathered from the four directions like clouds; how do you perceive it?"
Your thoughts should be appropriate, gentle and harmonious, pure and without blemish; how could you remain free from doubt and hesitation?
Regarding these essential teachings, surely there is noble conduct that does not rely on others—how could you fail to look up to them with reverence?

Not following the teachings of others, they are uneasy in their advancement or retreat; harboring chronic illnesses that cannot be cured, they remain firmly ensnared in the net, have not emerged from the deep moat, and are beset by the sixty-two doubts, the four inversions, and the five hindrances. Dwelling in the forest of fire and the chamber of serpents, caught in the twelvefold entanglements and the ten-fold pavilion, they wander aimlessly through the wilderness of the three pits, the three gates, and the three torrents, having not yet turned toward the Buddha-gate; even if they were to hear this Dharma, they would hesitate and fail to advance.

Furthermore, there may be some persons who, upon hearing of this inconceivable abiding in the Way, each harbor divergent thoughts; having heard it, they are filled with doubt and refuse to believe it steadfastly. Due to such confusion, they remain restless through the long night, forever losing the benefit of the true meaning, and abandoning the root to grasp at the branches.
Therefore, I remained silent just now out of compassion for these beings; I have no words to speak, for I abide in bliss where there is nothing to be desired.
He further spoke in verse:
“How could one see within this assembly One whose wisdom is pure and stainless?”
He skillfully expounds the Noble Path; his faculties are penetrating and profoundly subtle.
He has nothing upon which to rely or look up to; he is as immovable and steady as a mountain.
His disposition is free from anger and resentment; his thoughts are as level and upright as still water.
What is the practice cultivated through training? It is wisdom beyond compare.
Abiding in that which is known as bliss, one seeks the faith of the wisdom of meaning.
Should one hear this and fall into hesitation, one will immediately descend into the evil realms.
"For this reason, out of compassion for them, he does not speak of the stage of abiding in wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Moon-Liberation then addressed Vajragarbha: "Virtuous One, please turn your attention to us;

receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, proclaim the intent of the Tathāgata so as to move the ten directions, turning [beings] away from the false toward the true, eliminating all defilements and dust, washing away obstructions and stagnations, tearing asunder the net of the triple world, and opening the path to infinite wisdom. Pray, expound upon it! Such inconceivable matters as these must be properly nurtured and sustained; those who are broad-minded and magnanimous will surely believe and rejoice in them without hesitation."
Why is this so? Sons of the Buddha, you should know!

If one expounds this teaching, it will lead to the Way and its Dharma; all Bodhisattvas will then mindfully recollect all Buddhas, penetrate the meaning of the sutras, and protect and uphold this stage of the path of practicing wisdom, such that none shall fail to receive its benefits and all shall attain peace and security.

Why is this so? That which is practiced here must ultimately return to equality. The Dharma of the Buddhas is like that of a Buddha’s son; all written records merely expound upon characters, yet these all have the mind as their primary source. They rely upon the causal conditions of intention, yet writing itself has no inherent pattern. The characters thus manifested are empty at their source within the mind, and what is proclaimed is but voidness.

In this way, O Son of the Buddha, all Buddha-dharmas have the dwelling as their primary source; they are accomplished through practice and depend upon the stages of the path until the attainment of spontaneous wisdom.

Therefore, it is said: out of compassion for all beings, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, empowers you with the power of his path to establish and distinguish these written words, so that they may be made clear, the True Dharma may be protected and long endure, and no further fetters remain.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
“Excellent is the exposition of purity, Which leads to the understanding and entry into all-knowledge;
Universally traversing the essentials of all paths, One reaches awakening and accomplishes noble wisdom.”
All the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, dwelling securely in the most supreme path;
having reached the ultimate realm of the chamber of wisdom, they all together take pity upon him.
Establishing this intimacy with wisdom, he practices this track that leads to the ultimate end.
The peerless Dharma of all Buddhas arises entirely from immeasurable karma.
Just as written characters are formed by the convergence of intention, with the mind and its object as the primary factors;
so too does this abiding of the mind lead, through thorough understanding and expansion, to the path of Buddhahood.

Thereupon, all these bodhisattvas each resolved their minds and joined together in mutual exhortation and support, desiring to proclaim the origin of benevolence and the arousal of the will. They vowed for the sake of all beings to labor diligently and accumulate merit, amassing immeasurable virtues.

Like space itself, they sought to rescue those in peril and distress; they did not find the passage of kalpas difficult, and though they wandered through birth and death, their minds were ever earnest, desiring to save all while remaining free from attachment.

Their practice was like a lotus in the mud: they were not constrained by the sufferings of the three realms, but harbored only compassion, seeking to uproot the very seeds of affliction so that the tree of the three periods of time might forever be left without remainder.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas simultaneously raised their voices to praise and exhort Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, speaking in verse:
"Most supreme and extraordinary, his resolve and awakening are far-reaching; His eloquence is immeasurable and his mind is fully endowed with mindfulness.
He proclaims the gentle teachings leading to the Buddha’s enlightenment— The foremost, the most true, and exceedingly subtle."
With firm resolve and pure conduct, you do not abandon the ten powers of merit;
through analytical eloquence, you cultivate practice—may you please expound the Dharma of the supreme path.
The thoughts of the mind are like bright pearls; with a tranquil will, one eliminates worldly desires.
Now this assembly is free from doubt, and all joyfully desire what you, O Benevolent One, have spoken.
Thirsting for the teaching like one longing for a spring, Starving, they serve the Benevolent One as the sick await a physician;
With sweet cakes right before their eyes, They thus rejoice in the flavor of the ambrosia.
Therefore, may you graciously turn your thoughts toward broadening his resolve, proclaiming this sublime dwelling to remove all defilements;

may he remain in tranquil composure and right peace, never abandoning the state of non-existence, and expounding the practices of the World-Honored Ones so that there be no further suffering or hardship.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One emitted a sublime and holy radiance from among the bodhisattvas, known as Power and Might (*Balavega*). From between his eyebrows, the Buddha projected this brilliance, giving rise to countless lights that universally illumined all buddha-fields throughout the ten directions. All evil destinies were extinguished; the sufferings of diligent toil were brought to rest, and no further punishments were meted out. All became peaceful and secure. This light shone upon the Tathāgata’s entire site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
in the buddha-lands of the ten directions, the Dharma was established and preached, pervading everywhere throughout the inconceivable realms of the Buddhas.
The light then returned, circled the Buddha three times, and ascended into the void where it merged into a great radiance; the brilliance was magnificent, forming an interlaced canopy of pearls.

Furthermore, there were Buddhas appearing in the world, naturally radiant with majesty; from between their eyebrows, they emitted such arrays as these, and the power and brilliance of the various bodhisattvas manifested in similar fashion. Through their supernormal transformations, they illuminated this Sahā world-system. This radiance from the Tathāgata illuminated the assembly at the site of enlightenment and the Lion Throne of Vajragarbha, which then remained suspended in the void, forming a canopy of interlacing light.

This is the Buddha Śākyamuni; from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, a radiance issues forth, vast and far-reaching, illuminating all darkness throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions and the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment. There are none who do not receive this brilliant light, and it clearly manifests before all the bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas, shining resplendently upon their dwellings.

Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, the radiance emanating from the space between the eyebrows of all Tathāgatas shone forth and illuminated this Sahā world, pervading the bodhimanda where the Sage Gathers his assembly and shining completely upon the lofty and vast lion throne.

Within the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, a great radiance appeared, towering and brilliantly shining. Canopies of interlaced pearls were suspended, each containing a seated Buddha. From their own mouths, they uttered these words of praise:
"Compared to him, nothing is equal; He is like the vast emptiness of space.
The Honored One of the ten powers’ realm Possesses merits beyond measure."
Exquisite, supreme, and extraordinary, it is unsurpassed throughout all worlds;
establishing the foremost of deeds, it is the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas.
The sons who dwell peacefully among the assembly have received the grace and compassion of the Teacher.
The Dharma King, sovereign among men, radiates light from between his brows;
He proclaims the wisdom of the Buddha-way, entering the wondrous state where all conditioned practices cease.
Relying on the grace of the Ten Powers, he discerns and universally transforms all beings.
Abiding securely, he establishes this teaching; having heard it, he can proclaim its illumination.
The Dharma-jewel is the most honored; such is the tranquility of his resolute nature.
Abiding everywhere without defilement, he fulfills his original vows to their full extent.
Because the Ten Powers are supreme, one resolves to seek the most exalted path.
The waters of the ocean may yet be exhausted, and all things may be known through calculation;
yet if one wishes to cross over this [ocean of suffering], it cannot be heard all at once.
Those who can leave behind volitions and thoughts, forever eliminating all doubts;
for whom there is no other compassion than this, they are illuminated by this sutra.
Therefore, the Honored One of Eloquence dwells upon the path of wisdom through these conditions.
Abiding wherever they may be, they uphold this practice; their every step relies upon their fundamental karma.
Through supreme conduct, they enter the realm and universally reach the holy wisdom of the Buddhas;
out of compassion for all sentient beings, they disseminate these causes of the Dharma.

Thereupon, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva surveyed the ten directions; wishing to cause the assembled multitude to once again experience joy and yearn for the Dharma with thirsting longing, he gave rise to great compassion and boundless kindness. At that moment, on this account, he uttered these verses of praise:
“The path and Dharma of the Great Sage Are subtle, wondrous, profound, and far-reaching;
Through non-thought and the relinquishing of thought, They are pure, limpid, and forever difficult to fathom.”
The Sage’s brilliance penetrates the profound and subtle; his wisdom understands all that is practiced.
Spontaneously his karma is tranquil and secure; gentle and benevolent, he is free from strife and turmoil.
The spontaneous dharma of emptiness and purity is still and silent, eliminating suffering and affliction.
Wandering and dwelling until liberation is reached, one attains the equality of *nirvāṇa*.
Its meaning is infinite and boundless; its expression approaches transcendence.
Having surpassed the three periods of time, its practice is equal to empty space.
The conduct of all the Protectors is tranquil and profoundly serene;
the path of all their deeds is difficult to comprehend.
Their practice is like the earth, and their resolute nature is likewise so.
It is exceedingly difficult to explain; how could one possibly discern it?
Having cast away mind and mental objects, there are forever no traces of words for the mind.
This is the practice of all the Protectors of the World: wisdom consumes the food of speech.
Furthermore, there is nothing practiced; there are no aggregates, no elements, and no sense-bases.
The noble one relies on the karmic activity of wisdom, and his mind is free from conceptualization.
It is like a bird in flight, traversing through the empty sky.
It cannot be expressed in words, let alone be seen with the eyes.
Abiding in spontaneous wisdom, one dwells thus practicing the Way;
the mental activities and thoughts therein cannot be known through conceptual discrimination.
What sphere of entry exists that is the ground of supreme wisdom?
With constant compassion and pity, one’s vows are universally fulfilled.
Gradually perfecting all practices, the mind remains free from conceptualization.
Just as the intrinsic nature of the mind is clarified by wisdom,
so too are the karmic actions of such practice subtle and exceedingly difficult to understand;
lacking the corresponding disposition within oneself, they cannot be suddenly grasped or known.
How much more so for those who can proclaim it, dwelling securely in its contemplation;
let all together show reverence and listen clearly to these profound and wondrous teachings.
By entering into correct and true wisdom, one dwells as one who treads the Path.
Even if one were to spend billions of eons, one could never reach the ultimate end [of this teaching].
May all together be filled with joy and listen attentively;
regarding the wondrous and true meaning of supreme sincerity, remain without weariness and without divergence.
Not regarding it as confusion, it is like the formation of a great ocean;
now I shall fully expound the path of practice of all the Protectors of the World.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim and declare the extraordinary sound of the Dharma.
Drawing forth a multitude of parables, with words that are perfectly true and equal,
their analytical exposition is exceedingly difficult to unravel;
established in the matters of practice and conduct, they are thus immeasurable.
"Now that we have attained entry into the natural state of the self, all rejoice as if at a single drop of water; listen now to what is proclaimed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha addressed the assembled multitude:

"O Son of the Buddha, observe! These assembled beings have accumulated roots of virtue and practice the true reality without hypocrisy; they perform deeds that are exceedingly good and provide protection; they constantly and diligently make offerings to the Buddhas appearing in the world; they are thoroughly united with all pure and white dharmas; they always consult and receive instruction from spiritual friends; they eliminate sorrow and grief, and their nature is broad and magnanimous; they possess profound faith in the subtle and wondrous samādhi of equanimity; they behold the present with compassionate pity; and their minds are constantly intent upon the noble wisdom of all Buddhas."

They transform all sentient beings so that they all resolve their minds upon the Way, causing them all to attain true excellence and love for all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). Possessing the ten powers (*daśabala*) with great strength and vigor, they are able to travel freely within great fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*). Their minds are serene as they attain the Buddha’s True Dharma, protecting and rescuing all sentient beings. They cultivate great compassion, whose pity is pure; throughout the ten directions without exception, they fully understand all things. The gate of brilliant wisdom is fully manifested before their eyes; all Buddha-lands are unconditioned and pure. In a single moment, they awaken to the events of the three periods of time, turning the Great Wheel of Dharma to heal the ailments of the multitude.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment even for a moment, he takes compassionate action toward sentient beings as his primary principle, exercising infinite great pity. His wisdom is clear and penetrating, most magnificently sublime; he constantly and diligently studies and receives skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), with a mind-nature that is harmonious and gentle, drawing near to the Dharma. The ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata are immeasurable; through careful reflection and discernment, he realizes that among all human powers, the power of the Buddha is supreme. The Dharma-gates he proclaims are without obstruction, employing a wisdom that is harmonious, compliant, and sovereign.

The Buddha fully understands the arising of all Buddhas; by virtue of this mastery, he establishes the supreme practice of the Dharma-realm within the teachings of the Path, reaching the limits of space. Whatever mind he brings forth, it clearly manifests the aspiration for Bodhisattvahood in the future.

Having just given rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and transcended the stage of ordinary beings, one attains transcendence of the stages of bodhisattvas and is thus born into the lineage of the Tathāgatas; for this reason, one is called "That Which Is Unarisen" (Anutpāda).

Being free from fault or transgression, they immediately turn back the worldly inclinations; having just transcended the mundane through world-transcending practice, they thereby attain and establish themselves in the Dharma of the Bodhisattva path.

Having already attained and established themselves in the Dharma of the Bodhisattva path, they are able to accord with the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, diligently applying their minds to the meaning of the Way with a mind that is always profoundly supreme.
When Bodhisattvas abide in such a Dharma of the Way, they rejoice in the stages of the Path.

"O Son of the Buddha, you should know! Thus established and abiding in the Bodhisattva path, one acts with immovability and enters into non-retrogression. One who dwells in the Bodhisattva stage of Joy (Ratiprīti-bhūmi) gives rise to much delight by virtue of this resolve; those who see him are without exception filled with joy. He is always honored and receives offerings; those who come to see him all rejoice together. He transforms and enlightens the multitude, who all accept his teaching. People gather from afar and near to enjoy his company, yet he considers them all as lacking solidity. He constantly maintains benevolence and harmony, never causing harm; his will is ever joyful and his mind harbors no resentment. With a gentle countenance and pleasant expression, he is free from anger—this is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy."
Abiding in the Way of the Buddhas, all the World-Honored Buddhas collectively keep them in mind, feeling the utmost joy;
contemplating the Buddha-dharma, they immediately experience joy;
recollecting the fundamental practices of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, they immediately harbor joy.
Recalling the practices of a bodhisattva, he immediately gives rise to joy;
recalling the six perfections that are pure and infinite, he immediately gives rise to joy;
recalling the extraordinary state in which a bodhisattva dwells, he immediately gives rise to joy.
Reflecting that the Way is most subtle and without peer, one experiences immediate joy;
because of sentient beings, one benefits through the principles of the Way, experiencing immediate joy;
advancing the mind toward the profound Dharma, one experiences immediate joy.
They reflect upon the teaching of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One; they reflect upon exhorting and transforming all sentient beings, and thus experience joy.

They reflect upon the diligent practice of entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata as performed by all bodhisattvas; they repeatedly contemplate how to lead those who have not yet reached it so that they may attain liberation. For this purpose, they speak of the realms cherished by all sentient beings, bringing them to enter the equality of all Buddhas. Having already emerged far from the ground of ignorance and drawn near to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they have severed all the hardships of the evil destinies. As leaders in exhorting and guiding all sentient beings, they have already beheld the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, and have fully accomplished the realm of the Tathāgata. Because they have all attained the vision of the equalizing practice of the bodhisattvas' meditative concentration, they are joyful!
Because all fears have been eternally eliminated and the hairs of one's body do not stand on end, one is thus joyful!
Why is this so? For this reason, O Son of the Buddha!

When the bodhisattvas train with such joy, they immediately attain and establish themselves upon the stages of the bodhisattva path. Because they have established themselves upon these bodhisattva stages, all fears and terrors shall never again arise;

they abide in security without fear for their lives, without fear of the mundane world, and without fear of death. They do not fear the evil realms, and when entering any assembly, they encounter no hesitation or difficulty, for they have forever eliminated all forms of dread.
Why is this? Because they are free from the notion of self and do not covet their own bodies, much less covet all the various honors and the karmic fruits that arise from them.

They do not fear the absence of life, nor do they harbor thoughts of hope or seeking fortune; rather, out of compassion for all sentient beings and their infinite karmic activities, they rescue those who are destitute. Their lack of craving and ignorance regarding the Path is what constitutes the absence of worldly fear.
Having perfected his spiritual illumination, he does not regard his own body, nor does he fear losing himself, for he is free from the notion of "I" and "mine," and thus he does not fear death;
even when his life comes to an end, he perfects the bodhisattva practice and never departs from the Buddhas. For this reason, he does not fear the evil realms;
he surveys the world universally and examines the mind of the Way, finding no equal to him, for his will and nature are benevolent and harmonious—who could surpass him?
For this reason, whenever he enters an assembly, he harbors no resentment or difficulty; he is free from fear and dread, and his hair does not stand on end.
O Son of the Buddha, you should understand this!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, possessing great compassion and harboring no intent to harm, cultivates the fundamentally pure mind and increases his diligence, gathering together the roots of all virtues.
The Buddha said:
"Because they have arrived with sincere faith, their majestic spiritual power gradually becomes complete, and there is much cause for joy.
Thus, those without faith are purified, and sincere faith arises.
Constantly practicing compassion, they take refuge in infinite kindness;
their minds do not weary of the hardships of birth and death, as they are dedicated to a sense of shame and remorse, thereby adorning themselves;
in whatever place their minds arise, they remain patient, harmonious, and benevolent.
They offer various kinds of articles to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
rising early and retiring late, they practice with diligent vigor;
never wearying of recitation and preaching, they accumulate the roots of merit.
Associating with virtuous friends, one finds delight in the joy of the Dharma;
seeking extensive learning without weariness, if one hears the Dharma, one contemplates it accordingly, and having contemplated it, remains free from attachment;
one does not hope for clothing or food, nor for various gains and offerings.
The mind harbors no greedy longing; its affection for the myriad things has been forever eliminated.

One yearns only for the Dharma and seeks the Three Jewels; from the very moment the aspiration is conceived, one does not neglect right practice. Diligently cultivating and delighting in the ground of all-knowledge, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one single-mindedly and earnestly practices the six perfections.
Abandoning falsehood and hypocrisy, one is free from flattery; one’s words and deeds correspond, never allowing the mouth to contradict the heart.
Wherever they go, they always act in accordance with their words and never bring disorder to the lineage of the Tathāgatas;
they constantly maintain a single-minded recollection of the bodhisattva precepts and the mind of omniscience, remaining unshakable like Mount Sumeru which cannot be overturned;

throughout the world, they have no attachments or delights, seeking instead the practice that transcends the world to transform those who have not yet heard the Dharma; they study the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas) without ever knowing satiety, their minds always diligent as they seek extraordinary and sublime matters.

This is the purification of the path through such karmic activities for the sons of the Buddha; it purifies the bodhisattva-dharma and enables one to immediately attain firm abiding in the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The World-Honored One further said:
"If one can establish oneself in the stage of joy, one accomplishes the bodhisattva-abiding and constructs the vast and infinite path."
"Such armor of infinite great vows and far-reaching pledges has ten further qualities. What are these ten? They are: proclaiming [the Dharma] inexhaustibly;
using harmonious and elegant speech; reaching the point of being beyond analogy; being all-encompassing and thorough; and offering all manner of rare treasures to all Buddhas."

With profound faith in the subtle and pure karma, the *dharmadhātu* is serene; their resolve is directed toward the realm of emptiness, and they have attained thorough understanding and mastery. Regarding the future limit, they are entirely free of conceptualization and harbor no expectations, yet they cause the Buddha-way to flourish. Having no thoughts of personal pleasure, those whom they serve provide for them infinitely. Their will is dedicated to the great vows, and they keep in mind the teachings expounded by all Tathāgatas. Holding fast to the eye of the Dharma, they protect the deeds of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, never deviating from the instructions of the Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Having been able to fulfill the aforementioned Dharma-instructions, they immediately attain rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Descending from that heaven, they enter the mother’s womb, abide within the embryonic chamber, emerge from the mother’s womb, and accordingly—
He took seven steps and raised his hand to praise himself as the most honored in the three realms; Śakra and Brahmā prostrated themselves before him, and the various nāgas bathed his body.
He mastered writing with a broad mind, and what he beheld during his travels led him to leave the household life and enter the mountains.
Having attained Buddhahood and subdued Māra, Śakra and Brahmā exhorted and assisted him as he turned the Great Wheel of Dharma and manifested the Great Parinirvāṇa—thus was he honored.
They venerated the relics, proclaimed the transformative teachings, and elucidated the meanings of the various sutras;
all at once they attained the stage of non-retrogression. The Dharma-realm is vast and expansive, beyond measure.

Abiding within the realm of empty space, they ultimately achieve thorough understanding for the sake of future generations; amidst all thoughts, they remain free from conceptualization, following from the countless...
Throughout kalpas, they shall together attain the Buddha-way, maintaining firm faith without weariness;

they shall go forth in unison to proclaim the sounds of the Dharma, with infinite great vows, extending even to all the practices of a Bodhisattva—vast and inexhaustible, immeasurable and innumerable—embracing all the *pāramitās*, abiding in the path of purity, and discerning the categories of assemblies, their voices, signs, and signlessness, as well as union and separation, the conditioned and the unconditioned. Serving as the foremost teachers for all Bodhisattvas, they abide in the true and wondrous Way; the chapters and verses they expound are the various *pāramitās*.

Regarding what they should proclaim and practice, they diligently cultivate right conduct without giving rise to [dualistic] birth; drawing near to the initial arousal of the mind, once they have fully perfected these dharmas, they will completely understand and elucidate the realms of sentient beings.

Regarding the realms of form and formlessness, non-perception, perception, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception; those born in water or on land; places of assembly and congregation; all that is produced; those who take form within the three realms; and the six destinations—all these take form and possess locations. Even for those beings who receive formless bodies and whose realms are beyond all analogy, one distinguishes them all. By transforming and entering the Buddha-dharma to sever all that is produced through conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), one establishes and achieves omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This is called the vastness of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); thus one comes to abide in the realm of empty space. The mind can thoroughly understand the ultimate limit of the future, maintaining firm faith without weariness toward all perceptions and the karma of conditioned existence.

They manifest sublime sounds and voices, even unto the deeds of their boundless great vows. They understand the realms of all sentient beings; whether mundane or supramundane, they attain realization such that nothing remains unpenetrated. Throughout all Buddha-worlds—whether vast or narrow, coarse or subtle, large or small, manifest or unmanifest, finite or infinite, profound beyond naming, or as remote as the very summit of the origin—they enter into equality. Having entered equality, they clearly comprehend the various faculties of beings. All nets of conceptualization are resolved like passing through a doorway. Entering the ten directions, they observe them universally with wisdom, thoroughly understanding the fundamental limit of the Dharma-realm and empty space, thereby attaining entry into the boundless great vows.

Furthermore, they treat all lands as a single land and a single land as all lands, governing them with equanimity; pure and free from defilement, their light shines universally upon immeasurable Buddha-lands, adorning all realms so that they are forever free from dust. They discern the destination of pure verses and phrases, and their hall of noble wisdom is immeasurable. Fulfilling the vows of sentient beings, they manifest transformations according to the fundamental practices raised by the masses, revealing the subtle and wondrous realm of the Buddhas. The Dharma-realm is vast and expansive; observing the void realm, it is eternally without boundaries. Regarding the ultimate limit of all conceptual thoughts, their calculations and assemblies never cease.
Moreover, they do not believe in or follow the karma of deviant practices; they cultivate purity and don the armor of great vows.
Transforming those who have not yet heard [the Dharma], they cause all bodhisattvas to enter the nature of tranquil harmony;
they should practice with utmost sincerity, accumulating merit and virtue, advancing by means of a single object of focus, exhorting, transforming, and guiding all bodhisattvas,
never abandoning the bodhisattva vocation, allowing their own understanding to unfold freely, manifesting the arising of Buddhas, and spontaneously generating their own resolve.
Contemplating the teachings of the Tathāgata, he no longer undergoes the cycle of coming and going; having attained supernormal powers, he travels universally through all lands.
His great and holy wisdom is inconceivable; he practices the deeds of a bodhisattva within the vast expanse of the dharma-realm.
As the realm of empty space is without limit, so too does he traverse the bounds of the future, penetrating all categories of conceptualization.
The number of Buddhas and their retinues, as well as the number of their practices, cannot be diminished or destroyed.
They enter into noble wisdom and manifest their verbal and physical conduct through infinite, great vows.

Practicing the Bodhisattva path, they attain the turning of the mind and the non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma; their body, speech, and mind have never been false. As soon as they behold the Buddha and hear the teachings of the Dharma, they proclaim them to the assembly of sages and expound upon the work of wisdom. Having attained joy and gladness, they eliminate worldly afflictions and reach the nature of true resolve. Just as a great king of physicians treats the illnesses of all beings, they cultivate all the practices of the Bodhisattvas; for this reason, it is called the Vast and Broad Dharmadhātu.

That realm of empty space is without limit or boundary, extending through the reaches of the future; it fully knows the conduct of all sentient beings throughout incalculable kalpas and the destinations of their good and evil deeds.

It encompasses the Buddha-lands of the ten directions where they attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become Most Perfectly Awakened Ones, entering into every pore of their bodies and pervading all the hairs, wherever they may be born.
Abiding beneath the Bodhi tree, he turns the Wheel of Dharma and manifests Great Parinirvāṇa;

cultivating the Great Realm and proclaiming the Buddha’s work of wisdom, he dwells within the realm of sentient beings, manifesting his form according to their fundamental practices to repeatedly transform and guide them, extinguishing all defiled conduct.
Once he has attained the Way of the Buddha, the Dharma universally pervades all.

The realm is characterized by humility, reverence, and obedience, encompassing all things without exception. With a single utterance of sound, it gladdens the mental natures of all sentient beings and manifests great parinirvāṇa.

Without destroying the ten powers, it proclaims and displays the entire treasury of all dharmas through the ground of great illumination, as well as the karmic activities of the supernormal powers, the dharma-wisdom, and the six penetrations.
They travel throughout the realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions; for this reason, it is called the vast expanse of the Dharma-realm.

Just as the realm of empty space has no boundaries, they extend through the future for incalculable kalpas until they attain the Buddha-way and achieve the armor of great supernatural powers and great vows; these are the ten vows of the Bodhisattvas, the children of the Buddha.

"By attaining proximity to the fulfillment of the ten vows, they cause the countless, immeasurable, and incalculable multitudes of bodhisattvas to harbor joy in their hearts, abide in the bodhisattva stages, and at all times manifest the teachings of the Buddha through transformation; this is the training of the bodhisattva, by which these vows are accomplished."
Furthermore, there are ten matters that can be proclaimed but cannot be fully exhausted. What are these ten?
The realm of sentient beings cannot be fully exhausted;
the realm of all Buddhas likewise cannot be exhausted.
The realm of empty space is also immeasurable;
the sphere of the contemplation of dharmas is also beyond full expression;
the sphere of the unconditioned is also limitless.
The realm of the Buddha cannot be fathomed;
the realm of the Tathāgata likewise has no limit;
and the causal conditions of his mind are also beyond measure.
The beginning and end of the practice of wisdom cannot be fathomed;
regarding the spheres of all Buddhas, their advancing and retreating, and the turning of the Dharma and the revolving of wisdom, they cannot be brought to a final conclusion.
These are the ten matters.

The realm of sentient beings cannot be fully exhausted, yet one forms great vows of vast magnanimity; these ten activities are all likewise inexhaustible. The various realms, empty space, the unconditioned dharma-realm, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, their mental wisdom and conduct, the turning of the world’s dharmas, and the attainment of wisdom and progress—all these great vows are both finite and infinite, for the realm of sentient beings can never be exhausted.

By means of this inexhaustibility of the roots of all these virtues, one thus ultimately perfects the wisdom of the Way. Because these roots of virtue are inexhaustible, one dons the armor of great vows that can never be diminished. One's mind becomes subtle and wondrous, harboring benevolence and harmony, always maintaining utmost sincerity, profound faith, and simple integrity.

By means of this faith and delight in the Great Transformation of the Tathāgata, one enters the original vows of Equal Enlightenment; furthermore, one has faith and delight in the various *pāramitās*, faith in entering the extraordinary practices of the stages of the Path (*bhūmi*), and faith in the Ten Powers that transform the ten directions. One has faith in the Four Fearlessnesses and the Four Things Needing No Protection, whereby one is fully endowed with solitary sovereignty throughout the three realms. One has faith in the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of all Buddhas, which are transcendent and without equal; one has faith in the inconceivable nature of all Buddha-dharmas, and faith that the realm of the Tathāgata is bottomless. One has faith that the proclamation of the holy teaching is inexhaustible, and faith in entering the immeasurable path-practices of the Tathāgata. One has faith that the practices of all Bodhisattvas are equal, without partiality or bias.

Abiding in the Tathāgata, he proclaims the teachings of the Way. He contemplates the Dharma of the Tathāgata as being thus: profoundly deep, subtle and wondrous, majestic and lofty; tranquil and boundless, serene and immeasurable; empty and pure without limit, such that it is signless (*animitta*); for the sake of cessation and non-attachment, it is supremely vast and expansive. Such is its infinity and the boundlessness of what it enters; how much more so the Buddha-dharma, which is difficult to withstand—who could possibly limit it?

These ordinary persons possess perverted views; their errors cannot be rectified. They contemplate only ignorance and darkness, seeking that which is of no benefit; their minds and thoughts wander amidst the dust and toil of the world. Seeking the net of affection and love, they conspire with flattery and deceit; their mental conduct is hypocritical, characterized by stinginess, jealousy, greed, and envy. Their wills long for birth and death, wandering to and fro while harboring the three poisons. Defiled by lust, anger, and delusion, they revolve through the cycle of existence without end. Arising with a mind of malice and harm, they flare up like a blazing fire, creating sinful afflictions through their inverted karma.

All attachments, ignorance, and the outflows constantly dwell within the mind, binding its consciousness. One wanders through the tribulations and calamities of the three realms; acts of usurpation and rebellion proceed without ceasing. Together with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), they arise from mutual production; because name-and-form grows and develops, there arises the abode of the decay-aggregate of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Because the six sense bases are produced, they successively flow together to form contact (*sparśa*), whereby sensations (*vedanā*) arise.
One redoubles one's craving for pleasure regarding these sensations; thus, through the karma of sensation, the cause of karma grows and is nourished by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Having just formed bonds of affection, one consequently brings about birth;
because of this birth, there arise aging, illness, death, sorrow, affliction, and lamentation; with the mind harboring distress and fever, these combine to form a great calamity;
considering sentient beings, it is for this reason that the suffering aggregate of affliction arises within the body.

If one is detached from the notion of "self" and examines the mind within itself, perceiving that this body of mine arises from ignorance and is like grass, trees, tiles, stones, or walls, and is merely like a form and its shadow—understanding it to be nameless—for this reason, one is liberated from the body of the five aggregates of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). One forever eliminates all views and the sixty-two doubts; by means of this, one achieves infinite great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

We should protect and rescue those who practice in this way, setting our will upon the stage of the Way that is eternally peaceful and firmly secure, thereby attaining great kindness, vast equanimity, and noble wisdom (*prajñā*).
“Because a bodhisattva is able to exercise such compassion, O Son of the Buddha!
they achieve benevolence and harmony, becoming truly compliant. From their first resolve, they abandon all worldly gain and profit, as well as any anxious attachment or stinginess.

They cultivate vast deeds, inwardly cherishing all that they possess: treasures, storehouses of gold and silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, various bright moon pearls, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, exquisite jade necklaces, rare *jiaoyao* gems, elephants, horses, carriages, and vehicles, as well as male and female servants, attendants, and retinues; they are able to give these all away universally, without any sense of attachment or regret.”

If one can bestow upon the commanderies, kingdoms, counties, towns, hamlets, villages, gardens, and groves; ponds, waters, and fruits; wives, children, and sons; and even that which one holds most dear—head, eyes, flesh, muscles, marrow, brain, and limbs—and is thus able to be unstinting with all that one possesses, then one delights in giving.
By providing for the poor and destitute, one enters the Buddha’s holy, luminous, and infinite Great Way; this is called attaining and establishing the first stage of the initial resolve.

He accomplishes vast giving; his disposition is such that he practices compassion, bestows kindness and benevolence, and rescues sentient beings. He provides protection for those currently engaged in the work of transcending the world, seeking out what is beneficial and righteous, and accords with the inclinations of all living beings. He never gives rise to a mind of weariness or aversion, nor does his heart ever grow weary; he diligently studies the various scriptures and subtle, profound texts. Having universally mastered all sūtras and clearly understood all karmic actions created, he governs his own advancement and retreat.

Regarding the treasury of all meanings and dharmas, he observes the multitudes according to their superior, middling, or inferior capacities and accords with their intentions, so that each may find their proper path. Adapting to their respective vessels according to their great or small capacity, he thus understands worldly affairs.

Having understood worldly affairs, one acts according to what is timely; protected by this, one dons the garment of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*). The fragrance of preceptual virtue naturally permeates them, their mind is harmonious through patience, and they are diligent without fault. With single-minded wisdom, their practice is vigorous, whether for themselves or for the sake of the multitude;

thus the conduct of shame and remorse is perfected. Through such cultivation, they again leave the household life; their mind does not waver, and no one can overturn it, for its strength is firm and resilient.
By virtue of this firmness, they make offerings to the Tathāgata and respectfully receive his teachings.

For this reason, one cultivates and purifies the stages of the path, causing them to be adorned and pure; one causes the True Dharma to flourish and manifest, up to and including the cultivation of firm faith, compassion, and generosity toward all beings. Having fully accomplished all these, one then dwells in the Bodhisattva stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). One is seen, illuminated, and remembered by countless Buddhas, and is protected by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas. Thereupon, one attains progress and manifestation, and one's vows become powerful; one comes to behold the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, even slightly;
and with a mind of benevolence and harmony, one serves him, accumulating the eternally peaceful karma of a Bodhisattva.

Whenever there are sentient beings in peril or distress, he goes to protect them; by means of these roots of virtue, he exhorts and assists them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

He makes offerings to all Buddhas and transforms sentient beings so that they may achieve perfection. Desiring to transform sentient beings, he first relieves their hunger and thirst by bestowing food and drink. He gives rise to the four debts of gratitude, being joyful and capable, honoring those above with respect and showing compassion and compliance toward those below. Through benevolent giving and loving-kindness, he benefits others as he benefits himself. All sins are eliminated, leaving no further calamity; he plants no more seeds of misfortune. Whatever he offers to the Buddhas is used to transform sentient beings until they reach ultimate fulfillment.

Abiding in this stage of the path, one uses these roots of virtue to assist toward all-knowledge; the various supernormal powers and compassionate wisdom become increasingly flourishing. Just as when a son of the Buddha takes purple-golden *jāmbūnada* gold and a master smith, having refined it thoroughly, places it in the fire so that its color becomes even more radiant, so too does the Bodhisattva, by making offerings to the Buddhas and diligently transforming sentient beings, cause his merit and blessings to flourish further. Adorning and purifying this Dharma while abiding in the stage of the path, he uses these roots of virtue to manifest the original source, until even the most fundamental origin is attained with complete freedom of advancement and retreat.
Vajragarbha said: "Listen, Son of the Buddha!

A bodhisattva, abiding in the stage of the first resolve, should seek in this manner: observing their conduct and inquiring into its origins and details; regarding all Buddhas and bodhisattvas as virtuous friends who protect them; practicing correctly without weariness to perfect the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma); and abiding in what is to be practiced. For these reasons, it is called 'abiding in the First Stage'."
"Next, regarding the second stage (*bhūmi*) that follows, one must inquire as to how its practice is accomplished.

How do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through wise teachers and virtuous friends, practice the Dharma without weariness to achieve the dwelling of the Way? To state the essentials: in this manner, for the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, one should inquire into their fundamental principles and details regarding what ought to be practiced, thereby attaining the accomplishment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."

With wise teachers and virtuous friends, practicing the Dharma without weariness, they accomplish the stages of the path (*bodhisattvabhūmi*). Regarding the categories of these stages and the spiritual practices to be observed therein, they cultivate the roots of virtue and understand the skillful means (*upāya*) pertaining to each stage of the path, discerning them one by one. With the purity of the stages of the path, their entry becomes extraordinary; as their noble wisdom advances, they each attain it and are rendered non-retrogressive. By abiding thus in the pure dwelling of a bodhisattva, they comprehend the immeasurable noble wisdom of the Tathāgatas and establish such skillful means according to the occasion. This is the first stage of the bodhisattva, from which there is no turning back.
Never regressing, they thus advance until they attain the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), never falling back into the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Their dwelling in wisdom becomes manifest and clear, drawing them ever closer to the infinite radiance of the Buddha’s knowledge. They are like a wise and enlightened guide among the sons of the Buddha, who protects a great caravan of diverse multitudes as they cross a perilous road. Having reached their destination and entered the great city, they fully comprehend every path traversed—the quality of the roads, whether they are fair or foul, good or evil, easy or difficult; which places are exceptionally peaceful and which are fearful and hard to pass; and they inquire again about alternative routes that should be established, as well as the vehicles, horses, elephants, and great chariots by which they may successfully cross over without wavering or overturning.

The first stage of abiding is likewise like this: it is as if that person has entered the great city and finds a secure dwelling free from all agitation. From the ground of the path established in the first stage, one honors wisdom in such a way that there is nothing one does not penetrate. With the inexhaustible enterprise of great wealth, one equally transforms the great multitude until they enter the great city; one is not submerged by impurities and, being able to act for oneself, does not endanger the other merchants.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

A bodhisattva is like a wise and enlightened guide; having attained abiding in the foremost stage of the path and thoroughly understanding all stages, he purifies and cultivates every stage of the path. Reaching the tenth stage, he fully comprehends all the bodhisattva stages, enters the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and gathers the infinite blessings and merit accumulated through the deeds of a bodhisattva. Having built up this noble wisdom, he has accomplished all that was to be done.

Acting as a great guide for the multitude, he transforms them according to their inclinations, causing them to transcend the endless wilderness of birth and death with its cycle of coming and going and its sufferings of hunger and thirst; thus, through his penetration of reality, they enter the boundless Dharma-city of omniscience.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a mind free from weariness, constantly cultivates diligence to reach the extraordinary, pure, and adorned stages of the path. This, O Son of the Buddha, is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s First Stage of Joyful Delight, wherein one enters the gateway to the Path and expounds the universally equal teaching.

When a Bodhisattva dwells here, wherever they travel throughout the world—be it a kingdom or a specific location—they attain great majesty and power to protect and sustain the Dharma. Through great and generous giving, they rescue sentient beings; through virtuous merit, they eliminate greed and envy. They cast off all defilements and proclaim inexhaustible giving. Establishing the roots of virtue, they provide relief to those in want. Regarding all things held dear, they sever their attachments to benefit the multitude. Practicing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they bestow generosity and benevolence. Benefiting others as they would themselves, they provide universal salvation. Gathering together the masses, their minds never abandon the Buddha; they contemplate the Dharma and the Noble Sangha, focusing solely on the deeds of a Bodhisattva. They resolve upon the Bodhisattva practices, the perfections (*pāramitā*), and the ten stages (*bhūmi*). They keep in mind the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas, until they fully realize all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).

By virtue of these merits, one attains all supreme, ultimate, and magnificent marks; becoming the most eminent, the highest, peerless, and without equal, one guides and transforms others, manifesting [the truth] to all people and accomplishing all-knowledge.

To rescue those in peril and distress, at the very moment of resolving the mind, one diligently cultivates all harmonious transformations through vigor. Having no longing for the worldly pursuits of wealth and profit, one adheres to the rectitude of the Way and the Dharma, leaving home to study the Path and upholding the teachings of the Buddha. In a mere instant, one attains countless samādhis and beholds the venerable Buddhas beyond measure.

By means of this establishment, he beholds thousands of infinite worlds; mindful of transcending countless lands, he illuminates all realms and transforms sentient beings. He perceives and remembers the kalpas of the past and the future, selects the gates of Dharma, manifests various bodies, and appears for infinite years as a bodhisattva surrounded by a retinue.

By means of the power established through this, the bodhisattva enters into extraordinary vows; in whatever manifestations they appear, they perform all manner of wholesome deeds and proclaim acts of giving, even throughout the events of countless billions of *koṭis* of hundreds of thousands of eons.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, reflecting upon and examining the ultimate destination of the meaning of these bodhisattvas’ abodes, immediately spoke in verse:
“Accumulating pure and white dharmas, Planting the roots of manifold virtues;
Prostrating and taking refuge in all Buddhas, Practicing the deeds of loving-kindness and benevolence.”
Entering into faith and liberation, the source of pure goodness;
with a mind that governs the limitless, the most supreme noble wisdom.
The Buddha, as the All-Knowing One, manifests his power of purity therein.
Having accomplished the dharmas that bring benefit to all, he guides and protects the masses of beings.
Practicing great compassion, he turns the most excellent wheel of Dharma;
the Tathāgata’s field is excellent and fertile, and his arousal of the mind [for enlightenment] is most sublime.
At one time they fully comprehend and contemplate the karma of nirvāṇa;
awakening various sentient beings, they manifest its meaning according to the occasion.
Gathering all virtues together, they are the leaders of the multitude.
The range of his mind pervades all, remaining equal to empty space.
His wisdom is most majestic and divine; he fundamentally practices compassion and skillful means.
His nature and disposition harbor profound faith, and his power of purity is immeasurable.
Beholding all without obstruction, he rescues beings outside [the Dharma];
planting the seeds of impartial karma, he dwells in contemplative mindfulness.
The jewel of the mind arises spontaneously; it is the natural wisdom of the Protectors of the Multitude.
Through comprehensive refinement and diligent practice, one brings the Buddha-way and its Dharma to ultimate completion;
giving birth to the lineage of the Ten Powers, one shall forever be free from all calamities and transgressions;
as the most supreme radiance of the True and Right, one attains the Honored and Sublime Way.
This is the harmony of the mind, which manifests and leads to the level ground;
unmoving like a mountain, one maintains equal conduct throughout the land.
Embracing much joy, one’s will cultivates profound faith.
One should cultivate joy extensively and universally; how excellent is this sublime meaning!
One must distance oneself from all fears and act without malice;
at the proper time, one should excel in casting off defilements and reverently follow the path of wholesome self-cultivation.
Delighting in saving the multitude of living beings, with noble wisdom beyond peer;
the heart harbors supreme exultation, casting away all that is improper.
By eliminating the five fears, one thereby attains the stages of the Way.
Even unto death one cannot preserve life, yet one remains far removed from the various evil realms.
By relinquishing fear of the assembly, one ultimately possesses no heart of dread;
for what reason has this been so until now? It is because there is no "self" (ātman).
If one can be free from fear, Dedicatedly practicing loving-kindness and compassion;
With utmost faith cultivating reverence, And abandoning the longing for wealth and fame;
Rising early and retiring late, One cultivates the roots of all virtues.
By establishing the dharma of sincerity and faith, one is not defiled by desire.
If the mind hears the sublime scriptures, it cultivates goodness without weariness;
forever eliminating the profits of craving and desire, it always delights in the Buddha-way.
Aspiring to the power of pure wisdom, one cultivates and refines the teachings of the Buddha’s sutras;
seeking all the *pāramitās*, one abandons the practice of flattery and deceit.
One’s words and deeds always correspond, and one never utters false speech.
Of the most excellent lineage and free from defilement, you shall swiftly train to reach the Buddha-way.
Having distanced yourselves from worldly affairs, do not delight in the various benefits of the world;
do not violate the pure and white Dharma, but diligently cultivate the supreme practice.
Diligently striving for the sake of merit, he delights solely in such a Dharma;
guiding himself through his own vows, he seeks to behold the Most Victorious One.
For the sake of upholding the Dharma for all, wherever he goes, he is free from envy.
Following with great vows, their physical conduct is always sublime;
they purify all Buddha-fields and transform all sentient beings;
thus they pervade all Buddha-fields, traveling together with all Buddhas.
The Buddha, by means of a single name, is neither false nor deceptive in this or that;
all things can be attained, for he has awakened to the supreme meaning.
With such immeasurable vows, he guides and benefits beings until they reach eternal peace.
This is vast, universal, and limitless, reaching the state of fearlessness.
Sentient beings are like empty space; all phenomena arise from them.
This is the most supreme ultimate conventionality, manifested upon the stage of wisdom.
The realm of that mind enters most deeply into holy wisdom;
having attained the three types of supernormal knowledge, it opens the way for all sentient beings.
Reaching the ultimate limit of great vows, may I cause myself to fulfill this aspiration.
Such is his thorough mastery, and his conduct is likewise so.
Thus he well preserves his kindness; his mind is harmonious and gentle.
With deep faith in the Buddha’s merits, he contemplates the primordial nature of sentient beings.
Conditioned by conduct, one enters into compassion and gives rise to great loving-kindness;
thinking, "I shall protect and nurture them, desiring to establish the masses in peace," for this reason one practices giving, bestowing various kinds of gifts.
Kingdoms, cities, and settlements, Various jewels, elephants, and horses,
Heads, eyes, hands, and feet, As well as the flesh of one’s own body—
One should be able to give all these universally, Without harboring any timidity or weakness.
Aspiring to the many scriptures, he never grew weary or weary of them;
understanding the worldly classics, he exhorted and transformed others in accordance with custom.
His wisdom transcends the three periods of time, and though he harbors a sense of humility, his resolve remains firm and strong.
Making offerings to those peerless and matchless ones, and reverently honoring all the elders;
the practice of the multitude of sages is thus: diligent day and night without ceasing;
their blazing merits are like gold within the fire.
He diligently practices these ten stages of the bodhisattva;
Aspiring to the unconditioned state, he transforms all that is conditioned.
Just as a skilled guide feels compassion for a great caravan of merchants, so does he act.
Having previously inquired about the path of peace and security, he therefore stands before one to point the way.
So too is the Bodhisattva: having first set out in the First Abode, he gradually advances through to the Ten Abodes, thereby attaining the Path of Non-obstruction.
By being able to abide in this meaning, one thoroughly elucidates the achievement of merit;
with a compassionate heart free from malice, one instructs the multitude through the Dharma.
Abiding in the world while knowing the proper time, one transforms others and provides universal protection.
He established the multitude to practice giving, causing them to delight in the noble wisdom of the Buddha.
In the mere instant that the Most Holy One resolved his mind, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced his royal palace;
entering the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma, he went forth to cultivate diligence.
Soon he attained samādhi and beheld thousands upon thousands of Buddhas;
he moved the Buddha-lands and, seeing the light, went to hear the sutras.
He purified countless multitudes, causing them to enter the gateway of the Dharma.
Wandering through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he manifests his body according to the times.
Through the fundamental deeds of all the Most Victorious Ones, he awakens those who are asleep;
just as the Buddhas of the past awakened those who were muddled and ignorant.
"This is the first dwelling, proclaimed by the Most Victorious One;
it is for the sake of universally pitying the world, for all the unsurpassed Bodhisattvas.

When the Bodhisattvas heard this unsurpassed path of practice, they admired and delighted in the noble conduct. Their hearts were filled with joy and they felt profound peace and security. Rising from their seats, they went forward to meet him and prostrated themselves. Leaping into the air, they scattered various celestial flowers and uttered these sublime words.
He exclaimed: "Excellent, Vajragarbha!

You are a noble hero, free from fear, who clearly understands the abiding of the Way and practices the Dharma of a Bodhisattva. The assembled multitude is filled with joy as they hear of the source of liberation. Now we inquire only of the supreme path: what is the practice of the second stage?"
"What you should contemplate and uphold is that Great Wisdom which is proclaimed alone; those who hear it attain tranquility, advance to the ultimate, and transform sentient beings.
Chapter Two: The Abode Free from Defilement (*Vimalā-vihāra*) from the *Sūtra on the Gradual Preparation of All-Wise Virtue*. Vajragarbha replied:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva has fully realized the first stage from its initial inception, he then takes delight in the second stage; with a mind and nature imbued with sincerity, he reverently cultivates ten matters.
What are the ten? First, his disposition is gentle and mild, free from coarseness and ferocity;
second, he cultivates upright and true deeds, without any perverse thoughts.
