to transform and enlighten sentient beings, such that their conduct is pure—
these constitute the ten matters.

Vajragarbha said: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the fifth stage, they then accomplish the cultivation of excellent and wondrous deeds; they practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and their mind becomes exceedingly pure.
Their spiritual career becomes increasingly superior, and their vows become vast and expansive; by the power of these aspirations, they draw near to the Tathāgata."
He has compassion for all living beings, never forgetting or abandoning them; he accumulates merit and virtue, gathering together sublime wisdom;

with diligent and earnest effort, he never slackens or desists; through skillful means and expedients, he guides those who have not yet attained, always delighting in abiding within wondrous radiance;
he secretly rejoices in the principles established by the Tathāgata, and his own mind has already entered the power of the Buddha.

Their thoughts are focused exclusively on non-retrogression; they thoroughly understand these Four Noble Truths—namely, the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
They are able to reach the ultimate through sincerity, renown, and virtue, discerning the noble truths and penetrating their fundamental limit.
They clearly comprehend all characteristics as the authentic noble truths.
Lacking skillful means, they proclaim [the teachings] in accordance with [their own views], yet they understand and discern the truth;
this is the Noble Truth of the Cause. To analyze those matters and that which is to be transcended is the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Furthermore, being able to practice and fully understanding all matters is the Noble Truth of Right Action.

Next, he further proclaimed the Noble Truths of the Path, expounding their meaning until the Truth of Non-arising was fully realized; having attained the wisdom of the Truths and the practice of the Path through thorough understanding and entry, they had all universally entered the stages of the Bodhisattvas.
Having achieved proximity [to enlightenment] up to eloquence, with the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata, they dispelled the fetters and afflictions, and widely proclaimed the Noble Truths.

Furthermore, he is able to transform the thoughts of others, causing them all to be joyful; understanding the appropriate timing, he thoroughly elucidates the Noble Truths. Having already attained entry into the meaning of the path of the single cause, he subsequently becomes enlightened and reaches the ultimate source—the truly authentic Noble Truth.

Having awakened to and understood one's own characteristics, one is then able to comprehend the noble truths regarding all phenomena; by understanding where the nature of the will tends, one penetrates the various kinds of the five aggregates, the manifold decays, and the emotional obscurations that arise from distinct locations. By means of the noble truths, one transcends and fully realizes the afflictions of the body and the multitude of sufferings.

Having fully understood the Noble Truth of Suffering, and having undergone repeated cycles of wandering, bondage, and confinement, one is then liberated; having practiced the source of all truths, with all burning fevers forever extinguished, one is then liberated through the Noble Truth of Cessation.

From the beginning there has been no duality of speech; what is proclaimed accords with the truth. Only then does one understand the noble wisdom of the Way, having fully awakened to it and reached the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Only then does one understand the Noble Truth of True Practice, clarifying the power of faith and wisdom, comprehending all that is inexhaustible, and ensuring that suffering leaves nothing remaining. If one discriminates and calculates according to these truths, through such skillful means, one subdues the source of birth and death and understands the place from which all things arise.

Due to these dharmas, they are hypocritical and deluded; their actions are not genuine. Having clearly understood the beginning and the end, they increase their compassion for sentient beings and draw near to great pity (*mahākaruṇā*). Abiding in the world, they give rise to boundless loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Having already attained this power of wisdom, strength, and wealth, they universally protect all living beings. Delighting in the Buddha’s wisdom, they contemplate the course of birth and death from the distant past, examining its original source and the origin from which sentient beings proceed. This leads to ignorance (*avidyā*) and the three realms of affection and craving; drifting in the current of birth and death, they are attached to the aggregates (*skandha*) and hindrances, moved and transformed by them, thereby increasing the aggregates of suffering.

If one can understand and penetrate that there are no sentient beings, no self, no person, no life-span, and no vital principle, having already abandoned the notion of "I" and fully comprehended all this—just as with past events, so it is likewise for the future and the present.
Delighting in the deluded practice of nihilism, they wander through birth and death without cessation or rest; it is forever without end, lacking any protector, and they possess no true knowledge.

They have no teachers or friends; even though they may have teachers and friends, they do not accept the teachings of the Dharma. Thus they are without wisdom, deluded and ignorant worldlings, bound by the hindrances of sleep, beyond all calculation.

Having extinguished all notions of self, they shall bring to an end that which is to be ended; no longer will they give rise to further existence, nor will anything more be born. Yet, they do not believe in the Buddha-way, and thus their [delusions] increase ever further.

They are afflicted by the suffering and tribulations of conditioned existence (*saṃsāra*), drifting along with whatever they perceive; they do not abandon the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), do not grow weary of the four great elements, and do not uproot arrogance. They have the wounds of various views, fail to distinguish between lust and anger, and do not extinguish ignorance (*avidyā*).

In this dark and obscure chamber, they do not exhaust the difficulties of the abyssal pool of craving and desire, nor do they seek the practice of the Teacher endowed with the Ten Powers; instead, they enter the conduct of Māra and fall into the ocean of birth and death, which turns back and forth.
Free from thoughts of goodness, one departs from self-mastery; such sufferings and afflictions are beyond measure.

Forever without protection, without refuge, without rescue, and without benefit, one is alone with no companions; thus should one practice. Through such deeds, accumulating merit and virtue, and through self-discipline in every birth, one is able to cultivate wisdom. Having attained the understanding of all sentient beings and realized their ultimate primordial purity, one then achieves the Ten Powers.

He thoroughly clarifies the wisdom of non-action (wuwei), its majesty and brilliance shining forth; having thus awakened his mind to this essential wisdom, he attains the fulfillment of the Way through the practices he has cultivated.

Accumulating merit and cultivating virtue, all was for the sake of sentient beings; he established protection out of compassion for the masses, universally bringing peace to all beings, extending his pity to everyone, desiring to deliver and liberate them.
Free from a mind of affliction or harm, they do not slander others; they exhort and transform sentient beings so that none fail to rejoice.
Acting as their guides, they lead them to extinction. Having diligently practiced these, they abide in the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjaya*).

"Having attained mastery, his mind is free from forgetfulness; he understands the various karmic activities of virtuous conduct; his resolve is firm and strong; he possesses excellent discerning wisdom; his intention reaches everywhere; he understands the sequence of the scriptures and the meaning of their chapters and verses; he harbors a sense of shame and protects both himself and others; and his will is courageous."

Nurturing and upholding the prohibitive precepts, one remains free from transgression; with clarity within the mind, one proclaims them everywhere. One should practice what is correct, entering fully among the multitude of sages, having nothing further to revere or look up to.
With wisdom that comes and goes, they proclaim and expound the meaning, distributing it according to the times, thereby attaining divine powers.

Through skillful means of inquiry and exhortation, they manifest the transformation of the Way; practicing expedient means, they guide others in accordance with worldly customs. Accumulating merit and virtue, they are never weary or satisfied; yearning for the wisdom of the Way, they never slacken or abandon their efforts. Upholding infinite compassion and gathering together pity and mercy, their minds are never indolent or exhausted as they seek the karmic deeds of the Way.
Without being indolent or withdrawn, they apply themselves with diligent and earnest effort, devoting themselves to the Buddha’s ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and his wisdom;
to the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas; and through constant virtuous conduct, they contemplate and deeply enter the adornment of the Buddha-lands.

Establishing various practices and accumulating the collection of all marks and secondary characteristics, they constantly practice diligence, aspiring to seek the Tathāgata’s adorned and pure conduct of body, speech, and mind; they cultivate infinite karma, revere and uphold the precepts, accord with all bodhisattvas, honor the many Dharma masters, and harbor no malice or harm.

By means of the skillful expedients of all bodhisattvas, they roam throughout the world, single-mindedly from dawn until night, abandoning thoughts of others and constantly using the Dharma to diligently transform sentient beings; they are able to cultivate in this manner.

By means of the karma of giving, they exhort and guide sentient beings with words that are affectionate, respectful, and beneficial, providing great benefit and salvation to them, and equally rescuing the masses.

They further manifest the form of a physical body to proclaim the Dharma extensively, thereby following and carrying out the great enterprise of the Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas to transform and enlighten the multitudes. Furthermore, they perceive the defects and impurities of birth and death, extolling the meritorious achievements of the holy wisdom of all Buddhas, and are thus able to practice in this manner.

By means of great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), they manifest transformations and stir the hearts of others; through various kinds of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they exhort and guide sentient beings, thereby teaching and transforming them.

Having attained such diligence in transformation, they enter the wisdom of the Buddha; practicing the path with a pure mental nature, they proceed without regression, cultivating the roots of all virtues and zealously seeking the extraordinary, true, and correct Dharma.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, wherever they may travel or dwell within the world—whether transcribing and explaining the scriptures, presiding over assemblies with seals of office, managing government treasuries, or engaging in various great physical labors—he attends to those who require healing. He provides medical treatment for all manner of ailments: colds, fevers, emaciation, afflictions by malevolent spirits, poisoning, and insanity. Whether pursued by calamities or wherever his body may be, he heals their forms through the application of arts and techniques, using acrobatics and humorous discourse to bring great joy to many. He attends to the regions, kingdoms, counties, and towns; the rivers, streams, springs, and ponds; the trees, flowers, and fruits; and the medicinal herbs that grow therein.

Gold, silver, bright moons, pearls, jade, crystal, and the manifestations of lapis lazuli; the various jewels, suns, and moons; cities, towns, villages, households, fields, and lands; earthquakes, sleep, and dreams of strange portents; and all the forms and locations of the bodies of sentient beings into which one enters.

Regarding all characteristics that are appropriate and those that ought to be cultivated and refined, one should practice them with vigilance; concerning wealth, property, goods, supernormal powers, and the formless realm, one should do so without negligence, practicing the four immeasurable minds with single-minded devotion and without causing harm.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, they cultivate eternal peace; through these practices, they take pity on the world and gradually establish them in the true Dharma of all Buddhas, being able to transform and establish them therein.

The Bodhisattva Duṣpradharṣa, through his practice on the stages of the path, served and made offerings to countless billions of trillions of Buddhas, providing them with robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness.
In the presence of the Tathāgatas, he renounced his household affairs, left home to become a śramaṇa, and having heard and received the sūtras from all the Tathāgatas, became a Dharma-master.

Furthermore, hearing it again, one attains the dhāraṇī; throughout countless billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one brings forth and manifests the roots of virtue, reaching ultimate purity.
It is also like the sons of the Buddha, who, like exquisite jewels of *śaṅkha-śilā*, when brought together and in close proximity, reflect and illuminate one another.
The Bodhisattva thus dwells in the Bodhisattva stage called "Difficult to Conquer.

By means of these roots of virtue, he cultivates skillful means and wisdom; his realization of the Way’s meaning becomes increasingly lofty, and he magnifies the Mahāyāna. He should establish meritorious achievements, and his conduct is peerless. Just as within a village there may be a night-luminous pearl that shines universally upon the fields, or like clouds and winds that blow across and cause the palaces of the various devas to drift and turn, so too does the Bodhisattva attain this Dwelling Difficult to Conquer.

By means of these roots of virtue, skillful means, and wisdom, their mental activities enter everywhere; they constantly dwell in the world, and none are able to disturb them. This is the practice of the great bodhisattvas, the fifth stage.

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they experience great joy and satisfaction. If they become a celestial king, they subdue all heterodox teachers and those of divergent views; toward those who establish themselves in the path, they practice generosity, affection, respect, benefit, and impartial aid. Observing the thoughts of sentient beings, their minds never depart from the practices and dharmas of the Buddhas.

He then further recollected and contemplated the all-knowing deeds of all the sages, considering by what skillful means he might deliver sentient beings, even unto the sublime and infinite Hall of the Way. In the mere instant of generating this thought, through a moment of diligent effort, in a single moment of time, he attained incalculable billions of samādhis. He beheld countless hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas surrounded by their retinues, discussing the sutras and expounding their meanings; having attained liberation therein, they established the power of their vows and all achieved the extraordinary transformations of bodhisattvas, such that no one could calculate or measure their virtue. Even throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, none could fully praise or exhaustively describe their meritorious achievements.
Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, wishing to further elaborate upon the karmic activity of this sūtra, spoke these verses:
“The fourth stage, Prabhākari, is thus exceedingly pure;
with a mind already equanimous, one contemplates the affairs of the three worlds.”
With this mind, one practices the precepts of conduct; cultivating the Way and its virtue with purity, one becomes free from fetters in a single thought-moment and enters the fifth stage.
Thus attending to the various faculties, even upon hearing [the teachings], one does not turn back.
By means of the four foundations of mindfulness, one masters the verses of the Dharma’s joyful melody.
Having already transcended and traversed the five powers, one remains entirely indestructible;
thus, through courageous and pervasive movement, one attains the fifth stage.
Shame and remorse serve as their clothing; the fragrance of pure precepts is their scent;
the flowers of awakened mindfulness form their garlands; and meditative reflection serves as their unguent.
By following the work of wisdom, they adorn their own countenances with the dignity of the Path.
Dhāraṇī is the garden, and meditative concentration is the practice of equanimity;
The four bases of psychic power are the stride, and the purity of mind is the crown aperture;
A compassionate and pitying heart is the eye, and sublime vision is noble wisdom.
Maintaining the grasp of selflessness, his mind subdues the dust of afflictions;
he then attains entry into the fifth stage, abiding as a lion among men.
Having just entered this fifth ground, the path of extraordinary distinction;
The path of practice is purified, and through cultivation it becomes ever more sublime.
If one can purify the nature of the will, one shall immediately seek the most excellent meaning;
out of compassion for the world’s afflictions, one contemplates detachment from mental conceptions.
Accumulating the root of merit, the honored wisdom is likewise so;
it rouses countless multitudes and illuminates the stages of the path.
Established by the Buddha, one should contemplate the noble intention free from pride.
Thoroughly understanding through natural liberation, one does not neglect the four noble truths.
Fully elucidating the meaning of the ultimate truth, one nurtures and protects the various faculties;
if one discerns what is truly real, one further proceeds to deliver all Buddhas.
Thus one eliminates attachment to the mind, as well as the truths of the path;
with an equal resolve, the Way becomes clear, reaching even to the state of non-obstruction.
With a subtle, true, and refined mind, one cultivates and refines these truths in this manner.
The Honored One, liberated through wisdom, is free from affliction and the hindrances of the aggregates.
Having cultivated the roots of merit, his practice of wisdom is vast and far-reaching;
he transcends all causal conditions to deliver all living beings.
Those who harbor a mind of truthfulness accomplish such reality;
having personally and thoroughly understood it, they realize the fundamental purity that is free from abiding.
Through compassion that finds nothing to be grasped, one then dwells in peace.
Because sentient beings suffer from toil and affliction, they seek the wisdom of the path of the Multitude’s Protector.
Diligently observe their origins and the source from which they arise:
ignorance stems from darkness, and they are confined within the seeds of craving and attachment.
Sentient beings greedily grasp at the aggregates, And thus form bodies of suffering and affliction;
Having attained the realization of non-self, They observe them as being like grass and wood.
From the dust of toil they give rise to existence, Recurring again and again through the various realms of rebirth.
Like the revolving wheel without end, there are manifold sufferings, afflictions, and distresses.
Alas! Once lost, all people are to be pitied;
scorched by folly and ignorance, they flow through birth and death without returning.
The five aggregates are like oxen, and various false views are their sores;
fire blazes within their hearts, yet their wills remain steeped in darkness.
Fallen into the river of craving and desire, they only then long for the light of clarity.
Abiding in the river of toil and suffering, one clearly seeks the Supreme Guide.
Seeing such hardships as these, one should practice without negligence;
all the deeds one follows and performs are used to deliver sentient beings.
With firm resolve and peaceful conduct, his gait possesses majestic power;
being brave yet possessing a sense of shame, he understands clearly and achieves wisdom.
Accumulating merit without weariness—such is the practice of the Honored Sage.
In the pure and white dharmas there is no weariness; power and vigor are its intent.
This is the most supreme field of merit, proclaiming the sounds and characteristics of the awakened mind.
Its deeds never reach satiety; with diligence, it pities all sentient beings.
In order to transform sentient beings, he intentionally entered among artisans;
whether as a painter, a carver, a calculator, or a physician,
when images were afflicted by malevolent spirits, he used these very means to eliminate the illness.
Established upon the essential points of the scriptures, he understood awakening, joy, compassion, and pity;
he composed rhymed prose and verses, as well as various kinds of playful songs;
[he described] flowing rivers and gardens, bathing pools, trees, flowers, and fruits.
He establishes countless karmas to bring peace to sentient beings;
he manifests immeasurable forms and colors, as diverse as various precious jewels.
He takes hold of the earth and causes it to tremble, so that the light of the sun and moon may be seen.
Sentient beings possess various forms, wandering through all lands and abodes.
Formless wealth is supreme, and their supernormal powers are immeasurable;
wishing to cultivate compassion, they bring universal peace to all sentient beings.
This is called "Difficult to Conquer," the wondrously sublime work of wisdom;
having made offerings to billions of Buddhas, they together heard and received the sūtras.
Those who cultivate a virtuous nature manifest pure and white conduct.
Like a chariot of purple gold and musaragalva, polished and bright and beautiful;
its dwelling is composed of many jewels, and its palaces move and travel;
before this wind turns, there is no one who can obstruct or hinder it.
Just as one practices worldly dharmas, yet does so entirely for the sake of sentient beings;
wandering among this circle of awakened companions, like a lotus flower in the water;
therein he employs skillful means, establishing himself as a noble and honored one.
Abandoning divergent doctrines and observing joyful practices,
all the manifold virtues one cultivates arise from supreme wisdom;
by protecting the masses of beings, one thereby attains the ten powers.
The Honored One has attained majestic power, with diligence as his supreme quality;
seeing many billions of beings, he dwells securely as the God among Gods.
Having attained the wondrous samādhi, he observes billions of lands.
Because their vows are exceptional, they further surpass these meritorious achievements.
This is the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), wherein they employ hundreds of millions of skillful means;
they subdue and transform all heterodox arts, manifesting their own radiance for the sake of sentient beings.

At that time, the sons of the Buddhas, having heard this proclamation of the various practices of the bodhisattvas, leaped up from the earth and stayed in mid-air. Rejoicing, they rained down flowers, bright moon-jewels, necklaces, and garments of pure radiance, scattering them as offerings over the Buddha while exclaiming in praise, "Excellent!"
All the deities, dwelling in the midst of the void, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, were without exception filled with exultation.

At that time, the various wondrous and exquisite jewels from the heavens were offered to the World-Honored One; incense, flowers, ointments, silken banners, pennants, and canopies were presented. The retinues of Māra, the sovereign sons of heaven, and all the celestial beings arrived together, traversing the void above him. They rained down various precious flowers, their hearts joyful and content as they made offerings to the Most Victorious One. With immeasurable intent, they proclaimed aloud, "Excellent!"
The sons of the Buddhas and all the deities gathered, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, also dwelling above;
they struck various musical instruments, their sounds pure and harmonious, and all the music resonated with such a melody.
The resonance of the Buddha was benevolent and peaceful, dispersing the dust of evil; it is fundamentally pure and empty-quiescent, dissolving all conceptualizations of phenomena, just like...
Like space, it is equal and without thought; its movement is pure, its standing is perfected.
It does not cling to the mundane, is forever without negligence, and is fundamentally equal and entirely authentic.
In phenomena there is no conceptualization; if one understands that all phenomena are utterly non-existent, then one realizes the fundamental non-arising. There is no... [end].
Regarding all karmic actions, they act spontaneously without deliberation; out of compassion for sentient beings, they diligently cultivate their salvation.

This is how the sons of the Buddha, the heirs of the Dharma King, practice the perfection of giving: they abandon all attachment to signs, their precepts are firm, and their mental nature is tranquil.
For the sake of sentient beings, they practice patience; with inexhaustible wisdom of the Dharma, they bestow diligence.
Through the power [of wisdom], one causes all phenomena to become tranquil, enters the gate of meditative concentration, purifies all defilements, and examines all things;
by believing in and understanding emptiness and non-existence, the power of noble wisdom is perfected, serving as protection for all.
These sons of the Buddhas, of lofty virtue and purified of defilements, emit hundreds of thousands of such sounds; they naturally proclaim gentle voices as the most supreme Great Sages.

When they subsequently enter silence, the various heavenly maidens, like those who have finished their meal and rest, return to the heavens. Vajragarbha praised their courageous resolve, which has transformed them so that their practice is perfected in the fifth stage (*bhūmi*); thus they reach the ultimate goal, and none can ever cause it to fail.
Chapter Six: The Stage of Presence. From the *Gradual Preparation Sutra*, Chapter Six: The Stage of Presence. Vajragarbha said:
"Listen, O Sons of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has been able to cultivate and perfect the fifth stage, they immediately transcend and enter the sixth stage, wherein they practice ten dharmas."
What are these ten? They are:
realizing that all phenomena are entirely without conceptualization and are universally equal;
that all marks are level and forever devoid of form or category.
All things are utterly unarisen and transcend all comparison;
they are entirely without origination, and thus are called "equal.
They are profoundly pure, perfectly regulated, and truly authentic.
All are free from negligence and do not engage in restless wandering;
there is neither what is appropriate nor inappropriate, neither pairs nor singles;
they are tranquil and serene, beyond compare.
Like illusions, dreams, reflections, echoes in the mountains, the moon in water, and manifested images, they are also like transformations;
the karmic deeds performed on the path are without dualistic intent—
these are the ten dharmas.

From the fifth stage, upon reaching the sixth dwelling, having performed these practices, one naturally contemplates all dharmas, calculating and reflecting upon them, examining them repeatedly so as not to allow confusion, thereby drawing near to the sixth dwelling.
Seeing this naturally with one's own eyes and attaining its fulfillment, one then obtains the penetrative and skillful *anulomikī-kṣānti* (receptive tolerance in accordance with the Dharma).

Not following delusion, yet not yet having reached the proximity of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (tolerance regarding the non-arising of phenomena), one gradually draws near to it and is able to achieve spontaneity. Entering into the locus of all dharmas, one is further able to advance toward great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), becoming a sovereign leader, manifesting and illuminating great compassion, and being endowed with infinite pity.
To understand the five destinies of the world—their existence and non-existence, their convergence and dispersal—and to contemplate them in this way is called the sixth dwelling.
One then thoroughly elucidates how worldly habits arise through dependence upon the self; it is brought about by the notion of "I" and "mine," whereby one perceives the affairs of desire.
In this world there is nothing that truly exists; yet those who harbor deluded thoughts rely upon and cling to a self. Due to their lack of wisdom, they fall into the darkness of ignorance.

Longing for and delighting in places of birth, they practice unwholesome karma; their wills are intent on flight and escape, and they engage in perverse conduct. Thus they accumulate various merits and demerits, as well as the cycles of rise and fall.

All things are impermanent, arising from the cultivation of non-beneficial conditions. Understanding what is practiced, one’s mind cultivates itself well; by eliminating all outflows (*āsrava*), one reaches the ultimate truth of original non-existence.

Because one gives rise to wholesome virtues, one shall return once more to wander through the realms of birth and death and karmic retribution. What is done constitutes the field, and the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) is the seed.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) as its root is darkness and obscurity; craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the moisture; and arrogance and conceit are its disposition, nurturing the various views and the net of manifold fetters.
Conditioned by this, name-and-form arises spontaneously;
as name-and-form further increases, the sense-faculties are formed;
once the sense-faculties are formed, various kinds of experienced objects arise.
Through the habitual engagement of activities, sensations arise;
from sensations, there arises joy and pleasure, which increases what is experienced;
through the increase of what is experienced, that which belongs to one is immediately established.
The convergence of the arising of intention constitutes the formation of thought; because of this, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the physical form of the five limbs are produced.
One then proceeds through the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), gradually giving rise to attachments until all manner of attachments are reached.
When all these dependencies are fully present, from this there arises the feverish affliction that scorches and roasts one with all the sufferings of grief, lamentation, and weeping.
All unwholesome karmas are fundamentally empty and formless; they are not understood as being acquired through habituation, nor is there any distinction between them and non-distraction.
They are all, moreover, spontaneous; by gradually practicing until there are no hindrances, one thus attains this state.
One who understands this meaning will have nothing further to long for.

In this way, the bodhisattva delights in gentleness and compliance; observing the twelve links of dependent origination, he reflects within himself that it is through such sincerity that consciousness arises.
Ultimately there is no wisdom; the karma of ignorance is fundamentally pure, yet it forms the retribution of conditioned activities.

As these activities are completed, the consciousness (vijñāna) precedes them; as a companion to this consciousness, there arises the reception of the four aggregates (skandhas), which then leads to the delusion of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
The various decays, the six sense bases, and the spheres of the faculties immediately give rise to consciousness.
Acting as its companions, they undergo contact with the outflows (*āsrava*); from contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises; through craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it grows; and thus what is received increases.

By governing that which is received, one forms outflowing karma (*āsrava-karma*); from these actions arises the arising of the aggregates of the body (*kāya-skandha*). Within this birth, one consequently undergoes aging and infirmity; when the aggregates of the body disintegrate, death ensues.

To dwell together with ignorance and delusion is truly terrifying. From this comes harm and peril, leading to dwelling within the net of fetters and resulting in verbal expressions; thus the five faculties arise. Suffering originates from the mental faculty (*manas*), and from that sorrow and grief, many afflictions and anxieties arise. Because of this, one undergoes existence (*bhava*). For these reasons, one regresses and is born into the tree of suffering. One establishes what is to be done and subjects oneself to self-examination; yet by relying on what has been done and through the knowledge of what has been done, one is only just beginning to act. To reckon that there is "action" is itself non-action; from beginning to end it is without marks, and it cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, he reflected that these three realms are the product of the mind; one should contemplate them through this twelvefold dependent origination.

The five destinies to which beings return have been fully explained by the Tathāgata, the Truly Enlightened One; moreover, all of this is of a single kind, a single mind, simultaneously and completely formed.

Why is this so? If the various sense faculties give rise to craving within the mind, it is entirely due to the delusion regarding the birth and death of the *vijñāna* (consciousness). Because it proceeds from ignorance (*avidyā*), that which is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) takes the mind as its companion and establishes delusion. From that name-and-form, name-and-form is further formed, becoming the six spheres of decay (*ṣaḍāyatana*). From these, contact (*sparśa*) arises; contact becomes the companion of sensation (*vedanā*). Sensation leads to craving (*tṛṣṇā*); because there is craving, one does not relinquish grasping (*upādāna*), which gives rise to manifold difficulties. Through the conjunction of these conditions, "existence" (*bhava*) is brought about; depending on this, "birth" (*jāti*) occurs, and from this the net of suffering is raised, leading inevitably to old age and death. Thus, from within consciousness, existence is produced; this is specifically known as the conditionality of name-and-form.

Furthermore, name-and-form each has its own destination; as the six sense-faculties decline and enter their objects, one perceives one's own realm and is able to enter into stillness because of further habitual conditioning.
From that further conditioning, mental volition brings about it, giving rise to the condition of sensation (vedanā);
from sensation, one then again performs formations (saṃskāra), whether wholesome or unwholesome, beautiful or ugly.
From the condition of affection and love, one brings about the affairs of worldly toil, craving, and lust;
from the condition of craving, one brings about the prison of fetters and bonds;
from the condition of existence (*bhava*), one brings about rebirth in another life, being born into the present realm from which it is impossible to escape.

Conditioned by birth, the causal factors arise, producing the five aggregates as their basis; this brings about the conditions for aging, leading to decrepitude, whereby the faculties ripen and death ensues.

Regarding those who have died, there are twelve matters: from the point where the conditions for arising are initiated, the aggregates of their bodies disintegrate, yet [the continuity] cannot be severed and has never been permanently cut off.

With ignorance as a condition, there arise volitional formations, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.
Due to ignorance as a condition, there is no severance; it cannot be fully exhausted, and thus there is a remainder.
When ignorance is extinguished, all formations (saṃskāra) then cease; because of this, there is hearing, and thus there is a remainder.

Because they receive [existence] through ignorance and craving, their worldly afflictions increase and flourish without a moment’s interruption; as for the actions they perform, there is a cycle of retribution and response, and as these responses revolve one after another, the root is never uprooted. For those who have not exhausted their remaining calamities, suffering immediately shifts from one state to another without rest, all because of ignorance.

Regarding the past, future, and present, the proliferation of the fetters of views should be severed. Thus, through these three turnings, one realizes the threefold absence of self; by being free from the notion of "I" and "mine," ignorance is extinguished, and the karma of spontaneity finds no place to abide.

It is like a reed hut; as if a pond were pure, yet due to the afflictions of suffering and the cause of ignorance, there arise volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). This constitutes the fundamental past. Never having experienced various pains before, it is because of consciousness (*vijñāna*) that sensations of pain and pleasure arise; this constitutes the present experience of sensation (*vedanā*).
From craving arises existence; this is the source of future sensation and feeling. Beyond this point, nothing further is produced.

When ignorance is extinguished, the various formations (saṃskāra) cease and are cut off. Thus, the three afflictions of suffering and the twelve links of retribution, which arise from causes and conditions, proceed from ignorance down to the six sense bases; by this, one is able to extinguish the formations.

When all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) have ceased, one attains separation through this; such are the formations. There remain two further matters: being bound by oneself, suffering, and further sensations of pain and itching.

Yet there still remains the suffering of separation from what has been exhausted. When ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished, all formations then cease, and the three types of suffering are forever severed.
From ignorance (*avidyā*), the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise; because they act as conditions, the various formations come into being. Thus there is a remainder.
When ignorance is extinguished, the formations are likewise extinguished; this is because all formations exist only so long as this remainder persists.
There is ignorance and volitional formations; through skillful means, one unties the great bonds. Because these remnants remain, there is cyclic existence.

One should therefore contemplate the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination and their destination, examining them repeatedly. Since [existence] arises from causes, one should diligently avoid attachment, governing body, speech, and mind. Through the conditions of one's own actions and the results of offerings, there is no further production of karma. Its threefold revolution shall not recur; fundamentally, there is no suffering, yet through habituation one experiences the three types of pain. This is merely the practice of the retribution of all dependently arisen phenomena.
Suppose there is a person who, having raised a debt, is released from bondage; observing that it is inexhaustible, there is nothing that can be exhausted.
He contemplates this condition: as the condition arises, he perceives future events and shall fully comprehend them all.

There is no self and no person; there is no life-span and no soul. All things are naturally empty, tranquil, and serene. Whatever actions are performed result in their corresponding retributions; thus, one follows the gate of liberation through emptiness.

Holding this in mind, one thus brings it to cessation and extinction, leaving nothing remaining in the present locus. With focused concentration, one contemplates the signless gate of liberation (*animitta-vimokṣa*);

through this, one knows that there is nothing to be craved or delighted in, and one’s sole intent is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to instruct and transform sentient beings according to their original roots. This is what is meant by embracing the wishless gate of liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*). By being able to practice these three gates of liberation, one eliminates the conduct of self and other as well as the signs of conceptualization; one removes attachment to the various marks of existence and non-existence, and further advances in embrace. Taking great compassion as the ultimate, one increases one's vigor to transform all ordinary people who have not yet attained the Way, enabling them to reach full realization.
Being able to achieve this, one immediately reaches the assemblies of the Dharma; having entered these assemblies, one proceeds through them without ever turning back.
Fully endowed with harmony and concord, one advances in benevolence and gentleness, achieving non-retrogression.

If one perceives this, the affliction of the defilement of anger that arises from such conjunctions—and how it is precisely through these conjunctions that these manifold sufferings are brought about—is like the flow of a river that never rests. One should think to oneself:
"I shall not employ other practices; I shall forever cultivate tranquility to transform and enlighten sentient beings."
"Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
If one can practice in this way, they will abide without resentment even amidst the calamitous and poisonous evil world, guiding others according to the natural order.

Observing that which is fundamentally pure as neither arising nor ceasing, they revere great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and transform sentient beings in accordance with their needs. Practicing the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it is called the Gate of Unobstructed Wisdom; gradually cultivating and maturing their resolve, they study until reaching illumination, uniting with the clarity of the Way, and thus perfecting wisdom."

The great enterprise of the Right Path brings benefit through the Way in accordance with the times; one who practices and follows the meaning of the Way does not associate with or conjoin with unwholesome activities.

Through universal observation, there is natural quiescence; yet one does not merely go toward that state, but fully possesses the factors of the Path, personally witnessing and understanding the ground of the Way right before one’s eyes, thereby entering into emptiness.

He alone understands the concentrated mind; that concentrated mind is named the concentration of entering natural emptiness, the ultimate concentration of emptiness, the foremost concentration of emptiness, the concentration of the boundless emptiness of mind, the concentration of the unified emptiness of mind, the concentration of the emptiness of practice, the concentration of true non-conceptual emptiness of mind, the concentration of the equal observation of emptiness, and the concentration of the emptiness of non-substantiality free from karma.
In this manner, he attained ten thousand gates of samādhi, which naturally appeared before his eyes; the signless (*animitta*) and the wishless (*apraṇihita*) were likewise so.

Progressing further in his cultivation, he drew near to and reached the various bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattvavihāra*). His mind was filled, its nature indestructible, the nature of his mind lucid, and his natural conduct upright and true. His nature was profound and far-reaching; his will could not be turned back, his will never rested, and his will was vast and expansive. His mental reflections were limitless, and his mind aspired to and delighted in wisdom. When his mind gathered together skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), he then became fully endowed with them all.

This bodhisattva nature becomes thoroughly harmonious; established in the path of the Tathāgata, they never turn back. They are able to transform those of heterodox views and all practitioners of evil arts so that they accord with the ground of wisdom, neither falling into the stages of the śrāvaka nor the pratyekabuddha. Single-mindedly progressing, they behold the Buddha-wisdom with their own eyes, which is peerless; they abandon the practices of worldly toil, attain firm resolve, and abide in the wisdom of a bodhisattva.

Having thoroughly cultivated and honored emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they uphold the teachings of the Dharma, acting with appropriateness according to the time; through skillful means and wisdom, they no longer disrupt or scatter the practices of the factors of enlightenment.

That Bodhisattva dwelling therein beholds the stages of the path with his own eyes; his perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) becomes even more transcendent and extraordinary. Today he achieves mastery, becoming proficient and attuned to the Way, swiftly attaining the third patience known as "Gentle Compliance" (anulomikī kṣānti); this is called the Dharma of the Path.
Turning and following accordingly, he dwells in this sixth stage of the Bodhisattva’s path, beholding it with his own eyes.

He beheld incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; immediately he made offerings to them, serving them with a humble mind, providing them with food, clothing, bedding, seating, and medicine for their ailments. In the presence of these Buddhas, he left the household life, renounced his worldly affairs, and became a śramaṇa. He received and listened to the sūtras, practiced the wisdom as he had heard it, diligently cultivated holy realization, and sought the ultimate meaning through his conduct. Thus he was able to attain it, and further cultivating awakening and progress, he entered the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata.

Upon attaining the great illumination of the Dharma, after incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons—limitless and boundless—they have perfected the roots of merit and thus manifested their majesty. Just as when a son of the Buddha takes a precious lapis lazuli gem and polishes it until its brilliance is revealed, its light shining intensely, so too does the Bodhisattva abide in this present stage of the Bodhisattva path; their virtue increases daily, they practice skillful means and wisdom with ever-increasing clarity, and through these roots of merit, they become increasingly tranquil, walking without peer like a son of the Buddha.
That moon’s great light illuminated the minds of sentient beings, causing each to become serene; as for the palaces governed by the four great winds, they stood solitary and without companion.

"In this way, the Bodhisattva, dwelling in the stage of the Bodhisattva path before his very eyes, increases his daily merit; he illuminates and eliminates the afflictions of countless sentient beings, uproots the blemish of craving and desire, and comprehends the paths of the four Māras. Walking alone without peer, this is the stage of the path attained by the sixth Bodhisattva, the Son of the Buddha, who dwells near before him."

Abiding here in accordance with this practice, he is skillfully able to manifest transformations; even when acting as a celestial king, the four great elements become tranquil upon seeing him. He walks alone through the three realms without peer; neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas dare to question him. Regarding the roots of virtue in his conduct—generosity, loving respect, and impartial benefit—he transforms the minds of sentient beings, never abandoning the Buddha-way until all perfections are fully attained.

Mindful of omniscience, what could he possibly fail to manifest? His foremost vow is of such firm and powerful force that he guides, transforms, and brings others to universal wisdom. In the mere moment of resolving his mind, through such peerless and infinite diligence, he attains hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis in an instant.

He enlightened countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas; beholding the power of the vows of these attendant bodhisattvas, he perceived their extraordinary nature and was moved by them in a way that cannot be calculated, even over the course of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, for it is beyond all analogy.
Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, wishing to extensively resolve the ultimate meaning of this teaching, spoke these verses:
"Because they are fully endowed with all things, They abide in the fifth stage of the path;
Taking the Dharma as their auspicious response, They are signless and unarisen."
Unarisen and profoundly pure, they are free from negligence;
Practicing with the intention of noble wisdom, they enter the sixth stage.
All phenomena are quiescent, Tranquil and devoid of conceptual thought.
Nature is like an illusion; one is liberated from birth and death.
By attaining the patience of pliancy, phenomena are naturally undisturbed;
as their wisdom becomes increasingly sublime, they diligently cultivate the six stages.
The wise abide in gentleness and repeatedly enter the power of clear wisdom;
they observe all worlds as arising from habitual tendencies and resulting in retribution.
Due to the blindness of ignorance, there arise the notions of self, persons, and things.
Desiring to deliver these beings, I have thus undertaken diligent practice.
From the selection of causes and conditions, both beginning and end are entirely empty;
the karmic retribution of what is done brings together conflict and disorder.
It is as if there were something being done, whereupon one perceives what is created;
one selects and draws near to the assembly, just as a bee gathers from flowers.
Even if one examines it with wisdom, its beginning and end are both dark and obscure.
Thought conditions merit and demerit, and one receives retribution as the fruit of delusion.
Because thought has already arisen, name-and-form become its companions;
thus one encounters difficulties, resulting in the suffering of the five aggregates.
Because of the mind and its objects, one falls into the three realms;
furthermore, all these destinations are entirely within the single mind.
Arising from lustful desire, the mental activities are likewise so.
Exhaustion is likewise thus; one is further deceived by the mind.
Due to the delusion of ignorance, the twelve links of suffering are constructed;
through the causal conditions of foolish darkness, various conceptualizations are repeatedly produced.
That which is thus brought about—old age and sickness together with the decaying body;
furthermore, all manner of afflictions—shall thereby be exhausted and utterly destroyed.
From the condition of delusion and ignorance, this [suffering] arises and is never severed.
When thought is extinguished, conditions are severed.
From the arising of delusion and craving, one is led through conditions into the dust of worldly toil;
the afflictions of diligent suffering are harms that persist within conceptualization.
From the various sense-bases (*āyatana*) arises delusion; thus there is the suffering of birth and death.
Further contact and sensation lead from suffering to further suffering.
There are yet other bodies to be received, through which suffering grows ever more extensive.
Having severed all suffering and affliction, There is then no "self" or "mine.
Fundamentally there is neither sensation nor feeling, Nor are there any conceptual perceptions;
That which the consciousness undergoes Is what comes and goes in the present.
Because one will receive and practice [the teachings] in the future, all manner of suffering and affliction are produced;
furthermore, that which is to be extinguished is forever exhausted through contemplation.
Through the conditions of ignorance, one naturally attains clear awakening.
Because of weariness with suffering, one eliminates all causes and conditions;
because of those causes and conditions, one thereby severs all conditions.
Observing all lowly persons, they are naturally and eternally empty.
The compliant and the ignorant follow the inclinations of their own karma;
once they reach the end of delusion, all such conditions are severed through this.
Regarding these profound and subtle causes and conditions, one understands them as being devoid of marks.
Examining and reflecting upon these ten matters, one realizes they cannot be distinguished as separate.
One calculates the various destinies where transgressions and blessings await in the future;
these three grades of wealth and karma have been transmitted and transformed from time immemorial.
Discerning the practice of the three sufferings, The locus of their arising and ceasing;
When there is nothing and the aggregates are exhausted, One complies with and understands dependent origination.
Dependent origination is thus; That which is entered is the thorough realization of equality.
Just as a magical illusion appears, so too are desire and karma;
like what is seen in a dream, so too are forms and shadows.
Those who are dark, dull, and foolish are naturally like a mirage in the desert.
When one understands and practices in this way, that wisdom realizes emptiness;
all conditions are seen as fleeting illusions, and one honors this lack of solid characteristics.
Being able to understand things thus, one is likewise free from any volitional aspiration.
I only wish that you would take pity on all classes of sentient beings.
With a great resolve that is vast and expansive, he practices such a gateway to liberation;
his mind further increases in compassion as he contemplates and delights in the virtues of the Buddha.
Diligently cultivating compassion for sentient beings, he truly contemplates their origin;
free from all afflictions of emotion and distress, he attains immeasurable merit.
Endowed with the samādhi of emptiness, he perceives the roots of consciousness across hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
The heroic one is thus: signless and wishless.
Establishing this work of the Path, he is compliant with the honored patience of the Dharma;
his wisdom accords with the unconditioned, and the gates of liberation are his excellent treasure.
With such a nature broad and vast, one makes offerings to the Great Sage;
One should remain tranquil and eliminate agitation, directing the will in accordance with the command of the Most Victorious One.
Attaining the concentration of the mind of enlightenment, one further increases in purity.
Like lapis lazuli and purple gold, refined and polished to even greater brilliance,
he illuminates the minds of sentient beings like the vast light of the moon;
as the winds of the four stages circulate, he walks alone without equal.
Because he has transcended the paths of Māra, his most excellent radiance is sublime;
he extinguishes all worldly afflictions and scorches away every suffering.
The Great Lamp of the Teacher of Gods proclaims this dwelling in wisdom.
Skillfully transforming, he establishes the intent for the Path; his transformative power dispels the winds of mental attachment.
That which he reveres is the sagely wisdom, expounding the chapters and verses as they are taught;
this hero has already transcended that which the śrāvakas cannot reach.
One must arouse the resolve with diligence; having attained stability in one's practice, one has already secured in past lives hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis.
In a mere moment, one beholds the countless Buddhas currently manifesting throughout the ten directions.
His virtue illuminates the world, like the sun or the autumn moon;
subtle and profound, it is difficult to fathom, surpassing the reach of the śrāvakas.
The various heroes teach with mastery this sixth stage of the path.
At that time, the devas, having heard the Dharma taught, felt serene in their hearts; abiding in the midst of the void, they rained down various kinds of flowers, incense, and precious jewels.
With soft and wondrous tones, he praised and extolled him, proclaiming with his mouth a voice of pure, complete, and venerable merit:

"Excellent! Your supreme contemplation of benefit and meaning, your accumulation of merit and virtue, your attainment of mastery through wisdom, and your extraordinary conduct are most sublime and magnificent."
Like a lotus flower, he takes pity on all living beings; his conduct is transcendent and beyond measure.
The Great and Wondrous Deity, dwelling in the void, rained down a shower of various exquisite flowers and fragrances, eliminating coarse and subtle defilements as well as the darkness of sorrow.
He proclaimed a rare and sublime sound: "Attain the most pure and supreme benefit."
"We have attained the stages of the Way through what we have heard.

At that time, the various musical instruments produced mournful sounds, and the celestial maidens felt their hearts leap with joy. By the holy command of the Buddha, all the gates of those heavens opened of their own accord; the manifold darkness was dispelled, and their minds were enlightened like the sun as they received the most honored Dharma.

Thereupon, the countless multitudes of that world and the sages of the secular realm all transcended the mundane; they manifested the supreme subtlety of the worldly way. Beholding his body from afar—serene, tranquil, and at ease—they perceived his form as the "bodyless body," and they took refuge in the Dharma, extinguishing their passions through meditative concentration so as to become free from conceptual thought.

Possessing a resonant voice and eyes of great brilliance, they traverse incalculable Buddha-lands to make offerings to the Buddhas and serve the various Teachers. Examining their own bodies, they remember them as most excellent; casting off all defilements, they attain mastery over wisdom. They transform and enlighten sentient beings, free from the notions of "self" and "other," and they uphold diligent practice in accordance with their karmic duties.
All the celestial maidens delighted in the meaning of profound silence; beholding the Honored One among Men, the entire assembly was filled with joy and addressed the World-Honored One:

"Having attained mastery over the body through making offerings to the Buddha, we pray that you will proclaim the extraordinary teachings of the True Dharma. Your merit is like the great ocean; please, at this opportune time, declare it and reveal the seventh stage."
The Scripture on the Gradual Preparation for All-Wisdom and Virtue, Scroll Three; Scroll Four,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: The Sublime and Mysterious Abodes.
Vajragarbha said: "O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has purified and fully established themselves in the sixth stage, and enters the seventh stage to practice skillful means and wisdom, they cultivate the profound and wondrous path through ten matters.

What are these ten? They are: practicing the deeds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); adhering to the True Truth (*satya*); accomplishing the power of patience (*kṣānti*); feeling compassion and pity; being mindful of sentient beings; upholding the Buddha-dharma; delighting in making offerings to the Tathāgata; having firm faith without deviation; embracing the gateway of wisdom (*prajñā*) in one's mind; constantly conforming to the meaning of emptiness; and accumulating merit and inexhaustible blessings.
Understanding that the three realms are empty and abiding within the three periods of time, one exhorts and transforms the multitudes so that they may forever eliminate defilement.

Through this tranquility and composure, one removes all the blazing fires of dust; desiring to extinguish the greed, hatred, and delusion of all sentient beings, one realizes that all things are like illusions, transformations, dreams, echoes, mirages, and the moon reflected in water—without duality.
The matters of sin and merit never decay; one contemplates the buddha-lands as being like empty space, guiding sentient beings and adorning the lands with a pure dharma-body.

Having attained the meaning of the ultimate destruction [of delusion], one gains entry into the names and titles of all Buddhas; one becomes fully adorned with the physical marks and secondary characteristics of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), practices without attachment, and remains detached from sounds and echoes. One places faith in the voice of the Tathāgata as fundamentally quiescent and pure, understands the languages of all beings, and brings about guidance, benefit, and adornment. In a single moment, one awakens to the three periods of time and enters into the activities of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Furthermore, one can universally enter various eons and kalpas, discerning all numerical reckonings and analyzing the inclinations, natures, and practices of sentient beings; these are the ten matters.
Cultivating this extraordinary path from the stages of the six realms up to the ten abodes is called the "Profound and Sublime."

"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should diligently practice and study the perfection of wisdom through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); by means of this, they shall enter and abide in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), exhorting and transforming countless classes of sentient beings. Using the infinite teachings of all Buddhas, they shall instruct immeasurable sentient beings afflicted by suffering and enter incalculable Buddha-worlds."
They purify countless Buddha-lands; they enter the teachings of the various categories of inconceivable scriptural treasuries;
they enter the path of practice and the noble wisdom of the perfect enlightenment of immeasurable Buddhas; they descend into immeasurable and incalculable kalpas;
they enter the past, future, and present activities of immeasurable Buddhas; and they exhort [beings] beyond measure.
Calculating the categories of sentient beings, he causes them to enter into the practice of profound and extraordinary faith;
he enters into the manifestation of the various forms of the immeasurable physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas; he understands the immeasurable faculties and natures of sentient beings;
he enters into the sounds and verbal teachings proclaimed by the immeasurable Buddhas, which can delight all; and he enters into the immeasurable sentient beings.
With whatever mental activities they contemplate, they enter the hall of immeasurable wisdom where all Buddhas, Great Sages, and Leaders provide guidance and benefit;
they enter the place where immeasurable Buddhas, according to the occasion, transform and benefit those who take refuge with sincere faith among the śrāvakas;
they delight in the immeasurable teachings proclaimed by the Buddhas that lead one skillfully into the Way; and they respectfully cultivate the transformation of countless pratyekabuddhas.
He causes this multitude to achieve accomplishment, entering the gateways to the Way expounded by the profound and essential wisdom of the countless, most holy Buddhas;
entering the practices of the countless bodhisattvas and *kāśyapa*-like pioneers;
proclaiming the immeasurable Mahāyāna deeds of the Buddhas; and spreading forth such guided wisdom as these—this is what they themselves claim.
It can be calculated that they have reached the name of Buddha, the profound and wondrous stage of the various Equal Awakenings;
their practice is extraordinary and beyond measure, such that even over countless hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* of *kalpas*, they have been able to accumulate such Buddha-dharmas.
They claim, "We ourselves have established this Path," yet they do not crave wealth.
Regarding karma, neither conceiving nor not conceiving, they fulfill all practices.

Contemplating with such truth, relying on the wisdom of supernormal powers, they constantly practice diligence and enter the path of cultivation. With skillful means and wisdom, they dwell well in the noble path;
their conduct is unshakable, and at all times they remain in tranquil stillness. They uphold and practice the Way of the Buddha, never becoming weary.
Having abandoned [all attachments], he acts according to his own will.

Such is his practice: whether sitting, rising, walking, lying down, sleeping, speaking, or remaining silent, he is without hindrance; he constantly maintains majestic deportment, never forgetting anything, and never departing from such contemplative practice of the Way.

In the mere instant of generating that thought, within a single moment of mind, he fully accumulates the ten perfections (pāramitās) of a bodhisattva and universally amasses meritorious achievements. Why is this so?

Because when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices by thus generating the resolve wherever he may be, he takes the arousal of infinite compassion as his primary principle; he gathers together the Buddha-dharmas, encourages the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and through these roots of virtue, bestows them upon all sentient beings.
To practice the Buddha-way is the perfection of giving;
to incinerate and extinguish all defilements is the perfection of precept-keeping;
to possess compassionate pity and inexhaustible wisdom, knowing that sentient beings do not exist, is the perfection of patience.
If one can diligently practice the root of all virtues and cultivate mindfulness to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, practicing these skillful means, this is the perfection of vigor;
if one does not abandon the Way and directs oneself toward omniscience, this is the perfection of meditation;
if one realizes the practice of original purity and spontaneity, the gate of non-arising, and attains the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), this is the perfection of wisdom.
If one can guide and benefit others through immeasurable noble wisdom for the sake of the ten directions, this is the *pāramitā* of skillful means;
if one can practice the most supreme and wondrous wisdom and proclaim the work of the Path, this is the *pāramitā* of vow;
if one can subdue all external heterodox teachings and conquer the hosts of Māra’s armies, this is the *pāramitā* of power.
To examine with utmost sincerity, to transcend all dharmas, and to give rise to the practice of compassionate meaning—this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

By being fully endowed with these ten perfections, one is immediately able to proclaim and prepare the deeds of the four debts of gratitude, to possess in their entirety the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma), and to reach the three gates of liberation. With a mind of constant equanimity, in the space of a single thought-moment, one gradually and universally prepares for, and establishes, such [attainments].
There was a bodhisattva named Vimukticandra, who had attained thorough mastery; at that time, he questioned the Mahāsattva Vajragarbha:
"By what practices does a bodhisattva fully complete all aspects of the seventh stage?"
"If one wishes to fully prepare and accomplish the path of a bodhisattva, must they necessarily study and advance to the ten stages?
He replied: "O Son of the Buddha!

All bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path must fully realize the ten stages of the bodhisattva grounds (*daśabhūmi*); it is by means of these that they achieve liberation—how much more so for a bodhisattva at this seventh stage.

Why is this? Furthermore, these sons of the Buddha, having fulfilled the practices of the bodhisattva stages, enter the wisdom of supernormal powers and are universally able to fulfill all factors of enlightenment, while also accomplishing all ten dwellings.
Fully endowed with the ten abodes and striving for liberation, from the first arousal of the thought of enlightenment, one is equipped with these seven abodes.
Why is this? Because these are the abodes of the Bodhisattva path for the sons of the Buddha, wherein all practices are perfected and wisdom and spiritual powers are fully prepared.

Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha who, from their first resolution and the initial first dwelling, gradually fulfill all their vows by drawing near to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Their minds take delight in the second dwelling, and they subsequently reach the third dwelling, the activity of the broad essentials; they attain the fourth stage of the Way, the activity of conforming to the radiance of the Dharma; they enter the fifth dwelling, the practice of following worldly conventions with luminosity; and they enter the sixth dwelling, the profound and subtle Dharma, wherein they exhort and establish all the teachings of the Buddhas.

Why is this so? If there is a bodhisattva who accomplishes the seventh stage and enters the wisdom of supernormal powers, they immediately abide in the eighth stage, fully and thoroughly mastering the ground that is free from worldly concerns. It is like a son of the Buddha who has two worlds: one is defiled and the other is pure. Their original limit is level and equally pure; what is traversed therein is of one kind. Between these two realms, it is impossible to cross over; only by means of great supernormal powers, the power of attainment, and the power of vows can one cross them.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

Only by means of the bodhisattva’s practice of supreme diligence and purity can one thoroughly master this; it cannot be achieved through negligence or indolence. It is only through the power of great vows, skillful means, wisdom, and spiritual penetrations that one can universally fulfill it.
He asked again:
"How is it that while dwelling in the seventh stage, one still feels a close affinity for the practices of worldly toil?
By what means should the karmic activities of the bodhisattvas be examined?"
He replied: "O Son of the Buddha!

From the first resolution of the mind, abiding in the stages of a bodhisattva up to the tenth stage, one completely eliminates all karma of afflictions and fortune or misfortune, and assists the source of the Way; one should contemplate in this manner."
It is like a son of the Buddha who distinguishes those on the same path; because his principles do not overstep or transcend [the truth], it is called the seventh.

It is like a son of the Buddha who is a Wheel-Turning Sage King, riding upon a great precious elephant as he travels through the four continents. He clearly understands right and wrong, and though he dwells amidst the afflictions of poverty and suffering, he resolves the various defilements and is not polluted by impurities. He commits no transgressions, perfects human majesty and virtue, and abandons the nature of worldly men to be born in the Brahma Heaven. Ascending to the palace of Brahma, he beholds a thousand worlds; dwelling in the Brahma Heaven, he manifests radiant light and does not enter the human realm again.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, while dwelling in the stages of a bodhisattva and riding upon the perfections (*pāramitā*), one fully knows the conduct of all sentient beings; one is not defiled by worldly dust and filth, ascends to the hall of the Way, and commits no transgression—this is called the seventh.

If one can abandon all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*), proceeding from the seventh stage to the eighth dwelling, and likewise uphold the vehicle of the pure Bodhisattva, fully comprehending the conduct of all sentient beings, remaining unattached to worldly toil (*kleśa*) and untainted by defilements, never committing any transgression, and immediately attaining transcendence, one shall enter the profound and wondrous Dharma.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva attains this seventh stage, even if they are among those of lustful nature, they transcend all desires; though they dwell amidst those desires, they practice the pure Dharma. One should not say that they have either dust or no dust. Although they habitually remain within desire, they are free from affliction (*kleśa*). Because their aspiration for the wisdom of the Tathāgata is not yet fully realized, one should not say that they have abandoned affliction.

Having dwelled in this stage, their disposition becomes pure; their physical conduct is clean and white, ultimately pristine. The words they speak and the thoughts they harbor are pure from beginning to end. Regarding all matters that come to mind, they act solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings. They praise and never disparage the Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones, whether manifest or unmanifest, and they comply with all the teachings of the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, never contravening them.

He no longer yearns for or delights in the worldly crafts and heterodox arts, being like a bodhisattva in the fifth stage who takes no pleasure in the mundane world. He serves as a teacher and friend to all, finding much to approve of; whatever he finds admirable reaches the level of the unprecedented. Delighting in the Dharma of ultimate reality, he dwells among the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the trichiliocosm and among bodhisattvas on the path of the eighth stage, where he has no equal. In his nature and conduct, he always maintains benevolence and harmony. That which his mind mounts is constant progress through meditative concentration, as well as supernatural powers and the three gates of liberation—all of which he cultivates with single-minded diligence. He practices the gates of the Path without any expectation of reward, yet he has not yet fully accomplished the ground of the eighth bodhisattva stage.

Having dwelt in this stage, all his initial resolves are fulfilled through the complete mastery of skillful means and wisdom; he then cultivates the factors of the path and attains the seventh stage of the Bodhisattva’s path, characterized by universally perfected karma. He achieves the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Skillful Selection, followed by the Samādhi of the Meaning of Good Mindfulness, the Samādhi of Superior Intention, the Samādhi of Discerning Meanings, the Samādhi of Thoroughly Proclaiming the Dharma, the Samādhi of Abiding Well in the Fundamental, the Samādhi of the Door of Wisdom-Penetration, the Samādhi of Cultivating the Precepts of the Dharma, the Samādhi of the Treasury of Various Meanings, and the Gate of Samādhis on the Unconditioned within Saṃsāra.

When a bodhisattva attains this samādhi-samāpatti, they thus fully master a million concentrations; their stages of the path (*bhūmi*) become pure, and by virtue of that samāpatti, through these concentrations, they attain pure skillful wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*). Furthermore, they enter the inexhaustible power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), transcend the stage of the śrāvaka, and surpass the stage of the pratyekabuddha. They draw near to the gateway of the gate of wisdom (*prajñā-mukha*), and by abiding in this concentration, they maintain the karma of immeasurable bodily conduct in accordance with the Dharma. They advance in reciting the auspicious responses (*prātihārya*), such that both their speech and mental reflections are likewise beyond limit.
"His vision of the truths is pure, his radiance is sublime, and he possesses the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena.
He asked again:
"When he first resolves his mind and attains the first stage, do his body, speech, and mind not universally transcend those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"

He replied: "For this reason, one diligently cultivates a vast and expansive mind; having reached the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one is then able to achieve mastery over one's own conduct, becoming peerless. It is like a person born into a royal family who becomes a prince; possessing extraordinary virtues, he is honored and revered by all the ministers, yet he does not act with self-indulgence on account of his own status."
Suppose one were to grow up and, by virtue of his own physical strength, surpass all ministers in their discourse on the position of state.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva, having first resolved upon enlightenment, transcends the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; his mental nature is gentle and supple, and his magnanimity is boundless. This is the seventh stage of the Bodhisattva.

When one’s own wisdom is sovereign, entering the seventh stage of a bodhisattva, it is exceedingly profound and also tranquil; it reaches the state of non-action regarding body, speech, and mind. Having attained the work of the Way, one no longer advances further to seek additional meanings. What is there to hope for or abandon? Neither hoping nor abandoning—this is the Great Way.
He asked again:
"Son of the Buddha!
What is meant by the stages of the path (bhūmi) wherein a bodhisattva dwells?"
"Up until the point where a bodhisattva achieves the tranquil extinction of true and correct practice? He replied:

"Having attained the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭha-bhūmi*), one is able to practice this Dharma and thereby reach the seventh stage of the bodhisattva path. At that time, they give rise to the thought of awakening; as the mind repeatedly contemplates, they immediately achieve tranquil extinction and true practice. However, one should not say that they have realized the cessation of all existence (*nirodha*). For this reason, the actions of their body, speech, and mind are inconceivable; it is in accordance with what they perform that this is so described."
If there is a bodhisattva who dwells at the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) yet does not realize it, he is like a son of the Buddha.

At that time, that man boards a great ship and enters the vast ocean; accompanied by a skilled captain who possesses skillful means and knows the proper conditions of the waters, he travels across the great ocean without encountering any maritime disaster.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva establishes their practice and reaches the seventh stage, they board the vessel of the Dharma of the *pāramitās* and travel to the ultimate limit (*koṭi*), yet they do not realize [nirvana]. Having attained such power of noble wisdom and sustained by the power of samādhi, they accomplish all practices and awaken to the mind of the Way. By the power of great skillful means and wisdom, they manifest within the gateway of birth and death; though they traverse toward extinction, their mental nature is spontaneous. Having manifested their bodies together with their retinues, they come and go in surrounding circles; even amidst the clamor of the world, they remain ever diligent and attain profound stillness.

By virtue of their original vows, they are born within the triple world yet remain unsullied by worldly things; whether entering or emerging, advancing or retreating, they dwell in profound stillness and detachment. Their light of skillful means shines everywhere, leaving nothing unilluminated, and they suffer no burning affliction.
They attain the wisdom of a Buddha and withdraw from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
