They realize the realm of the Buddha-treasury; though currently appearing within the realm of Māra, they have already transcended the four māras, moving among their ranks while performing deeds that deliver them from the works of Māra.

Now, regarding the various heterodox teachers, all manner of errors, the ninety-six types of practitioners, and the sixty-two views—by transforming and enlightening these outsiders, I cause them to abandon their false studies so that they do not deviate from the Buddha-way.
Now, regarding all worldly secular activities, he guides and benefits them with the Dharma that transcends the world,
manifesting it before all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
In accordance with local customs, their clothing and dwellings were adorned, pure, and exquisite; yet their minds never abandoned the joy of the Dharma.

Such was their wisdom, as they fully mastered and thoroughly realized the stages of the Bodhisattva path, abiding in the profound, far-reaching, and sublime Dharma that is difficult to attain. Thus they made offerings in measureless ways.
To the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *gai* of Great Sages, the Buddhas, who offer superior robes, food, bedding, and seating,
as well as medicines for the sick and frail to provide them with comfort— I take refuge and bow my head to these Tathāgatas,
receiving their Buddha-way transformation and surpassing the dharmas of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, walking alone without peer.
He answered the questions of his companions at the appropriate time.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva, through the purity of the dharma-patience used to gather in sentient beings, subsequently became increasingly radiant; his roots of wholesome virtue flourished even further over countless billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, becoming pure and magnificent, just like a son of the Buddha.
Yet there is a rare treasure among all jewels whose light alone shines with singular brilliance, towering and peerless.
Even so, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this wondrous dharma—the path of practice for a bodhisattva that is difficult to attain—they rely upon these roots of virtue to achieve skillful means and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), thereby further increasing their renown and manifesting the Unsurpassed Way.

That which the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot attain is like the vast light of the sun and the palatial abode of the moon, O Son of the Buddha; the radiance they shed pervades the world, causing all things to ripen in abundance, and can even dry up the lands of mud and mire. The light of the sun and moon is likewise without obstruction; there is nothing it cannot penetrate or illuminate.

Thus, O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this profound, subtle, and difficult-to-attain path of practice for enlightening beings, the foundation of their merit is such that none can equal it; their virtue becomes ever more majestic, transforming all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas so that they feel a sense of shame, eliminating their various afflictions and defilements, and causing their natures to become pure. This, O Son of the Buddha, is the seventh stage of dwelling for the bodhisattva mahāsattva—profound, subtle, and difficult to attain.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the seventh stage, they further gain mastery. If they become a celestial king, through wisdom that accords with the times, they establish all things and perform deeds of diligence. Whether practicing giving, showing love, respect, and benevolence, or providing encouragement and benefit, they impartially bestow the meaning of profit and advantage. Their minds constantly recollect the Buddha, never forgetting or abandoning him, even up to universal wisdom, singular knowledge, and compassionate wisdom. From the very beginning, their minds never entertain the thought of when they might fail to attain the most perfect enlightenment of Buddhahood; rather, dwelling among sentient beings as the most holy and honored one, they guide and benefit them, demonstrating all-encompassing wisdom.

At the very moment he resolved his mind [on enlightenment], his diligence was so transcendent that in a single instant, he attained hundreds of thousands of billions of trillions of samādhis and meditative absorptions. He beheld the bodhisattvas, each surrounded by retinues of hundreds of thousands of billions of trillions; through the power of this vow, he sustained the extraordinary manifestations of the bodhisattvas and displayed spiritual transformations beyond measure. The merit and virtue cultivated over hundreds of thousands of billions of trillions of kalpas were truly immeasurable.
When Vajragarbha had finished expounding this Dharma, wishing to further elaborate upon its meaning, he spoke these verses:
"The profound and wondrous sagely wisdom Accords with the meaning of the foremost phrase;
The mind realizes the sixth stage, Diligently conforming to one's own conduct."
Diligently cultivating the Way of the Buddhas, one should employ skillful means and wisdom;
thus one readily and skillfully enters the seventh stage of the bodhisattva path.
Abiding in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one’s resolve is to practice loving-kindness and compassion.
If one practices and makes offerings to the path and teachings of all Buddhas,
understands the wisdom of the various sages, and never tires of their virtuous power;
by practicing in this way, one enters the seventh stage of the path.
Yet within the three realms, there is tranquility amidst great turmoil;
all sentient beings are extinguished, and the fever of afflictions is stilled into stillness.
Like reflections illuminating illusions, they exist within dreams through the practice of dharmas.
By entering the seventh stage, one manifests the karma of compassion;
the Buddha-fields are purified as empty, and the nature of the world is devoid of conceptualization;
fully realizing the most excellent marks, one abandons all wavering phenomena.
Thereby producing wondrous sounds, they remove the defilements of sentient beings;
contemplating that the essence of wisdom is fundamentally empty, these most excellent ones provide equal guidance and benefit.
By practicing this Dharma, they attain such brilliant illumination.
Pervading the sublime stages, they are what sentient beings delight in.
Having already dwelt in these stages, the practices of sentient beings are immeasurable;
selecting and contemplating the dharmas of peaceful abiding, their observations are beyond limit.
In countless and immeasurable lands, the various thoughts and conceptions differ;
their dispositions harbor sincere faith, and their mental activities comprise many varieties.
He proclaims the teachings of the Three Vehicles, guiding and benefiting beings in measureless ways.
We shall all advance together, reciting and transforming these followers.
With such a mind of wisdom, we shall attain the sublime and wondrous Path;
observing the four matters of dignified conduct, we shall follow skillful means and wisdom.
In every moment of mental reflection, one attains the meritorious achievements of the Way;
thus one is able to fulfill these ten perfections of boundless action.
If one gives rise to such a thought, it is an exhortation for sentient beings to practice giving.
Precepts extinguish all worldly afflictions; patience is free from discursive thought.
Through diligence one zealously practices and cultivates, further increasing one's karmic conduct;
the Path is unshakable, as wisdom and merit establish the resolve.
The Noble Honored One of stainless wisdom has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena;
may he exhort and assist us with skillful means so that we shall forever be free from doubt.
Possessing sovereign power, he universally delivers all through his holy brilliance.
The merit of the Way is thus: all things are bestowed according to the time.
When prior practice is thus established, its fame becomes manifest and complete;
one uproots the defilements of the mind and cuts off the source of strife and contention.
Equally honoring the Way in these four ways constitutes the establishment of the fifth karma;
through non-arising and non-discrimination, one then fully develops the sixth.
This is the attainment of the seventh stage, wherein his meritorious achievements are perfected.
Able to follow various practices, with vows beyond measure;
for what reason does one receive this noble work of wisdom?
By attaining the eighth stage, all things become entirely pure.
The profound and subtle practice is difficult to attain; wisdom is without limit.
It is like entering a second realm, transcending that which lies between.
One practices the dharma of the seventh stage, remaining unattached like a burning lamp.
If one abides in the meaning of the Path, with valor one transcends all.
Having attained entry into the eighth stage, the preceding was the Stage of Noble Wisdom;
having transcended the sphere of mental conceptualization, one dwells in the activity of wisdom.
Constantly observing in the Brahma-heaven, they do not rely on the mundane world;
the practice of the worthy and holy is thus—unattached like a lotus flower.
Abiding in these various stages, they transcend all worldly afflictions.
This practice is free from defilement, and there is nothing therein to be exhausted or extinguished.
Abiding thus in the ultimate Way, one is without the conduct of defiled stains;
this most supreme illusion has no root, for it eliminates defects through wisdom.
Regarding the various crafts practiced in the world, he understands them all clearly;
transformed, he abides by the teaching of the World-Honored One.
With single-mindedness he pursues supernormal powers, receiving instruction and practicing with diligence.
Practicing according to various stages, he advances through the three grades of concentration;
transcending all śrāvakas, the practice of the pratyekabuddhas is likewise.
Abiding in the seventh stage of action, he cultivates the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Abiding in the fundamental nature of the mind, one brings forth this true illumination of wisdom;
thus accomplishing all noble sons, one nurtures the power of the Path.
Consequently, increasing diligent practice, one attains entry into the profound and subtle.
The mind takes refuge in cessation, yet does not create or grasp at realization.
It is like one who has entered the great ocean and remains upon the prow of a ship;
beholding all the waters, they neither increase nor decrease.
If one can diligently receive and practice these supreme skillful means and wisdom,
no class of sentient beings will be able to limit their treasury of virtue.
By making offerings to billions of Buddhas for ten million years, one’s path of practice becomes ever more purified.
Like various necklaces made of countless precious jewels,
the wise one abides in this practice with the light of supreme wisdom;
having dried up the source of craving and desire, he shines like the full moon.
Having already entered and dwelt in this stage, he acts as a sovereign sage-king;
cultivating the ultimate meaning of the Path, he proclaims the fruits of wisdom.
In the mere instant that his mind is resolved, he exerts the power of diligent effort.
One sees thousands of Buddhas, numbering in the hundreds of billions of koṭis;
Having well cultivated compliance with one's own person, one perceives all throughout the ten directions;
Increasing one's supreme vows, one’s meritorious achievements become infinitely sublime.
"The universal world is difficult to comprehend; One proceeds freely through the conditions of the Way.
This is the seventh stage, Adorned with the wisdom of skillful means.

The assembly of Bodhisattvas, of most honored rank, was divine, wondrous, and majestic. Immeasurable devas and nāgas, and countless people, hearing what was said, were all filled with joy. They made offerings of flowers, incense, banners, and streamers; they presented blended powdered incense, precious jewels, and robes; and they stood holding innumerable parasols beyond measure.

A rain of various necklaces fell, and the gods above proclaimed wondrous sounds and gentle voices; they spontaneously produced beautiful, soft, and harmonious tones to honor the Protectors of the Multitude and the sons of the Buddhas:

“We extol the immeasurable World-Honored One, the Capable One (Śākyamuni), who is seen by all as the supreme among the most holy beings. Beholding the realm of the Buddha, he takes pity on sentient beings; his voice is like falling rain, spreading the roar of great thunder, while musical instruments and flutes produce manifold sounds. There are infinite hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, and the lands of their imperial kingdoms are likewise as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all making offerings to these Buddhas.”
His buddha-field is peerless and most magnificent, and his sovereign power can manifest transformations that enter into a single pore.
When the Buddhas proclaim the stainless and inexhaustible Dharma, it is as easy as expounding from a single hair; how could it ever be difficult!

The lands and their locations, as well as the regions of the four quarters, various kinds of species, springs and great oceans, billions of Iron Ring Mountains and Mount Sumerus—all these appear spontaneously without any crowding, and all enter a single pore, where they move about at will.

Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; gods and humans, as well as various spirits and malevolent demons, and asuras—though their karmic retributions of sin and merit differ—they all come together within the realm of the Buddhas. Traveling through all lands in every district and county, they spontaneously manifest the sublime and wondrous Wheel of Dharma, preaching with gentle words and abiding in harmonious resonance, in accordance with the mental inclinations and the practices of sentient beings.

The multitudes of beings are diverse, their bodies each differing; within the lands of the World-Honored One, these beings possess bodies that take form wherever they dwell. Born among devas and humans, they are each distinct from one another. All this is according to the Dharma teachings proclaimed by the Buddha: to eliminate the defilements of subtle conceptualizations and various impurities, to give rise to the aspiration for the Way, and to manifest vast Buddha-lands through the spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) of the Buddhas. Such transformations are beyond the capacity of all worldly people to fully describe; such is the inexhaustible wisdom of the Buddhas' Path.

The sound of his voice was resonant, gentle, and subtle; as he entered the assembly, all were silent and filled with joy, gazing upon him with reverence. He was the most extraordinary and holy being among the multitude. As they contemplated in profound stillness, it was like the moon after an eclipse, its light restored. They desired only to hear further about the eighth stage (*bhūmi*); may you, at this time, expound upon that which the practitioner enters.
Chapter 8: The Station of Immovability (*Acalābhūmi*) from the *Gradual Preparation Sutra*. Chapter Eight on the Station of Immovability.
Vajragarbha said: "Listen well, Son of the Buddha!

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can successfully fulfill the seventh station, through a resolute aspiration for the truths, seeking pure karma with skillful means and wisdom, reverently conforming to all practices, delighting in what is given, and through infinite great vows, they rely upon and uphold the intent established by the Tathāgata; by virtue of their past roots of merit, they attain power—the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, mindfulness of perfect enlightenment, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."

His disposition is benevolent and harmonious; he contemplates purity, and his merit, sagely wisdom, and majestic power increase ever further. He gives rise to great compassion, pitying the realm of sentient beings, yet does not abandon the joy of the Dharma. He penetrates and enters all immeasurable dharmas, reaching the state of non-arising and signlessness. There is no composite formation, nor is there any loss of luminous wisdom. There is nothing to be fully realized, nor is there anything to be extinguished; yet, being without possession, he enters equally into the primordial source. Progressing upward, he attains deliverance, universally eliminating all mental conceptions, perceptions, and cognitions. Equally encompassing the fundamental purity of his disposition, he thereby transcends and, at that moment, attains the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas). This is what is meant by this.

When a bodhisattva attains such dharma-patience, they enter this dwelling of the bodhisattva stages, becoming unshakable. They achieve the profound and essential practices of a bodhisattva—mysterious and subtle, difficult to comprehend—which no one can destroy. They eliminate all conceptualizations, encompassing all thoughts to reach ultimate perfection.
Immeasurable and peerless, the entire assembly of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can never attain his state of profound stillness, for he is pure and refined.

He manifests spontaneously, like a son of the Buddha—a bhikṣu with supernormal powers—whose thoughts are sovereign; gradually advancing forward, he eventually enters the meditative absorption of the samādhi of cessation, completely eliminating all desires and deluded imaginings.

When a bodhisattva has thus attained this dwelling, they abandon all worldly activities and acquire the wealth of non-action—the Dharma of ultimate reality. They leave behind the pleasures practiced by body, speech, and mind, and abide in profound stillness. Just as a son of the Buddha, even while in a dream, recognizes upon attaining great merit that it arises from the power of great diligence, so too does he universally transcend through it; having attained it, he realizes awakening. He cultivates skillful means and reflects day and night in order to eliminate attachment to pleasure.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained such boundless diligence and dwells in this Bodhisattva stage, remaining thus immovable, far removed from all karma, gradually practicing what is appropriate, they become non-dual in their conduct.

Furthermore, they practice with equanimity and have no attachments; like the sons of the Buddha, even if they are born in the Brahma Heaven and dwell in the Brahma palaces, they do not cling to sensual conduct, nor do they possess worldly afflictions.

In this way, the bodhisattva, dwelling in this stage of the path, causes his mind to roam universally through all practiced activities; though he remains within these activities, he is not defiled by them, for his intellect clearly understands the nature of the actions performed in each instance.
The practice of a bodhisattva consists in practicing within *nirvāṇa* while not regarding it as a practice, let alone worldly practices.

Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has entered this stage through the power of his original vows, he reaches the Tathāgata’s awakening, the infinite Great Sage. This is the gateway to the Dharma-scriptures; he follows the path of the Tathāgata’s Dharma and establishes noble wisdom, speaking these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Noble son! This foremost dharma-patience of these true beings culminates in the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, noble son!

The ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the exalted station of the Buddha-dharma—these you do not yet possess. Therefore, practice with diligence, aspire to supreme effort, and be careful not to fail or lose them.
This is the gate of patience in the Path; for the sake of sentient beings, one honors its cultivation.
Furthermore, son of good family!

You have indeed attained this, yet while you practice such tranquility, foolish ordinary people lose their composure; they habitually engage in countless afflictions and are harmed by various conceptualizations.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If sentient beings should recall their original vows from past lives and, out of compassion for those dwelling in darkness, seek the Way and practice the gate of the inconceivable, noble wisdom of stillness and solitude, they shall never grow weary or abandon it.
Furthermore, son of good family!

This is the root of all dharmas; it has issued forth from the Dharma, giving rise to and perfecting the Tathāgata, and establishing the Tathāgata. Abiding within the dharma-realm, the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, does not practice anything apart from this. No śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can ever attain this dharma of non-differentiation.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Observe my body, which is beyond measure; its wisdom cannot be discussed, its lands are immeasurable, its radiance is immeasurable, its place of enlightenment is immeasurable, and its pure resonance is likewise immeasurable. For these reasons, that which is practiced through benevolence and compassion is manifested through the power of karma.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Regarding that which is definitively called "luminosity": it is said that all phenomena are without conceptualization; this is what constitutes luminosity.

Sons of good family, such is the illumination of the Dharma; the conduct of the Tathāgata is boundless, his retinue is bottomless, and the entry into these states—from the time they first set out in practice—has been as magnificent as this.
Furthermore, son of good family!

You should observe these immeasurable Buddha-lands of the ten directions and their infinite sentient beings; the sutras they distinguish are incalculable, universally entering into all things, with their words and deeds in perfect accord.

Thus, O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, practice these bodhisattva deeds; such analogies for their immeasurable guidance and benefit of the gateway to the Way are used to transform and enlighten the multitudes. If there are bodhisattvas who analyze and explain immeasurable noble wisdom, they will fully accomplish the task of guiding the assembly.
O Sons of the Buddha! I entrust this to you:

even if all Buddhas were to transform these Bodhisattvas and cause them to enter among sentient beings to guide them through the gates of the Way, it is by virtue of this that the work of bringing sentient beings to extinction (nirvāṇa) will naturally flourish and expand.

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, exhort and transform beings herein; through these dharmas of the bodhisattvas and their immeasurable wisdom-karma, they cause all those whom they guide and benefit to take that sacred karma as their foremost priority."

From the initial generation of the thought of enlightenment until the completion of the seventh stage, if one were to combine all skillful means and calculate the resulting merit, it would exceed [the former] by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, and even hundreds of billions of times; it could never be equaled, for there is no analogy to compare it with.

Why is this so? Because through these past lives, he has led the multitude with a single body, accomplishing the work of guidance and benefit, and attained this dwelling. He encourages and advances all bodhisattva practices with equanimity, discerns the affairs of the body, and achieves the power of practice. He proclaims and disseminates the teachings of the True Dharma through immeasurable sounds; his cultivated wisdom is immeasurable, his guidance and benefit are immeasurable, the lands where he is born are immeasurably adorned and purified, and he transforms immeasurable Buddha-lands.
Furthermore, among the classes of sentient beings, those who make offerings to and revere immeasurable Buddhas give rise to immeasurable awakening.

The gates of the Way of all dharmas and the power of their spiritual penetrations are beyond measure; they analyze and transform the hardships and calamities of sentient beings, causing them to expand immeasurably.
The assemblies and the sites of practice where they dwell and roam are likewise immeasurable.
Their maintenance of body, speech, and mind, and their accumulation of all essential practices of a bodhisattva, are also immeasurable.

It is like a son of the Buddha on a great ship who wishes to enter the great ocean; remaining secure and free from negligence, he proceeds with steady composure and acquires immeasurable treasures, rare and exquisite jewels. Upon reaching the great ocean, he raises his sails in accordance with the wind; the wind being favorable, within a single day he traverses the great ocean. All the wealth and treasures thus obtained fill countless treasuries, which can never be exhausted.

In this way, the bodhisattva accumulates and perfects infinite, vast roots of virtue; gathering together the Mahāyāna, they attain the ocean of wisdom regarding the bodhisattva path. In a single moment, they acquire the treasure of holy clarity and the infinite jewels of the Path, entering into all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). The worldly wealth and treasures accumulated over past lives cannot be compared to this; even if one were to contemplate and calculate for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, or incalculable kalpas, it would still not serve as an adequate analogy.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva establishes themselves in the eighth stage of the path, they shall observe the great skillful means and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), proclaiming and exhorting others through the principle of non-material action.

If a bodhisattva understands and honors all-knowledge, they thoroughly know all buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, as well as distinguishing the disintegration and dissolution of those buddha-fields. Whether observing the world’s dissolution or its formation, by what cause does the world dissolve and disintegrate?
By what causes and conditions does the world form?
One is able to see and know them all: whether the earth element is small or great, finite or infinite; and one knows each of these individually.
It is likewise for the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.

They clearly understand the extent and magnitude, the finite and the infinite, and the subtle nature of all atoms; they discern their locations and fully comprehend the numerical limits of these atoms at any given time. They universally know and distinguish the various kinds of atoms within as many worlds as there may be—atoms that are infinite, subtle, and difficult to fathom—and they understand how these various categories of atoms naturally combine together, knowing the total number of atoms contained within all the Buddha-worlds.
He is able to know the number of sentient beings, the dimensions and forms of their lands, and the length, size, and stature of their bodies.

He knows the locations of the hells, the natures and behaviors of beasts and hungry ghosts, and the causes by which they fall into these states, as well as the extent of their respective karmic actions.
He is fully able to know the combined numbers of all sensory objects, the movements of the asuras, the abodes of the devas, and the dwellings of worldly people.

He knows all about their gatherings and their instruction, as well as the conjunctions and disjunctions within the desire realm, and the conjunctions and disjunctions within the form realm and the formless realm.
Whether few or many, large or small, finite or infinite, he knows them all.
He is able to accomplish the task of dwelling and wandering through the three realms, understanding the principles of selection and rejection, and transforming sentient beings.
He thoroughly understands the skillful means regarding the various bodies of sentient beings and their physical forms; wherever they may be, he clearly comprehends them all.

He knows the places where they are born through their past conduct and the realms where the Buddhas roam. According to the types of sentient beings, the abodes where they are born, and the accumulated actions of their bodies, he establishes [teachings] in accordance with those bodily conducts.

One’s own body and land are established according to one's own person; their intention is inexhaustible. One establishes one’s own body as the "body without a body. One must establish one’s own body as the body of the land, the body of transgression and merit, and the body of the retribution for transgression and merit. Having established one’s own body, the intention of the inexhaustible body is the "body without a body. One’s own body is inexhaustible: the bodies of the various classes of sentient beings, the body of the land, the body of conditioned retribution, the body of the śrāvaka, the body of the pratyekabuddha, the body of the bodhisattva, the body of the Tathāgata’s holy wisdom, and the Dharma-body are all established according to the occasion.

Manifesting these various bodies, they fully understand the body of sentient beings' sins and blessings, the body of retribution, the body of afflictions, the form-body, the formless-body, and the land-body; whether small or large, defiled or pure, vast and immeasurable, diminished or balanced, and how they impartially guide and benefit others—they know all of this, including the exposition of karmic retribution.
He also thoroughly understands the bodily actions of merit and demerit and the retributions they shall receive, as well as their convergence and dispersal and how they form distinct destinies.
He fully knows the practices undertaken by those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and the convergence and dispersal to which they return.

The Tathāgata’s holy body—his body that has attained supreme perfect enlightenment, his body of vows, his body of parinirvāṇa, his established body, his body adorned with physical forms and marks of excellence, his body of the practitioner, his agreeable body, his magnanimous body, his humble and reverent body, his body of merit, his body of noble wisdom, his body of retribution, and his body of noble wisdom resulting from careful conduct—he knows all those who have been delivered through them.

The Dharma-body is equal, the body of no-body; it is immeasurable and universally enters all things. Whether possessing a body or lacking a body, there is nothing it does not discern, understanding each and every instance with complete clarity.

With his body having attained such karmic activities, he achieves mastery over life; his mind acts according to its own will to accomplish what it intends, acting with full autonomy and without difficulty, his conduct being unrestrained, his births following his own volition, brought about by his original vows and the power of firm faith, through the grace of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and sustained by the practice of noble wisdom and the guidance of the Dharma—by these means, he attains this state, which constitutes the ten kinds of mastery of a bodhisattva.

Having attained mastery, they become sages of immeasurable wisdom and light, inconceivable, vast, and universal; these sages have no peer, and by entering thus, they ultimately abide forever in the body of non-arising.

One transforms the habitual practices because they are ultimately without arising; thus, by transforming all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*), one takes wisdom as the foremost. Transforming the habitual practices of the body, one takes wisdom as the head; transforming the habitual practices of speech, one likewise takes wisdom as the head. To state the essential point: the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the great lamp of light, with Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its primary guide.

He thoroughly understands skillful means and does not abandon his ultimate vows; established by the majestic spiritual power of all Tathāgatas, he should never rest. His wisdom accords with all sentient beings as he travels through boundless Buddha-worlds, proclaiming the meaning of the Dharma and dispersing their knots of affliction.
“O Son of the Buddha!

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva constantly cultivates the dwelling in the path attained through equanimity, which is unshakable. He accumulates all the Dharma-scriptures of the Buddhas, and his actions of body, speech, and mind further increase in merit. Having attained this dwelling, the power of his will and nature remains steadfastly established.”
All have eliminated every defilement; their minds are imbued with benevolence and harmony, and their power is firm and strong as they stand at the head [of the assembly].

By the power of great compassion, they freely transform all living beings; in whatever they establish, they do so for the sake of sentient beings without expectation or attachment, further increasing the establishment of the power of great loving-kindness.

Protecting and sustaining all classes of sentient beings, they maintain firm abiding through the essential power of dhāraṇī; never abandoning sentient beings, they dwell with true stability in all Buddha-dharmas by the power of their vow.

Discerning through analytical selection, establishing with skillful and precise clarity, and abiding for infinite eons by the power of spiritual penetrations, they protect all classes of sentient beings at the very root of all conditioned phenomena; steadfastly dwelling in the power of their vows, they practice all the deeds of the bodhisattva path without ever abandoning them.

The power of the perfection of deliverance is firm and stable in its practice; it compiles all the sūtras of the Buddhas, correctly abides by the power established by the Tathāgatas, and accomplishes the omniscience of perfect enlightenment.
"By entering this practice, through such power and majesty, one universally manifests all infinite spiritual transformations and is immediately reborn in all places of destination.

Vajragarbha said: "This is the work of the sons of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas who abide in the Stage of Wisdom (prajñā-bhūmi) and cannot be shaken; this is called 'having no peer,' and it is also termed the 'Stage of Non-retrogression' (avaivartika-bhūmi)."

When wisdom does not regress, it is called "difficult to withstand"; that which no sentient beings can attain is the Stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūmi). It is the stage where there is no birth yet it is the ground of birth; the stage where the fulfillment of vows is mastery and where cessation is perfected; the ultimate stage of non-action. By accumulating true wisdom, it is the unconditioned stage; by skillfully cultivating one's aspirations, it is the stage of establishment. Transcending non-action, it is the state of being without possessions or karma. Through practices of past lives, all sufferings are eliminated, and the wicked are subdued.

Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters the lineage of the Buddhas, they inherit the Buddha’s meritorious achievements and are illuminated by his distant spiritual power. By taking refuge in the gate of the Tathāgata’s majestic conduct, ultimate deeds, and the realm of the Buddhas, they are constantly established by the Tathāgata. They gain entry into the palaces of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings; the Vajrapāṇi spirits constantly follow and attend upon them from behind. Having attained the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), their bodies become limitless; they subdue the treasury of form (*rūpa-kośa*) and disperse immeasurable fetters, being forever liberated from them all.
Through the power of all bodily actions, they possess infinite majesty and great supernormal powers; regarding the retributions of their conduct, they attain mastery.

With unrestricted intention, they receive immeasurable predictions of enlightenment; acting freely according to their own will, they encounter no obstacles. In accordance with their purity and goodness, they awaken and deliver sentient beings, manifesting the meanings as they appear.

By entering into this practice, one attains entry into the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and possesses boundless great wisdom. Through the performance of the deeds of great wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one constantly manifests the light of the Great Sage’s wisdom, bestowing upon others chapters and verses within the realm free from obstruction.

They discern the chapters and phrases proclaimed throughout the lands of the ten directions in all worlds; they manifest the virtue of the merit of all karmic deeds; they attain mastery in the arousal of the bodhicitta; they contemplate with profound clarity, understanding the past, future, and present; and they turn back all the paths of the various māras.

Descending into noble wisdom, they enter the sphere of the Tathāgatas throughout the regions of provinces and prefectures and the boundless lands; in the lecture halls where they dwell, they uphold the bodhisattva practices, and that which they inspire others toward is such that none can regress. For this reason, it is called "Entering the Immovable Ground."
Vajragarbha said: "Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva attains the stage of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*), they abide eternally in the boundless; they behold the Tathāgatas, who are beyond measure or limit, never being far removed from them. Having brought those practices to completion and achieved samādhi, through the entry of their majestic power, they behold the Buddhas, making offerings, serving, and taking refuge in them, never forgetting or abandoning this."

In each and every world within each successive eon, the lecture halls he beheld each manifested various Buddhas, and he made offerings to countless billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas.

Bestowing peace upon all, I bow my head and take refuge, paying homage to the Tathāgata. He who thoroughly understands the world as its sovereign leader, who yearns for and guides through the light of the Way, and who receives and upholds the teachings of the Dharma, further increasing them until the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—his practice is peerless, his majesty transcendent and far surpassing the multitude, distinct from all others as he consults and receives the ways of the world.

Through teaching, questioning, and proclaiming, one follows the roots of merit accumulated over countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, advancing further and becoming ever more radiant. O Son of the Buddha!

It is just as if there were a bright moon-jewel atop this Jambudvīpa, whose value equals that of the entire continent; when worn around the neck, it is peerless, such that among all the necklaces worn by the multitudes of people throughout the world, none can equal it.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Immovability, they perfect a great illumination through these roots of virtue, such that it cannot be attained by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, regarding the practices of a Bodhisattva in the seventh stage, a Bodhisattva who has entered this ground of the path relies upon infinite wisdom to eliminate all the afflictions of sentient beings. He discerns the subtle gateways of the noble wisdom, just like a son of the Buddha presiding over the Brahma Heaven; his practice of loving-kindness pervades the great trichiliocosm, and its radiance shines everywhere.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise.

Abiding in this Bodhisattva stage of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*), they illuminate hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within them; their radiance completely pervades immeasurable Buddha-lands, exhausting all the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings and gradually eliminating the poisonous stains of the mind. Such is the son of the Buddha; this is the eighth path-stage of Bodhisattva merit, wherein the Bodhisattva abides in the impartial and upright conduct of immovability.

Extensively praising and extolling [this practice], throughout boundless kalpas it cannot be fully exhausted. That which the Bodhisattvas abide in serves as the Great Brahmā King for the Brahmā Heaven, presiding over a thousand worlds. Among the practices of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, there is nothing that can equal its true essence. It is the perfection of deliverance (*pāramitā*), the discernment of worlds, and the cultivation of peerless qualities. Upon hearing what is preached, one understands the causes and conditions that arise, the karma of skillful means, and the acts of giving, reverence, and affection. Bringing equal benefit to others, providing universal rescue and relief, one constantly contemplates the Buddha, never forsaking him. With all practices fully perfected, one reaches omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
I focus my mind solely on the Great Way; by what practice does one become honored among sentient beings, distinguished above all?
To accord with the universal sages and provide protection throughout the ten directions, one should, at the very moment of generating the resolve, follow such an example as this.

Diligently practicing with vigor, in a single moment he attained the samādhi of perfecting the number of atoms filling hundreds of thousands of lands throughout ten thousand worlds, as well as the meditative absorption of correctly receiving [the vision of] bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms filling ten thousand times ten thousand three-thousandfold world systems, surrounded by their retinues. From this he made a vow; the power and majesty of his resolve were so extraordinary that all were moved, and his wisdom was clear and bright beyond measure.
Reflecting thus, for immeasurable kalpas—beyond the limit of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons—one’s meritorious achievements would be bottomless, beyond all analogy.
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, wishing to further elaborate and analyze this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Gradually preparing for the seven stages, With pure wisdom and skillful means;”
Truly upholding and guiding their activities, they establish infinite vows;
accumulating merit and piling up virtue, they steadfastly abide as the supreme among men;
delighting in noble wisdom, they immediately enter the eighth stage.
Planting the roots of virtue with great sage-wisdom, practicing diligence and compassion;
their minds are immeasurable, and their thoughts are like space.
Hearing the Dharma, they can understand it clearly and enter the power of the Great Sage.
The power of patience is without arising; it is tranquil and accords with the subtle and wondrous.
That which is received does not originate; it is non-arising and devoid of marks.
It is non-extinguished and indestructible, and likewise there is nothing to be fully realized.
The dwelling place is spontaneous; there is no fundamental storehouse, nor is there abandonment or mindfulness.
Having already departed from the nature of mind and thought, one's contemplation is equal to space.
With such patience as this, one’s conduct is free from negligence.
Practicing the profound requires a stirring of the spirit, leading to the attainment of tranquil conduct.
Sentient beings are unable to understand this, due to their habitual dwelling in worldly activities;
yet by maintaining the mind’s contemplations, one clearly realizes the nature of all practices and thoughts.
When his intention is established in this way, the mind is free from conceptual thought;
like a bhikṣu who has brought about cessation, he attains non-attachment.
Whatever the mind conceives and imagines is like what is seen in a dream upon waking.
If the Brahmā realm is fully perfected, so too is the desire realm.
Abiding securely in one's original vow, one repeatedly exhorts the multitudes;
this is the foremost patience, which leads to the attainment of the stage of Avinivartana.
Our wisdom is profound and far-reaching; we understand the Dharma through the power of our resolve.
They are free from the notion of "mine" and practice with diligent vigor.
Devoted to the state of tranquility, they dissolve the entire web of craving.
He extinguishes the great blazing fire, the worldly fires of dust and toil.
Recognizing his own original vows from past lives, he practices compassion for sentient beings;
establishing himself through sharp wisdom, he employs it to deliver the masses.
One who can always honor this Dharma abides in fundamental non-existence and the absence of conceptualization;
the Buddha understands the abiding of all things and thus transcends the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Among the worldly powers of influence, none can equal these ten powers.
Wisdom alone is beyond limit; throughout the three periods of time, it is free from obstruction.
Being thus peerless, they are honored and revered by devas and humans;
gathering them together for guidance and transformation, they practice through countless gates of wisdom.
Having accomplished the most supreme Dharma, they enter the infinite further shore;
having practiced the Buddha-way in previous lives, even as they accord with the times,
they thus attain sagacity and reach the extraordinary and holy ground.
At one time, they pervaded everywhere, reaching throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Thus they attained the destination of wisdom and acquired all supernormal powers;
they were like the waters of the great ocean, or like the celestial flowers and divine vessels.
Having eternally eliminated the mind’s greed, one establishes the practice of the path of wisdom;
selecting various buddha-fields, one dwells in clear discernment.
Regarding the fourfold sphere of experience, one remains free from manifold cravings for gain.
Subtle and coarse alike, they enter equally into the understanding of consciousness and its objects.
Within all the three thousandfold worlds, as numerous as the atoms filling them, one discerns the fundamental nature of sentient beings: bodies born of the four great elements.
The calculations of all attachments and pleasures are limited in this way across the six realms;
yet the sphere of wisdom is beyond measure or limit.
Wisdom discerns the mind and its intentions, reaching unto every state of consciousness.
Having cultivated his own conduct, he leads and guides sentient beings.
Throughout the entire trichiliocosm, with its manifold colors;
he perceives clearly the forms of all classes of beings, even across infinite worlds.
Just as the sun travels its circuit, moving through the void above;
so too does this palace proceed, its radiance shining everywhere.
Guided by the wisdom of original non-being, it remains unmoving within the dharma-realm.
The nature of the common people is pure, universally illumined by the light of the Way.
Just as the fundamental nature of sentient beings resides within each of their bodies,
so too does [the Buddha] manifest before all multitudes, illuminating and transforming the heavens and the world.
Having attained mastery over one’s own body, one excels in the practice of non-substantiality;
manifesting a body that dwells in peace, it is adorned with all the marks and signs.
The lands of sentient beings are likewise so: bodies are received according to their transgressions and merits.
Various kinds of noble natures constitute the essence of the wisdom of the Dharma.
Taking emptiness as the realm of the body, one receives it through impartial karma;
manifesting various transformations of supernormal powers, one eliminates the manifold defilements of the common people.
The Ten Powers are vast and sovereign; through wisdom, they are infinitely expansive.
Having attained the noble illumination of wisdom, he gives rise to compassion and sympathetic pity.
This most supreme teaching of all generates the path of practice through the Dharma.
Guarding the three matters with vigilance, remain as unshakable as Mount Sumeru.
This is called the power of the World-Honored Ones; the gentle practitioner possesses a strength free from anger.
Such a person does not waver, and no maras can withstand them.
That which the Buddha has established is revered by both Śakra and Brahmā;
the Vajrapāṇi spirits constantly attend him with their power and might.
Thus, in this place of land, virtues are combined in an immeasurable way.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, one could not exhaust their limit.
I bow my head in refuge to all the Buddhas, numbering in the hundreds of millions and nayutas;
they have accomplished the supreme path, adorned as if in the robes of a sovereign king.
This is the ultimate ground of the Way, where Bodhisattvas gather;
having attained the state of a Great Brahmā, they possess the merits of various realms.
Proclaiming the activities of the Three Vehicles, they reach an infinite assembly of companions.
With a mind of loving-kindness as pure, The light of wisdom dispels all dust.
In the brief moment a thought is stirred, One reaches hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands;
Attaining the source of all meditative concentrations, As numerous as the atoms within a full world-system.
The valiant one beholds the realms, transforming sentient beings throughout the ten directions;
his vows are likewise thus, adorned with infinite majesty.
This is spoken as the essential summary: the eighth supreme mastery.
"Even if one were to spend a full billion kalpas, one could never exhaustively describe them.
When this eighth stage was being taught, at that very moment, ten billion buddha-fields shook; established by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, his inconceivable merit was most sublime.
He manifested immeasurable, wondrous radiance, universally appearing in all manner of physical forms to illuminate all lands and bring peace to all sentient beings.
Countless thousands of bodhisattvas dwelt in the void, their offerings surpassing those of the heavens.

The offerings presented to the Buddha were profound, transcendent, and extraordinary; the Great and Wondrous Devas, together with their retinues and the sovereign celestial beings, were all filled with joy, and they made offerings to the Honored One in various ways, serving that Ocean of Virtue.

Countless billions of celestial maidens, filled with joy and leaping for gladness, their faculties serene and harmonious, played exquisite music and struck heavenly instruments to make offerings to the Great Sage.

These various musical instruments, delighting the great and holy ones, produce hundreds of thousands of such sounds; their resonance is gentle and harmonious, tranquil and serene, dispelling all afflictions and weariness, and freeing one from all defilements and impurities.

Having relinquished his land, he has reached the ultimate truth and stands preeminent; for the sake of sentient beings, he travels throughout the ten directions, manifesting the supreme conduct revealed by Great Penetration. His resolve is like empty space, and his mind is likewise so.

The most honored among devas and supreme among humans, awakened with the utmost clarity, his profound and wondrous realm is bottomless in its merit; he adorns and purifies the ten directions, serves the gateway of the Way, and is the refuge for all sons of the Buddhas. Through the Way he reveals the immeasurable merits of the Buddha.

Practicing noble wisdom, they do not crave fixed paths; though remaining unmoved within a single buddha-field, they pervade all lands without defilement, universally approaching all classes of sentient beings with compassion and acting as their leaders.
He extinguishes all sounds and is free from conceptualization; yet the voice he utters is resonant, its expressions numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
If there are inferior sentient beings who hear his teaching, though their minds are base, they will turn their hearts toward him in devotion.
If they hear his voice, he appears before them as a holy being and transforms them according to their original conduct.

If there are sentient beings whose faculties are clear and penetrating, who take pleasure in causes and conditions, yet have no fixed aspiration, for them he manifests the meaning of the stainless clarity of wisdom.
If there are sentient beings whose hearts harbor compassion and whose minds cherish kindness and benevolence, the Buddha remains in their presence and diligently demonstrates right practice.

If there are sentient beings whose aspirations are directed toward the Most Honored One and whose minds delight in this Dharma, he manifests immeasurable Buddha-bodies for them, appearing through such transformations like a master of illusions.
Wherever he travels, he guides countless billions of trillions of beings.

In this way, the Son of the Buddha delights in the illusion of wisdom; manifesting all practices while remaining detached from all possessions, he proclaims hundreds of thousands of such voices—voices that are gentle, harmonious, and benevolent.

The devas and celestial maidens submitted themselves in the world; they remained silent and delighted in stillness. The assembled multitude rejoiced, singing praises of his peaceful dwelling; his meritorious virtues were so lofty and immeasurable that they could not be fully described.
It is said that this Bodhisattva, in the eighth stage of the path, practices the True Dharma and attains penetration into the Mahāyāna.
Chapter Nine: The Stage of Excellent Resolve. In the *Anupūrvasamudgata-parivarta*, Vajragarbha said:
"Listen, O Son of the Buddha!
The wisdom-practices of the Buddhas for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas are thus immeasurable.

Increasing further still, they dwell in profound stillness, with their resolve set upon the gates of liberation. Through the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, they augment supreme virtue; furthermore, by means of a benevolent mind, they practice that which is the secret of the Tathāgatas.

Because one can enter this Great Way through wisdom that is inconceivable, selecting the ultimate essentials, maintaining the pure samādhi of dhāraṇī and right reception, relinquishing all that is non-virtuous, and performing pure deeds to guide and benefit all; one achieves great supernormal powers that are vast and far-reaching, discerning the worlds and instructing the masses, proceeding alone and unaccompanied.
The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas are without equal.
Having perfected the foundation of the Path, the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, turns the wheel of Dharma and leads beings toward the realm of ultimate destination.
Establishing great compassion and abiding in the great vows, they do not forsake the ten directions and enter the ninth stage of the bodhisattva path.
Having dwelt in this stage, they possess conduct that is neither fixed nor wavering; regarding the minds of good and evil, they know them with thorough discernment.

They make offerings to the sutras and serve the Truly Realized Ones, as well as all phenomena with outflows and without outflows—each according to mundane laws and the laws for transcending the world.
Their contemplative practice is inconceivable; they follow and uphold the ultimate, yet do not seek definitive resolution regarding phenomena.
They follow the teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas while practicing as bodhisattvas, honoring this path and making vows according to the stages of the Tathāgata’s way.

Arriving at the proper time, they approach conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) while their aspirations are set upon unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), knowing them with precise discernment.

With such luminous wisdom, they awaken to and understand the destination of all things; they discern and know the mental activities of sentient beings, their inclinations toward acceptance or rejection, the defilements of worldly toil, and the fortune or misfortune they receive. They grasp the functioning of the various faculties, have profound faith in the various destinies and the nature of the mind, and understand the locus where the various fetters and karmic formations arise. They clearly comprehend the places of birth and reception, the abodes where one dwells, and they definitively resolve the three clusters [of suffering].
He knows with precise discernment the destinations to which karma leads. He observes the minds of sentient beings and their conduct, whether right or wrong;

he perceives the various types of mind, how that mind advances or recedes in an instant, whether it coalesces or disperses. That mind has no physical body and cannot be delimited; it arises universally, manifesting its brilliance. Whether the mind is like dust or free from the afflictions of dust (*kleśa*), whether it is bound or liberated—knowing the mind to be like a magical illusion, he understands its points of return and abiding, its causes and conditions, and its advances and retreats. Furthermore, regarding those afflictions that wander far into the profound depths, he treats them for the sake of the future, so that those of similar kind may become free of karma. He understands the causes and conditions of all fetters, the places where they dwell and roam, and how the mind gathers together in a single location.

If there is separation, wherever one is born, and throughout all present activities—whether moving forward, stopping, walking, or coming—one shall discern the sufferings of the three realms: the sicknesses of craving, ignorance, and various views; the pride, folly, and boundless sins and calamities. These shall be severed and extinguished, as one comes to understand and know with certainty the treasures of the Tripitaka.

Entering into the calculation of permanence, there are eighty-four thousand varieties of defiled and afflictive conduct; before the meanings of sin and merit, good and evil, have been resolved, one instructs and informs ignorance, causing the faction of the distracted mind to engage in no other activity, contemplating the manifold blessings so as to bring about retribution, and accumulating various benefits such that the actions performed by those one holds dear do not fail to yield their fruits.
What is reported is without report; darkness is clear and bright, and there is no attachment to white through obscurity. Such words and the karmic retribution for one's conduct have their limits.

The field of merit for offenses is immeasurable; as the worthy and sages dwell in the world, they carry out their governing deeds, wherein present sins and blessings, as well as those to be cultivated in the future, may be further traversed.
He understands the destination toward which the vehicle proceeds, yet he does not grasp at that destination; he clearly comprehends and distinguishes skillful means according to the times.
He constantly and equanimously recognizes the eighty-four thousand varieties of offenses, knowing with precision their origins and their destinations.

He thoroughly understands the roots of the faculties—whether weak, middling, or clear—and to state the essentials: according to the original nature of sentient beings, their past lives, their deeds of destruction, their indestructible karma, their subtle or middling states, their inferior conduct, their association with the defilements, and their lack of wealth or merit.

From the mind of fundamental practice, one is able to achieve decisive understanding; yet if one does not achieve decisive understanding, though one may transform others with true sincerity, the net of the sense-faculties will lead to differentiation and regression, causing one to grasp at manifold conceptualizations.

Regarding the various marks, whether noble or inferior, he moves and returns with unimpeded progress and retreat; he understands and elucidates the three periods of time, traveling infinitely far and wandering alone without peer. Toward the various categories of beings, he always maintains equanimity, and he is fully able to know the eighty-four thousand diverse types of faculties.

To state the essentials: whether their faith and joy be of the superior, inferior, or intermediate kind, and whether their faculties be clear and penetrating, he always follows the eighty-four thousand variations of those faculties; whatever deep faith they harbor, he fully understands and clarifies it all.

There are various kinds of conduct among sentient beings; their realms may be weak or inferior, or they may be intermediate and discerning. Following the eighty-four thousand faculties, the various types of the four great elements, and the superior, middling, and inferior dispositions, as well as the nature of their good and evil conduct, he thoroughly understands the destinations to which these faculties lead. He comprehends their mental natures and behaviors, the companionship of their minds, the factions they form through their aspirations, how their minds converge, and how they may also be separated.

Traveling far into the profound and remote reaches, he may appear to have self-importance, yet he has no self-importance; his mind is harmonious and compliant, free from all weariness, and never lax or negligent.

All [beings] rely upon the gate of single-minded liberation, the samādhi of correct reception, and the appropriateness of supernormal powers; yet they lack true union and remain bound and attached to the three realms. They aspire to reach the heart of reality, where they do not practice various conditioned activities, but practice entering the gateway of the Way, which is beyond verbal instruction.

Not relying on factions or parties, possessing no wealth, occupation, or affairs, being without distinction or companions, he cultivates the gateway to the Path and knows with precise discernment what is correct.

Regarding the conduct of sentient beings, there are various categories; according to the conduct in their places of birth and how they abide in that conduct, they are born within the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

He fully understands the abodes where asuras, devas, and human beings take refuge, the places of birth for those in the realms of form and formlessness, and the places of birth for those with perception and without perception.

The retribution for sins and blessings arises from affection, desire, and lust; through the darkness of ignorance, the spirit undergoes rebirth again and again. With name-and-form as its companion and employing no path of practice, one is deluded by the cycle of birth and death. By associating with those who are fond of affection, one incurs greed and desire, yearning for emotional love. If one does not long for worldly glory—the pleasures of sentient beings within the three realms—and maintains a mind fixed upon ultimate reality, remaining free from harm, one will thoroughly and clearly understand the abiding place of one’s own will and conduct.

That which one ought to practice is the destination toward which the Tathāgata turns; it is bound to where habitual tendencies reside. Following the conduct of sentient beings, each according to their demerit and merit, they habituate themselves to worldly afflictions.
Good and evil have not yet been proclaimed; the deeds performed from beginning to end revolve without limit, turning and circling back again.

Returning to the fundamental conduct one has practiced, there is no traveling far away that can sever what is difficult to sever. To uproot the dust of lust and the empty affairs of greed and jealousy cannot be accomplished abruptly.
When the mind becomes clear and enlightened, one is then able to transcend; regarding all that is done, reaching the state of non-existence, one knows it all with thorough and precise discernment.

Regarding the conduct of sentient beings—whether their resolutions are firm or wavering, whether their will is set upon wrong actions, or whether they rush toward contrary views—one applies the karma of folly and delusion to right view, remains fixed in right action, and eliminates all fears, such that there is nothing that does not reach ultimate completion.

Furthermore, regarding the calamities that arise between the five heinous crimes, one thoroughly investigates and clarifies the five faculties to attain the practice of true and correct enlightenment; thereby, one abandons fear and reaches the ultimate state.

He clearly understands the cessation of the deviant and the sublime tranquility, as well as the matters of transgression, causing them to incline toward karma that leads to stillness and ultimately return to nowhere.

Yet, having fallen into deviant karma and turning back from their practice, he guides and shows them the unsurpassed right path of the worthies and sages; if they do not reach a definitive resolution, he unties their entanglements according to the occasion, protecting their karma.

All that has been proclaimed should be known with complete truth: if a son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, takes refuge in this wisdom, he shall attain the establishment of the excellent stage of mind, the dwelling of a bodhisattva.

"Once one dwells in this stage, one is able to fully comprehend the karmic activities of all sentient beings; according to their accumulated practices, one should liberate and transform them as they ought to be liberated."

He is able to enlighten sentient beings by instructing them according to the proper time; he knows how to encourage and guide śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and transforms bodhisattvas by expounding the stages of the Tathāgata. He preaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to their dispositions, leading, benefiting, and liberating them in accordance with their respective natures and behaviors.

From the fundamental root and source, one should preach the Dharma for the sake of liberation; according to their conduct, one further traverses from the beginning to the end to bring about transformation and enlightenment.
According to the vehicle upon which they ride, one cultivates the gates of contemplation and liberation; by means of those gates of liberation, one proclaims and disseminates the Way and its Dharma.
Abiding in this stage of the path, one beholds the flourishing of the great Dharma-preacher, who protects the Tathāgata’s infinite treasury of the Dharma.

If one should go to where that Dharma-preacher dwells, one shall consult him regarding the entry into the immeasurable, clearly comprehend noble wisdom, and practice and proclaim it; through the four analytical eloquences, one shall carry out the conduct of a bodhisattva.
In accordance with the Dharma they preach, they constantly practice it without any impairment.
These Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas possess the four analytical eloquences and roam within the stage of non-retrogression.
What are the four? First is the discernment of phenomena; second is the thorough understanding of meaning; third is following the proper sequence; and fourth is the mastery of eloquence.
What is called "discriminating phenomena" refers to clearly proclaiming the natural characteristics of all dharmas;
"understanding the meaning" refers to being able to explain and elucidate the ultimate destination of the dharmas;
and "following the sequence" refers to speaking with unimpaired discernment regarding the profound and far-reaching wisdom that analyzes all dharmas.
One who possesses the eloquence of liberation is without any fetters or bonds and knows that phenomena are uninterrupted.

To discern and eloquently explain the Dharma and to clearly understand phenomena means to realize that phenomena are of the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), and that this is the body of spontaneity.
One who understands the definitive meaning knows through illumination that all things return to the scriptures.
One who follows the proper sequence elucidates all dharmas; they should be expounded and proclaimed without interruption.
As for those who analyze and debate, they propagate [the teaching] boundlessly according to its path, without any expectation of gain.
As for those who understand and expound the Dharma, they penetrate the present phenomena and clarify the ultimate destination of what is proclaimed.
One who clearly understands the definitive meaning knows the principle of the retribution and response of dharmas past and future.
One who follows the proper sequence explains and resolves all dharmas of the past, future, and present without causing any contradiction or destruction.

As for the one who excels in analytical discernment, in every single teaching they deliver, they remain free from dualistic thought and without limit; they radiate the light of the Dharma, clarify and expound the sound of the Dharma, are able to recognize all phenomena, and analyze and distinguish all matters.
One who understands the definitive meaning discerns all meanings so that none fail to receive compassion.
One who follows the proper sequence preaches the Dharma according to the sounds, languages, and distances of sentient beings.
As for those who analyze and debate, they observe the mental activities of all sentient beings and thus expound the sutras.
As for those who understand and elucidate the Dharma, they are proficient in skillful means, clearly discern the wisdom that disperses phenomena, and do not destroy the various virtues.
One who clearly understands the definitive meaning possesses the wisdom that is fundamentally non-abiding and non-dual; thus, for the sake of the common people, each may come to understand it.
One who follows the proper sequence expounds upon karma, which is the indestructible wealth of noble wisdom.
One who excels in analytical discernment thoroughly elucidates the principles of various doctrines according to their timely significance and understands both the beginning and the end.

One who thoroughly elucidates the Dharma knows that all phenomena are fundamentally one; having lost sight of this original source, they follow the current into the cycle of birth and death, revolving without end.

One who thoroughly understands the definitive meaning is able to transcend the five aggregates and the four great elements, as well as the eighteen kinds of decay and the various sense bases; through skillful means they attain liberation, clearly perceiving that the twelve links of dependent origination are entirely without beginning or end.

As for the sequential order, it proclaims the origin of all sentient beings, their circulation through the five destinies, their gentle and refined dispositions, and their soft voices, which are universally received by those who hear them.

As for those who analyze and debate, they expound the essential teachings; their illumination increases further and further without limit, its radiance shining afar to dispel the darkness of ignorance, such that there are none who do not receive its light.

Those who understand and expound the Dharma guide and benefit beings of a single class; there are no distinctions among these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who give rise to infinite compassion, establish inexhaustible pity, and develop the Mahāyāna.

One who clearly understands the definitive meaning distinguishes the various vehicles and brings beings across their respective limits; through vast and transcendent practice, they are serene and peerless, walking alone amidst the great assembly.

As for following the proper sequence, one proclaims all the various vehicles according to their respective aspirations; without causing any disruption among those of superior, middling, or inferior learning, one gradually guides and encourages them to enter the Great Way.

As for those who discern and debate, they establish the One Vehicle which is without limit; they proclaim the True Dharma, brilliantly illuminating the calamities of suffering within the three realms, removing the hindrances of the aggregates, and attaining samādhi.

Those who comprehend and elucidate the Dharma honor the karmic activities of the noble wisdom of all bodhisattvas; they cultivate and practice the path with such transcendent clarity that it is lofty and immeasurable.

Those who understand the definitive meaning expound upon the origins and conclusions of the ten stages of abiding, providing insight so that learners each attain their proper place, do not lose their resolve or conduct, and achieve liberation from the mundane world, reaching mastery in all things.

As for those who follow the sequential order, they proclaim the prohibitions of the Dharma so that each may pursue their aspirations; they cherish the teachings of the Way without causing any destruction.

As for those who possess analytical discernment, they proclaim all practices without limit, expounding upon fundamental karma until the attainment of true and perfect enlightenment, rather than remaining within the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

One who thoroughly understands the Dharma attains realization spontaneously; all Tathāgatas are but a single Buddha, and their powers are immeasurable. Having awakened to this meaning, they consequently turn the wheel of Dharma, reaching omniscience and thereby delivering sentient beings.

One who thoroughly understands the definitive meaning can further discern the various types of consciousness, establishing them in the correct and true state; in a mere moment, they distinguish the destinations to which they lead, as well as the right and wrong of both the monastic and the secular, proclaiming them all without exception.

As for following the proper sequence: according to his perfect awakening, he analyzes and explains through speech; he contemplates their roots—the superior, middling, and inferior capacities, and the depth or shallowness of their minds—and thereby brings them to transformation and enlightenment.

As for the one who possesses analytical eloquence, the dharmas he proclaims—each and every chapter and phrase—expound manifold meanings with wisdom that is boundless, uninterrupted, and satisfies all hunger and emptiness.

One who elucidates the Dharma universally invokes the teachings and exhortations spread by the Tathāgata: all the ten powers and fearlessnesses, the dharmas of the Buddhas, the eighteen unique qualities, the cultivation of great compassion, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the infinite, penetrating wisdom of all things.

One who thoroughly understands the definitive meaning recognizes the eighty-four thousand various types of conduct among sentient beings; according to their dispositions and natures, and by examining their roots, they proclaim the voice of the Tathāgata in accordance with their inclinations and faith, thereby dispersing their knots of affliction.

As for following the proper sequence: regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one does not cause them to be destroyed; one utters the lion’s roar, produces the voice of the Tathāgata, and the sounds of the eight classes of beings are heard throughout the ten directions, penetrating and perceiving the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

As for the one who discriminates and expounds, he manifests the majestic spiritual light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, eliminating the darkness, obscurity, blindness, and obstructions of the multitudes. Relying on the power of his own practice at the site of enlightenment, he transforms beings according to their inclinations and faiths, causing each to attain their proper place.
Vajragarbha said: "Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
For the ninth bodhisattva who is established in the ninth stage, the foundation of his wisdom and virtue is as magnificent as this."

With eloquence such as this, he has attained the Tathāgata’s infinite treasury of the Way and become a great Dharma Master. He establishes the vessel of meaning and acts as a sovereign of meaning; having realized the phrases of meaning and the profound, wondrous dhāraṇīs, he gathers and rescues the three realms as the Lord of Dharma who upholds all.

To state the essentials: by means of noble wisdom and supernormal powers, one employs them for deliverance; the *dhāraṇī* of illuminating light shines throughout the ten directions; the *dhāraṇī* of benevolent intention encompasses all intentions; the *dhāraṇī* like the earth has conduct as vast as space; and the essential *dhāraṇī* of sovereign majesty is an infinite Dharma-gate that is difficult even for a celestial lord to attain.

That which is directed toward total retention (dhāraṇī) and that in which one wanders infinitely; the revolving dhāraṇī through which one circulates and comes and goes; and the attainment of various kinds of skillful means (upāya) dhāraṇīs—one is fully endowed with and possesses all such categories.

He has attained ten hundred thousand incalculable *dhāraṇīs*; his voice reaches all according to what is appropriate, and the gates of his discernment are immeasurable. He proclaims the sūtras beyond the capacity of words to record; such are the *dhāraṇīs* that cannot be limited or recorded, for they are the gateway to the Path of the True Dharma.

They hear the immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifesting their bodies to expound the Dharma, and hearing it, they do not forget; what they have heard they proclaim extensively beyond the reach of ordinary discourse, and in the presence of each and every Tathāgata, they inquire, receive, recite, and chant ten times immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇīs.

Just as there is no limit to the number of beings who can be transformed and guided by a single Tathāgata, so too is the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, equal and without distinction.

While he was prostrating himself, his merit increased even further; from countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, he received dharma-gates that neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas could fully describe or record, as well as the vast learning, the reception of sounds, and the dhāraṇīs he had cultivated.

One who attains this dhāraṇī establishes acts of grace; through the dhāraṇī of virtue, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they attain such a retention and achieve eloquence, thereby establishing it.

When such a majestic Dharma and its assembly of noble ones gather together, they fill the entirety of all three thousandfold world systems, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate for the minds of sentient beings to be transformed.

Seated upon the Dharma-throne, he received the instructions of the Tathāgata and attained the stage of the tenth dwelling, the *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) ground. Among all others, he was sovereign and peerless; his majesty had no equal. His radiance reached everywhere, shining upon all things. Seated upon the Dharma-throne, in a mere moment, at the very instant he first resolved his mind, he manifested various sounds from a single voice, proclaiming them universally to the assembled multitude. Simultaneously, light issued from his mouth, and from all his pores there issued forth every sound, spreading the transformative teachings of the Way so that there was nothing they did not understand.
It illuminated the trichiliocosm as well as the realms of both form and formlessness, everywhere proclaiming the sound of the Dharma.
