At that time, all sentient beings throughout that great trichiliocosm came together at once to inquire about the principles of meaning; each expounded their own views and questioned on countless matters, yet without needing to ask twice, everyone attained understanding and liberation.
At that time, in a single moment, the Bodhisattva received all sounds; whatever voices were proclaimed, he universally announced them all through a single word of teaching.

To state the essentials: throughout two or three thousand great chiliocosms, or four, three, five, ten, twenty, fifty, and even up to a hundred thousand great chiliocosms—indeed, across incalculable numbers of great chiliocosms.

The Light performs Dharma-activities, establishing the majestic power and holy intent of the Tathāgata; always acting in accordance with the proper time, it brings forth Buddha-works for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having been initiated and established, it further progresses; through such noble wisdom, it receives and radiates light while practicing diligence.

Suppose that from each and every pore there were as many atoms as would fill boundless Buddha-worlds; suppose one were to behold such an incalculable number of Buddha-lands, along with their assemblies gathered at the sites of enlightenment, proclaiming the scriptures. Each and every Tathāgata therein would, for the sake of countless classes of sentient beings and various multitudes of people, untie the knots of their afflictions.

The mental dispositions harbored by each and every sentient being are beyond measure; their minds are each different. Yet, one exhorts and benefits them with the Dharma, transforming and enlightening them just as a single Tathāgata brings them to liberation.

All Tathāgatas are likewise thus, equal and without distinction; as it is with a single pore, so it is with all, for they all proclaim the sound of the Dharma. We who study should also be like this: we shall broaden our resolve, contemplate the meaning of the Vaipulya sūtras, and lead those who have not yet reached [enlightenment]. At one and the same time, all Tathāgatas universally manifest their bodies, and all receive the illumination of the Dharma. This is all through a single voice, according to what each delights in and in accordance with what they praise.

When assemblies of sentient beings fill the site of enlightenment, and those who wish to hear the Dharma are fully present in their entirety, we too shall likewise act in that same manner toward them.

With the light of wisdom and penetrating eloquence, through pure deeds, they gladden and liberate sentient beings in a single moment. Their bodies traverse various worlds, reaching all sentient beings who have attained this stage of the Bodhisattva path.

Day and night they advance further, their thoughts remaining unwavering; they enter the practice of the Buddha-way, attain the Tathāgata’s teaching of equality, and reach the profound and wondrous gates of liberation of the bodhisattvas.

By entering into this wisdom, one constantly beholds all Buddhas and is never separated from them; within each eon, one perceives countless billions of hundreds of thousands of kotis of Tathāgatas, making offerings to and serving them.
Questioning all Tathāgatas and receiving their teachings, they uphold the sūtras and proclaim them far and wide.

The root of their merit thus flourishes even more, surpassing all without peer; it is like a Buddha-son or a master craftsman of supreme skill who can fashion necklaces, refining and adorning them with beauty to present as an offering to a Cakravartin King.

The precious jade woman was tied around his neck; she was magnificent beyond compare, radiantly brilliant, and while he stayed atop all the high terraces and towers at dusk, she shone universally upon all the four quarters of the world.
The necklaces of sentient beings are obscured and do not appear, while [the bodhisattva] alone shines forth brilliantly.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the practice of this, he dwells in the path of the noble-minded *kalyāṇamitra*.
The root of his merit becomes increasingly flourishing, surpassing all comparison and exceeding the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Transcending the stages from the initial aspiration through the seventh and eighth abodes, the clarity of his root of virtue extinguishes the afflictions of sentient beings, illuminating them all.

From this they receive grace, turning from evil toward good and abandoning the secular world to enter the Path, becoming like sons of the Buddha. Like the light of Great Brahmā, which pervades all the three-thousandfold world systems, its brilliance reaches everywhere, and all people are illumined by it.

In this way, the Bodhisattva dwells in this "Excellent" stage of the Path of the Kāśyapa-like Bodhisattva; with the radiant brilliance of all roots of virtue, he universally illumines sentient beings. His noble wisdom reaches afar, and by the light of the Dharma, he dispels the dust of darkness for all, causing everyone to turn away from the mundane and proceed toward the Path.
This, O Son of the Buddha,
is called the ninth stage of the path for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, known as the Teaching of Equanimity and the Vast and Profound Practice of the "Excellent Mind."
To proclaim its virtues would be impossible to exhaust or reach the limit of even throughout incalculable kalpas;
no one could ever fathom it. "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, whether as a Brahmā or as a Mahābrahmā King, he attains sovereign mastery over the trichiliocosm."

He establishes the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and the practices of the bodhisattvas; he expounds the *pāramitās* with peerless clarity, inquiring into the fundamental nature and origins of sentient beings' inclinations and their cultivation of the path. He bestows gifts upon others with kindness, treats them with love, respect, harmony, and gentleness, benefiting and enriching them, and equally encourages the sharing of wealth. By means of these four debts of gratitude, he universally rescues all beings.
By accumulating such merit, one constantly evokes mindfulness of the Buddha; with the mind never straying far, one eventually attains full mastery and achieves all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

Never forgetting this contemplation, how can one reach the state of supreme and infinite honor among all sentient beings, becoming a universal sage (*samantabhadra*) who leads those who have not yet reached it? At the very moment of resolving the mind, such is the manifestation of these forms and images.

Diligently cultivating vigor, in a single moment, he fully and completely attains the meditative absorptions of the ten countless hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands, filling them with as many atoms as there are.

He saw all these bodhisattvas gathered as an assembly of great beings, numbering like the dust motes in ten incalculable Buddha-lands, brought together through the power of their supreme and wondrous vows. The aspirations of these bodhisattvas were so extraordinary that their transformations and manifestations could not be fully described; they remained inconceivable even throughout incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* of infinite eons.
At that time, Vajragarbha, wishing to expand upon this meaning and further elaborate its intent, spoke these verses:
"This power is immeasurable; It is the practice of the Buddha’s essential path.
This subtle and wondrous wisdom is supreme, Yet difficult for sentient beings to comprehend."
Thus abiding in the secret treasury, the World-Honored One personally upholds it;
for the sake of sentient beings, one attains entry into the ninth stage.
By this, one reaches the dhāraṇī and the unsurpassed sovereignty of samādhi.
The vast and universal karma of supernormal powers pervades all lands;
Through the power of decisive understanding of noble wisdom, he manifests in the most excellent abodes;
With a resolute vow and a heart of compassion, he correctly dwells and enters the ninth stage.
By penetrating this stage of the path, one attains the supreme, victorious treasury;
it is the essential core of the truly wondrous Dharma, wherein the meaning and virtue are not conceptually differentiated.
This pertains both to those in conditioned, outflowing practices and to the bodies of worldly worthies and sages.
This mind is inconceivable; the Honored One has awakened to the ultimate meaning.
He discerns and elucidates all phenomena, contemplating them to their final conclusion;
he accomplishes the works of the Three Vehicles, weighing and calculating all that is done.
Whether conditioned or unconditioned, one understands through realization what ought to be practiced;
engaging in both matters, one enters accordingly in accordance with the world.
By entering such wisdom, the mind becomes subtle and extraordinary.
Gathering in the minds of sentient beings, one contemplates their origins and ends.
The mind is manifold like a painting, shifting and revolving afar;
its consciousness is limitless, radiantly pervading all.
The various gateways of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are difficult to cure even with companions;
they are the locus where the many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are received, and the source of suffering through constant association.
Their various manifestations enter into the analysis of karma.
Below this, there is no retribution; causes and conditions have been extinguished.
There are those who enter through the faculties of clear penetration—whether weak, inferior, or intermediate.
Having eliminated all that is past, they penetrate downward to the meaning of the future.
With profound faith in the immeasurable, whether pure or impure;
Pervading the eighty thousand practices, and further, the four thousand matters.
If one enters into various categories, one becomes a fool, a dust of false views.
Because of this, one undergoes wandering, boundless and impossible to sever.
The fetters of the mind roam together with its factions;
when the mind thus reflects upon them, its bondage is without end.
The path of their dispositions and natures is such that the manifold fetters still obscure the moon;
they have no permanent abode, nor do they dwell in fixed residence.
For this reason, it is difficult to transform them through assemblies, and the realm of men does not return to its source.
Severed by the diamond sword, its path remains undifferentiated.
Entering through various divisions and following their courses, one is born within the realms of the six destinies;
the moisture of desire and passion, and the fields of merit for the sins of ignorance.
The divine consciousness sows the seeds; conditioned formations constitute name-and-form.
Abiding within the three realms, its wanderings are boundless.
Even reaching the seats of the gods, it follows the movements of the mind amidst the dust of affliction.
Wandering everywhere throughout all realms, one thus returns once more to birth and death.
Sentient beings abide within the three categories, which causes them to come and go;
the fires of various false views then plant the traces of the consciousness-essence.
Practicing in this manner, they abide in this stage of the path;
according to the mental dispositions of sentient beings, they understand their various faculties and respond accordingly.
For their sake, they preach the Dharma and proclaim its various distinctions.
Discerning this principle and meaning, with skillful means and true eloquence;
if one approaches the place where the Dharma Master dwells, he immediately arrives at his abode;
his speech is free from attachment, like Mount Sumeru.
The rain is soft and moistening; the nectar universally drenches all beings.
The faculties and powers of the awakened mind are as full as the ocean.
Understanding the wisdom of excellent meaning, the comprehension of phenomena is likewise so.
All things are utterly extinguished, and one attains supreme eloquence;
having acquired countless insights and ten thousand dhāraṇīs,
by grasping the essentials of all dharmas, one rains them down like a great ocean.
Possessing such dhāraṇīs, they attain the pure samādhi;
in a single moment, they behold countless hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas.
Having heard the treasure of the Dharma, they proclaim it repeatedly.
Their speech is fluent and pure, with naturally wondrous voices.
In the brief span of a single thought, they know the three thousandfold world-system;
they perceive the various inclinations of all beings gathered in the assembly.
He can delight all beings according to their minds and faculties;
his entry [into the world] is likewise, like the great oceans of the four quarters.
His virtue surpasses even this; in brief, he brings about the perfection of diligence.
His contemplations are like the sands of the Ganges, truly beyond all measure.
Abiding securely, he speaks only the Dharma to transform ordinary sentient beings;
hearing it, they immediately receive and uphold it, just as one sows seeds in the earth.
Even if all sentient beings, dwelling throughout the realms of the ten directions,
were to be gathered so that they all sat together in one place—
their respective natures, conducts, and thoughts could all be fully and universally known.
Then, with a single sound, they can universally satisfy all;
the Honored One among Men abides herein, the Supreme Dharma King;
advancing further through all lands, he brings the Sons of the World-Honored One to fulfillment.
Always at peace day and night, they attain victory in accordance with their aspirations;
dwelling in profound, wondrous tranquility, they enter the gate of liberation through courageous wisdom.
They serve with single-minded devotion, making offerings and paying homage to billions of Buddhas.
His realization is as lofty as the Way; his adornments revolve like a wheel.
His radiance dispels the toil of afflictions, and what he receives manifests majestic brilliance;
like the light of Brahmā, it illuminates the three thousandfold world system.
Merit and virtue abide herein; he upholds the infinite Brahmā-heaven.
The Buddha analyzes and explains with liberation, establishing the three vehicles.
Diligently practicing what there is to be done, he takes pity upon the masses of living beings.
By entering into all-knowledge, one attains the virtue of noble wisdom.
Though lands are incalculable, even reaching as far as the city of Rājagṛha,
one contemplates their majestic power all at once through a samādhi that pervades the ten directions.
Beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions, whose voices as benefactors are gentle and soft;
they give rise to subtle and wondrous vows, their minds being without limit or boundary.
This is the ninth dwelling, profound, subtle, and difficult to comprehend.
Having established himself in peace, he himself proclaimed the practices of the Mahāyāna.

Billions of devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens gathered for this assembly; hearing such unsurpassed and correct teaching on practice, they remained in the air, their hearts leaping with joy, and with reverence and humility, they attended upon him as he dwelt in peace.

The assembly of bodhisattvas, numbering immeasurable billions, dwelling in the void, their hearts filled with joy, rained down a profusion of flowers and incense that brought infinite delight and utterly scorched the defilements of the afflictions of sentient beings.

The Sovereign King of Heaven was filled with great joy; dwelling upon it together with billions of attendants, with hearts of profound reverence, they scattered various exquisite robes. The Brahmā heavens and others, in silent wonder at these rare treasures, single-mindedly took refuge.
The hosts of jade maidens, with countless joyful countenances, played hundreds of thousands of millions of musical instruments and likewise prostrated themselves.
All together they produced such sounds as these; the retinue of the World-Honored One sat pervading the Buddha-land, their radiance shining forth and illuminating all the buddha-fields.
Throughout billions of kalpas, his various bodies are supple and pervasive throughout the entire Dharma-realm, reaching everywhere without exception.
When the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, emits light from a single pore, that radiance is so brilliant that it extinguishes the dust of sentient beings.

The dust motes of the buddha-fields may yet be counted to their end, but the number of people in this assembly cannot be measured. At times, the Buddha’s body—with its subtle and wondrous marks—is beheld by all;

and when the various wheel-turning kings travel to other lands, performing supreme and most magnificent deeds, they behold celestial beings, sages, and great divine honors. Abiding in the Tuṣita Heaven, he manifests his descent into the mother’s womb, and again his birth; though still within the womb, he manifests in countless billions of lands. Upon being born and falling to the ground, he manifests his buddha-field. By the original vow of the Guide, for the sake of sentient beings, he renounces the world, attains the way of the Buddha, becomes the Most Perfectly Awakened One, turns the wheel of Dharma, and manifests all buddha-fields.
For countless billions of years, he was like a master illusionist who, having skillfully learned the arts of incantations, manifests countless illusions throughout his entire lifespan.

In this same way, the World-Honored One cultivated and studied wisdom; for the sake of sentient beings, he further left the household life. All phenomena are empty, tranquil, and silent, fundamentally pure and signless, equal in all respects, just like space.

The Buddha’s teachings and precepts are fundamentally and most beneficially non-existent; his manifestations are supreme, and his dwelling places and all modes of abiding in peace are entirely spontaneous.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, he attains the realization of the sūtras; he perceives the mark of all marks as the mark of equality regarding all phenomena—the supreme signlessness, the meaning of the benefits for all beings, and that from which noble wisdom proceeds. Having completely relinquished all marks, whether they pertain to the realm of perception or non-perception, he understands all conditioned formations with equanimity and swiftly achieves preeminence among the masses.
Such sounds, numbering countless billions, proclaim a voice of harmony and gentleness; dwelling in the world, they subdue the hosts of Māras and celestial maidens, thereby making known the assembly.
The Perfectly Realized One is tranquil and still, like the full moon shining fiercely upon the world.

Furthermore, Vajragarbha, when various chapters were being expounded, the sons of the Buddha—who cultivate the tenfold karma of the Mahāyāna—should put them into practice. As they perform these various household-like deeds and meritorious works, and as auspicious signs appear, their hearts are filled with joy; those of superior and noble wisdom all join in singing praises.
The Scripture on the Gradual Preparation for All-Wisdom and Virtue, Scroll Four; The Scripture on the Gradual Preparation for All-Wisdom and Virtue, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Western Jin Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master from Yuezhi, Zhu Fahu.
Chapter Ten: The Questions of Vajragarbha on the Bodhisattva Abodes. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra:
"In this regard, O Son of the Buddha, the noble wisdom-intent of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas is sublime and immeasurable; such are their practices and deeds, continuing even unto the ninth abode."

He purifies the stages of the path, fully possessing the pure and radiant Dharma that is without limit; accumulating merit and virtue, he disciplines himself in every birth. Thinking, "If I do not benefit sentient beings, by what skillful means can I rescue those in the three realms? he carefully and rightly gathers them in.
Possessing boundless wisdom and virtue, his compassion is inexhaustible; the scope of his entry is vast and expansive, circulating everywhere without exception.
He discerns the worlds with clarity regarding their boundlessness; he enters the realms of sentient beings, moving in silent cycles, ending and beginning again.

This refers to opening the first treasury of the Tathāgata’s path of practice, the contemplations one reflects upon, the powers and fearlessnesses, the sūtras of all Buddhas, the emptiness and immeasurability, as well as all keen wisdom—fully accomplishing and attaining the state of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is what it means.

Furthermore, O Sons of the Buddha! Entering such noble karmic activities of Bodhisattvas, they draw near to the stage of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having just settled therein, there is a samādhi named "Stainless" (*vimala*). The Bodhisattva personally manifests and proclaims the Dharma-realm; the Bodhisattva’s site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is called "Pure Adornment," "Vast Ocean Treasury," "Ocean Seal," "As Vast as Space," "Accumulation of All Dharmas Spontaneously," and "Mental Activities of Sentient Beings. Through such categories, they attain nearly hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya concentrations of the True Dharma. Having attained these various concentrations, they employ correct reception (*samāpatti*) to personally manifest the samādhi of manifold virtuous qualities and bestow various skillful means upon all beings.

By means of these causes and conditions, such a state of meditative concentration thoroughly and fully manifests all keen wisdom in a most extraordinary manner; this is therefore called the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Approaching the Stage of Non-retrogression (A-vyaya).

Having attained this proximity, through this samādhi, the thirteen thousandfold world-systems naturally produced hundreds of thousands of infinite and inexhaustible wondrous jewels, pure lotus flowers, and the abodes of all things; these were the natural treasures of the Way, by which one transcends the entire dharma-realm, practices the principles of the Way to reach the truly correct Dharma, becomes fully endowed with the roots of all virtues that deliver the world, achieves ultimate perfection, and attains the profound spontaneity.
Furthermore, its Dharma-realm is well-cultivated and pure, radiating holy light; its stem is exceedingly vast, composed of lapis lazuli and bright moon-jewels, surpassing all the heavens.

Immeasurable sandalwood and various precious gems were interlaced together; with infinite agate and purple-polished true gold, they grew as flowers and leaves, their brilliance shining so radiantly that it could not be measured.
The lotus blossoms shone brilliantly, all composed of various precious gems.

Above them, in the void, canopies of exquisite jewels transformed into latticed pavilions, filling the entirety of the thirteen thousandfold great trichiliocosm. Within these, multitudes of beings as numerous as motes of dust were beyond calculation. Hundreds of thousands of lotuses were arrayed throughout the void of the ten directions; their fragrance was sweet and exquisite, perfuming the bodies of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and endowing them with all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).

If one attains this samādhi of the dwelling in the ultimate sovereignty (an-avaivarta), one will immediately appear seated upon this great lotus flower; once seated, all those to be transformed will likewise spontaneously arrange themselves in a complete assembly around him.

There were great lotus flowers beyond measure, surrounded by retinues of various bodhisattvas; seated upon these lotuses, they stood tall and majestic on all sides, and each individual bodhisattva attained hundreds of thousands of samādhis, remaining in meditative absorption.
Observing all the bodhisattvas who have thus attained meditative absorption, the boundless Buddha-fields of the ten directions are spontaneously pure.
The Tathāgatas, within their respective assemblies at the sites of enlightenment, illuminate them with the light of perfected teaching.

Why is this so? Furthermore, as soon as that bodhisattva sits upon these great lotus flowers, from the soles of his feet there issue ten incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, which illuminate the ten directions as far as the Avīci Hell, the great niraya, extinguishing the afflictions and sufferings of sentient beings.

The light emanating from his left and right knees was likewise exactly as described before, without any difference; it illuminated all hungry ghosts and animals, causing their diligent suffering and pain to cease.
From each of his left and right flanks, there issued forth infinite and countless rays of light, illuminating the people of the ten directions, so that all were bathed in radiance.
From the palms of his two hands, he likewise emanated light, which shone upon the palaces of the devas and asuras.
From his two shoulders and elbows, he emits light of the second grade, illuminating the assembly of śrāvakas.
From his back, the fontanelle, and his neck, he radiates light that illuminates the minds of the pratyekabuddhas throughout the ten directions.
From the gateway of his mouth, he emanated wondrous light that illuminated the assemblies of Bodhisattvas in the ninth stage throughout the ten directions.

From the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, he emanated a great majestic radiance that shone upon all the palaces of Māra throughout the ten directions, causing them all to be eclipsed in darkness.

With the body of an Avaivartika Bodhisattva, he ascended into the void and illuminated hundreds of thousands of incalculable trichiliocosm Buddha-fields in the ten directions. He circled the Buddhas—whose number was equal to the dust motes filling those fields—and their assemblies at their places of enlightenment ten times. Remaining in the void, he manifested a great radiance, a jeweled canopy of interlaced pearls called "Great Light."
Resplendent and brilliant, he used these to offer as a tribute to the Tathāgata, thereby increasing his merit and virtue.

By virtue of this offering, from the initial generation of the aspiration for enlightenment until reaching the ninth stage, he served and followed the Tathāgata, remaining tranquil and in harmony with the times; this merit was hundreds of thousands of billions of times greater, beyond all comparison.

The great luminous pearl-canopy was of such towering brilliance that its light reached all lands throughout the ten directions; it was spread everywhere with various flowers, mixed incenses, powdered perfumes, garments, banners, canopies, and streamers, and strewn with precious crystals and bright moon pearls, pervading all worlds in the ten directions to form a universal realm.

The roots of goodness and virtues of that unsurpassed, true, and correct [enlightenment] rained down great masses of flowers; each flower rained down various kinds of objects, making offerings to all the sites of enlightenment in the great assemblies and presenting them to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. Among the classes of sentient beings, whoever saw or knew this all conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment.
This rain of various flowers was thus subtle and wondrous.

Its light circled the assemblies and *bodhimaṇḍas* of all the Buddhas ten times; having completed these circuits, it entered beneath the feet of the Buddhas. The flower-light suddenly illuminated all the Tathāgatas and their multitudes of Bodhisattvas, who beheld those Buddha-worlds and saw the names of the Bodhisattvas established in such practices.
When he had attained the stage of *A-vyaya* (the Invincible), all the bodhisattvas from the boundless ten directions and those bodhisattvas of the ninth stage gathered together for this assembly.

These bodhisattvas and their retinues performed great offerings and, through the correct reception of samādhi, observed the situation throughout the ten directions. They beheld the assembly of *A-vyaya* bodhisattvas, whose heads were adorned with what is called the "Illusion-Crown," upon which a vajra was erected to subdue the hosts of Māra. From that single radiance, hundreds of thousands of lights were emitted, each producing countless brilliant attendants that illuminated the infinite Buddha-lands of the ten directions, manifesting great transformations.
That light, appearing in an instant, entered the illusory head and adorned the crown of the Bodhisattva.
Not long after it had vanished, the Bodhisattva was immediately suffused by its radiance; through its majestic spiritual power, his splendor became even more flourishing.

"At that time, O Son of the Buddha, there was another great light named 'All-Wisdom' (Sarvajñā), a holy lord of supernatural powers, which emerged from the *ūrṇā-kośa* between the eyebrows of each of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Each emitted an infinite retinue of radiance that illuminated the boundless worlds of the ten directions. Having circled the various Buddha-fields ten times, it manifested the infinite supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*) and transformative manifestations of all the Tathāgatas."

He addressed the assembly of countless billions of trillions of bodhisattvas; the buddha-fields shook in six ways, all evil realms were utterly extinguished, the palaces of Māra were eclipsed, and the buddhas of the ten directions all appeared spontaneously.

He universally manifested himself at the sites of enlightenment within the assemblies of those who have attained true and perfect awakening; majestic and pure, supreme throughout the Dharma-realm, he pervaded all of space, illuminating every world in the ten directions. The light then returned and, ascending into the void, circled clockwise around the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, manifesting great majesty and purity. These rays of light suddenly appeared above them and immediately entered the crowns of the heads of all the assembled bodhisattvas.

When this radiance vanished, these bodhisattvas, having never before experienced such a thing nor received such concentration, immediately attained one million samādhis by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic power.
These rays of light, when measured against the passage of time, descend upon the Bodhisattvas; they are all equal and without distinction.
When these lights vanish, the Bodhisattvas attain the state of *anuttara* (the Unsurpassed), which is called the realm of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One.

Possessing the ten powers and the perfect enlightenment, he is as level as space; like a son of the Buddha, he is like the eldest son of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), born from the womb of the noble and true queen, endowed with all the marks of excellence, and destined to be a holy king.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King sat upon a bed of purple gold atop a celestial jewel-elephant; he took the waters from the four great oceans and brought them there, holding a great parasol over him and adorning the scene with banners, streamers, and musical performances.

Taking a golden water-pitcher, the Wheel-Turning Sage King used the waters of the four oceans to wash the crown and body of the Prince; as soon as the bathing was completed, he was accordingly named King Śirighaṭa.

As for the Wheel-Turning King, because he is endowed with the ten roots of goodness, he is called a Divine Emperor and a Holy Wheel-Turner; such is the Buddha-son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who has accomplished great wisdom.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva practices for incalculable hundreds of thousands of eons, undergoing diligent hardships;
having thus fully perfected such meritorious wisdom, he further advances to the stage of the Path established therein, which is named "Dharma Rain," the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva dwells in the stage of the Way of the Rain of Dharma, they penetrate and understand the realm of desire, comprehending it exactly as it is; they practice the realm of form, practice the formless realm, the realm of sentient beings, the realm of non-perception, the realm of the conditioned and the unconditioned, and the realm of empty space; they practice the dharma-realm, comprehend nirvana, and know it exactly as it is.

He clearly understands that all views are a deceptive net that obstructs the five destinies and the defilements of worldly toil; he practices the various modes of arising and ceasing, the conduct of the śrāvakas, the conduct of the pratyekabuddhas, and the conduct of the bodhisattvas; he attains the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the form-body and the dharma-body, as well as omniscience; he achieves supreme perfect enlightenment and turns the wheel of Dharma; he manifests parinirvāṇa, yet always enters into all phenomena with equanimity; he discerns and transcends them, thoroughly understanding all habitual tendencies, and examining them as they arise from their origin.

By entering into this wisdom, their minds are further elevated, causing all classes of sentient beings to be free from the karma of self-importance. Furthermore, through thorough discernment, they transcend and attain liberation; they do not give rise to arrogance regarding the root of worldly afflictions. Abiding within mundane dharmas, they harbor no fear; abiding within the dharmas of the Path, they do not become conceited. They do not abandon great compassion, nor do they become conceited regarding the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of the Tathāgatas.
Amidst the midst of both anger and joy toward the multitude, he remains neither increased nor diminished, attaining the ultimate truth and deliverance.

Furthermore, he clearly understands the scriptural works established by the Buddha; whether amidst the defilements of worldly toil, he accords with the timing of his vows, makes offerings through various practices, contemplates the duration of kalpas, and establishes noble wisdom. Knowing things as they truly are, there is nothing he does not penetrate.

The various Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas enter into the profound and wondrous; that is to say, their wisdom is subtle and far-reaching. Having circled through birth and death, they have clearly understood the subtle and marvelous; when manifesting their birth, they renounce their kingdoms and abdicate their kingship to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.

Through transformations they deliver beings, explaining subtle and wondrous wisdom; they turn the wheel of Dharma, and whether their lifespans are long or short, whatever they establish in their minds, up to their final nirvana and the extent of the Dharma they institute—all is subtle and wondrous wisdom.

Furthermore, they fully understand the secret repositories of all perfectly awakened Buddhas—the Dharma-treasury of the Way, as well as the secrets of body, speech, and mind, whether manifest at times or not, and their various modes of conduct.
When a Bodhisattva receives the prediction of enlightenment, their grace flows toward all sentient beings, and they rescue and gather them in.

There are various categories of beings, shrouded in obscurity; according to the conduct of the multitudes, the distribution of their faculties, and the karma they grasp and create, there is the practice of the Perfectly Awakened One—the majestic, divine treasury.

Furthermore, they clearly understand the number of kalpas in which they reside, as well as the extent of their coming and going—whether it be one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or incalculable kalpas—they recognize and know them all.

Within incalculable kalpas, one can enter a single kalpa; furthermore, by calculating and enumerating the countless, one perceives them through mindfulness and consciousness, such that they cannot be reckoned, yet the limits of these tranquil kalpas are all fully known and remembered.

In the kalpas of tranquility, whether there is a kalpa or no kalpa, he is without thought; yet regarding kalpas where there is thought, he fully cognizes and recollects the thoughts of existence and non-existence.

Whether it be the attainment of perfect enlightenment, the absence of perfect enlightenment, or supreme perfect enlightenment, he fully cognizes and recollects them all. Regarding the past, future, and present; the past, the future, and that which is yet to come; and the events of the past, the present, and the current moment—he fully cognizes and recollects them all. Furthermore, concerning the present, the past, the future, and that which is yet to come, whether kalpas are long or short, he knows them all as they manifest with equality.
All kalpas, whether near or distant, years, and the formation and destruction of heaven and earth—beyond all measure or record—he fully understands and penetrates.

Regarding all Tathāgatas, wherever they manifest their influence, he grasps them as if they were a single hair or a minute speck of dust; with the wisdom of supreme perfect enlightenment, he enters universally into the wisdom perfected by the awakening of the bodies and minds of all sentient beings.

He manifests ultimate realization and displays compliant wisdom; he knows the conceivable and the inconceivable, the Buddha-worlds, what is known by śrāvakas, what is understood by pratyekabuddhas, and what is attained by bodhisattvas, as well as that which is beyond reach—the light of the Tathāgata’s path. He fully comprehends the sublime wisdom he has bestowed; this, O Son of the Buddha, is the immeasurable, vast, and boundless wisdom of all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of the infinite path, they enter inexhaustible wisdom.

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, by entering such a stage of the path, the bodhisattva enters the inconceivable liberation-entrances established by bodhisattvas; there is the liberation-entrance named "Unobstructed," the liberation-entrance named "Pure Realm," and the liberation-entrance named "Universal Illumination."

It is also called the Tathāgatagarbha; it is called the Invincible Treasury; it is called Entering the Three Times; it is called the Dharma-realm Treasury; it is called the Radiance of the Path of Liberation Shining Afar; and it is called the Universal Entry into the Bodhisattva’s Gate of Deliverance that Reaches the Limitless. These constitute the ten gates of liberation established by the bodhisattvas, which are beyond measure and calculation.

Reaching hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* doors of liberation, if there is a bodhisattva who dwells in the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they will immediately attain such samādhis, reaching hundreds of thousands of millions, with infinite dhāraṇīs and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
By means of this wisdom, his mind understands that which he enters; he wanders extensively throughout the immeasurable, and the skillful means he contemplates are fully endowed with all virtues.

Having at once received the principles of the Way proclaimed by the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, he expounds the light of the limitless holy Dharma; the radiance of the scriptural canon shines forth as he rains down the moisture of the Dharma. He immediately receives and maintains it, just like a son of the Buddha: when the various dragons in the ocean wish to rain, nothing else can bear the weight, and only the great ocean receives it.

In this way, O Son of the Buddha, if one enters the secret treasury of the Tathāgatas and all Buddhas, one can then immediately rain down the moisture of the Great Dharma. Other sentient beings are unable to bear or receive it; only those with the conditions for karmic response who maintain various practices can do so, yet even they cannot sustain or bear it until they reach the stage of the Bodhisattva in the ninth dwelling.
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, dwelling in this ground of the Way, rain down the Dharma to provide moisture and sustain the minds of all sentient beings, just like the sons of the Buddha.

Within the great ocean, there is a great rain-cloud named Supreme Truth Infinite; it embraces those of the two vehicles and, in a single moment, releases sweet rain everywhere throughout the lands, thoroughly moistening the boundless earth beneath heaven and reaching all great cities, provinces, and kingdoms.
Why is this so? Because that great ocean is immeasurable.

In the same way, O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this rain of Dharma, the Tathāgata’s single body embraces this rain of Dharma to transform those of the two vehicles, and even the infinite wisdom of all Tathāgatas—which is countless, inconceivable, ineffable, immeasurable, boundless, limitless, transcending the unmanifest, and beyond all analogy—is contained within it. All the bodies of the Tathāgatas are thus encompassed.

"In a single moment, he shakes forth the great light and rains down the rain of the holy Dharma, universally moistening the ten directions; who could possibly calculate the number of those Dharma rains?
He asked again:
"Is there anyone able to calculate this Bodhisattva’s practice—how many Buddhas he has served, or the quantity of the Dharma rains he has discussed?"
"Will it be finished in a mere moment? He replied:

"It cannot be measured or limited by any collection of analogies or calculations. Suppose, O Son of the Buddha, that there were as many worlds as there are grains of dust filling hundreds of thousands of billions of *ya* of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions; and suppose the number of sentient beings were equal to the limit of those grains of dust, with not a single one diminished. If each and every one of these sentient beings were made profoundly learned and attained *dhāraṇī*, such that they all became the foremost attendants of the Tathāgata—"

Among the great disciples, he was most honored for his vast learning, like a lotus atop a vajra, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha. There was a bhikṣu named Mahāprabha who established such an image; his vast learning and skillful means were of firm and powerful strength. If every single person possessed wisdom such as this, and if all classes of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions were made entirely like him, with their merit and wisdom so sublime and immeasurable that each would receive the moisture of the Dharma from all things—what do you think, Son of the Buddha? What would be the result?
"Among these sentient beings, would their extensive learning not increase greatly? He replied,
"It is limitless."
Vajragarbha said: "I entrust this to you with earnest exhortation.

When a Bodhisattva attains this great rain of Dharma and dwells upon the stages of the Bodhisattva path, in a single moment, from the body of a single Tathāgata, there falls a rain throughout the Dharma-realm that expounds the infinite Dharma of the treasury of the three periods of time. The radiance of this Dharma—compared to the previous metaphors of extensive learning and skillful means—is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, and a hundred-thousand-ten-millionfold beyond comparison. It is just as if, for a single Tathāgata, the lands of the ten directions and all Buddha-worlds were filled with the dust motes therein; it is likewise so."

The number of Buddhas is as vast as these particles, yet it even exceeds this; from incalculable Tathāgatas, all at once, they shake down the great rain of Dharma and the radiance of light, such that their dharma-benefit cannot be compared to anything else.

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage of the Way called "The Path of the Rain of Dharma," from their residence in the Tuṣita Heaven until their Great Parinirvāṇa, all of this is through the Tathāgata’s own vows, the power of his majestic spiritual authority, the arousal of great compassion, and the boundless moisture of the Dharma. He emits the great light of the Dharma, sends forth the thunder of the sacred scriptures, and relies upon the six supernormal powers, the three types of perfect knowledge, and the four fearlessnesses to illuminate everywhere. With infinite radiance, he dispels the darkness of the multitudes of defilements; with the brilliance of great merit and noble wisdom, he cuts through the web of doubts of all beings.

Amidst various assemblies, he manifests diverse bodies and proclaims the Great Dharma, never forsaking the gathering; he removes all hindrances and obscurations, extinguishing the blazing fires of all ten directions.

As previously stated, throughout as many Buddha-worlds as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-lands, and extending beyond that, a great ambrosial rain shall fall. According to the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings, it shall eliminate the defilements of worldly toil and extinguish the blazing fires of affliction; by receiving the moisture of that Dharma, there shall be no one who does not attain eternal peace.

"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva has established this ground of the Great Way and spreads the rain of Dharma, from one world up to the Tuṣita Heaven and the ground of Great Parinirvāṇa, they establish the activities of all Tathāgatas. According to the minds of sentient beings, they transform and guide them as is appropriate. In every single world, for as many atoms as there are, across hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-worlds, they descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to the Great Parinirvāṇa, universally establishing the activities of all Tathāgatas."

In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, they should provide instruction and transformation; having attained mastery over wisdom, they employ supernormal powers and sublime clarity to reach the ultimate. In the mere moment of a thought, they can take a nearby small land and establish it as vast, or take a vast world and manifest it as small. In the mere moment of a thought, they can transform a defiled and turbid world into purity, or manifest a pure world as defiled; all worlds are likewise so transformed.

Establishing their respective realms, in the mere instant of a thought, they use a single mote of dust to manifest a single Buddha-land, universally establishing all the Iron Ring Mountains, Great Iron Ring Mountains, and various moats, ravines, and streams—whether one, two, three, up to ten, fifty, a hundred, or even countless Buddha-worlds—and thus establish them.
It enters into a single atom; though it is within a single atom, it is neither vast nor expansive, neither increasing nor decreasing, yet it is manifested through that which is created.
In the mere instant of forming this thought, a single Buddha-world is manifested in its pure adornment;
his body appears in every single Buddha-land, even throughout all infinite worlds.
Furthermore, in a single moment of thought, he pervades all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, yet he does not disturb a single nation or a single Buddha-world among those beings.

It is likewise with these and other such beings; reaching as far as incalculable Buddha-worlds and pervading the boundless Buddha-lands of the ten directions, they manifest entry into a single hair-pore without causing any harm.
In the space of a single thought-moment, they manifest entry into all Buddha-realms within a single hair-pore, displaying their majestic purity in the space of a single thought-moment.
Once these transformations were completed, their number was as vast as the countless atoms filling all Buddha-worlds.
Each of those transformed beings manifested their own bodies in such infinite measure that they now stood within my palm.
With this palm, I made offerings with supreme diligence to the Buddhas of the ten directions. One.
With one hand, he displayed flowers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges atop his robes to offer them to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
He established all such acts of pure adornment: various fragrant flowers, blended incenses, powdered incenses, garments, banners, canopies, and silken streamers.
Each of these bodies further emanates several heads, and each of these heads emanates several tongues, extolling the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions.

In the mere instant of generating the resolve, they pervade the ten directions; within the span of a single thought-moment, they cause incalculable beings to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment and even establish the pure karma of great parinirvāṇa.

Abiding throughout the three periods of time, they establish countless and immeasurable bodies; thus, by means of their own bodies, they manifest infinite Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in limitless Buddha-lands, establishing them in purity.

Furthermore, he manifests his own body, transforming all Buddha-lands so that they are dispersed, destroyed, and reconstituted; he establishes within his own body all the universally complete lands of the Buddhas and places them within a single pore without disturbing sentient beings. In the mere instant of a thought, he transforms and manifests boundless Buddha-lands, turning them into a great ocean, wherein he establishes a multitude of lotus flowers.
Furthermore, those lotuses possess pure radiance that illuminates immeasurable Buddha-fields in their entirety.

Moreover, within them, they manifest various Buddha-fields, even those as sublime as all-encompassing sagacity; their bodies reach universally throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions. Like the sun and moon, they shine everywhere, establishing gateways of light in every direction. In each and every location, throughout all quarters, they establish visions of infinite worlds, never fearing sentient beings, even during the dissolution of the ten directions.

Manifesting these transformations of disintegration—namely the calamities of wind, fire, and water—in the mere instant of a thought, they demonstrate them to all sentient beings. According to their aspirations, they construct and transform physical bodies, adorning their will and nature; they are able to manifest the body of a Tathāgata by means of their own body, manifest their own body by means of the body of a Tathāgata, and establish their own body by means of the body of a Tathāgata.
Within the Buddha-field, one establishes the field of one’s own body within the body of the Buddha.
Listen well, O Son of the Buddha!

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in the practice of the stage of the Path of the Rain of Dharma, they manifest this transformation as well as countless hundreds of thousands of other miraculous displays.

At that time, all the bodhisattvas in the assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the four great kings, the great and wondrous deva-kings, and the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, each thought to themselves:

"If even the spiritual power and transformative teachings of a bodhisattva, with such immeasurable and sublime virtues, are like this, how can they be compared to the majestic transformations established by the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One?"
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly, asked the Mahāsattva Vajragarbha Bodhisattva:
"I pray that you, Son of the Buddha, will sever the net of doubts of this assembly at this time; it would be well to resolve them."
"The manifestations revealed by the purity of Bodhisattvas are peerless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered the samādhi known as the "Natural Body and Majestic Power of All Buddha-lands" and remained in meditative absorption.

Once this meditative concentration was established, at that very moment, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the four heavenly kings, the great and wondrous heavenly kings, and the kings of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, each saw their own bodies within the person of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Furthermore, he observed that the trichiliocosm was also contained within his body.

The pure deeds performed therein could not encompass his entire body; throughout billions of kalpas, he cultivated the practice of vigor at that Buddha-tree. That Buddha-tree was vast and long—thirty thousand *li*, or perhaps one hundred or three thousand—and it was universally expansive, boundless, and complete.

Furthermore, just as three thousand million lands are suspended in the vast and extreme distance, so too is this lion throne at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; it is as majestic as that.
There is a bodhisattva there named Sarvābhijña, who shall become a Tathāgata named Cittarāja, and he has come to the tree at the site of enlightenment.
Thereupon, all those gathered there saw him from afar; the splendor they beheld was perfected through billions of kalpas, and they marveled at his virtue, unable to exhaust its praise.
Having manifested this transformation, he immediately returned to the assembly and was once again in his original place.
At that time, the entire assembly marveled at this unprecedented event; they remained silent and speechless, observing the bodhisattvas dwelling in profound stillness.
Then the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked Vajragarbha:
"How extraordinary! O Son of the Buddha!"
“This samādhi-concentration possesses such majestic brilliance and its realm is so exquisite; what is the name of this bodhisattva concentration?
He replied, “It is named ‘The Majestic Splendor of the Natural Body in All Buddha-lands.’”
He asked again:
"By what means does this samādhi-samāpatti travel, and how is its sphere of activity pure and adorned? He replied:

"If one is able to fully practice this, suppose there were sons of noble family, or bodhisattvas, who have skillfully cultivated this samādhi; such as these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, filling all the atoms within a trichiliocosm, may these bodhisattvas pervade all the trichiliocosms and manifest their own bodies therein."

Furthermore, if one attains this stage of the Way of the Rain of Dharma, any bodhisattva dwelling in this stage will obtain hundreds of thousands of incalculable meditative concentrations, such that no one can limit or know them.

Regarding the number of bodies manifested by these bodhisattvas, the practices they undertake, their excellent and wondrous intentions, and the abodes of the bodhisattvas—one cannot know their bodily actions, verbal expressions, or mental thoughts; nor can one know the power of their spiritual feet (*ṛddhipāda*). Even when examining the samādhis through which they enter, the sphere of their noble wisdom, their methods of transformation, and the dharmas they establish, these are beyond the limit of knowledge.
In their constant conduct, whether lifting or lowering their feet, there is none who can comprehend it.
They proceed with the practice of supreme vigor; this is the bodhisattva’s course of action, abiding in the wondrous intention of "well done" upon the stages of the bodhisattva path.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When this rain of Dharma, the stage of the bodhisattva path, is expounded in its state of equality, its meaning is vast and immeasurable; that which is proclaimed as correct and true is inconceivable.
"Proclaiming the correct words extends to hundreds of thousands of boundless realms, beyond all analogy.
He asked again:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
The practices and spheres of all Tathāgatas are profound and subtle; how can they be described?
Now, the practices established by these Bodhisattvas and their spiritual transformations within their spheres are as boundless as this.

He replied: "Suppose, O Son of the Buddha, there were a man who displayed his body as large as the four quarters of the world; he took up great staffs as large as the four quarters of the world—two or three of them—and holding these great staffs in his hands, he carried them to a rock and, taking hold of this rock, spoke these words: 'I shall cast this rock into as many Buddha-worlds as there are atoms in the ten directions, even unto infinity, until they are filled with these atoms. Would it be possible to calculate or know the number of these atoms?"
Having attained this infinity, one fully understands all that exists and reaches everywhere; this is what is called "equanimity.

One accomplishes the stage of the Bodhisattva Path of the Dharma Rain, which is immeasurable and surpasses all such metaphors. When the wisdom of all Tathāgatas reaches the point of being beyond calculation, one then attains supreme, perfect enlightenment and practices the dharmas of all Bodhisattvas with equanimity.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is as if there were a person who took a small amount of earth from the four quarters of the world, while the remainder was infinite; even so, O Son of the Buddha, now as I proclaim this stage of the Bodhisattva’s path of the rain of Dharma, though I sing its praises for a few moments, if one were to extol its merits throughout countless eons, one could not exhaust its blessings, let alone [fully describe] the stage of the Tathāgata.

I now entrust you with this matter, earnestly commanding you: as you stand here before the Tathāgata, to speak of the essential point—if there were a son of the Buddha in every single region, throughout incalculable Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the atoms filling all those buddha-fields, and you were to cause them all to attain such a dwelling in the Way; [then you would have fulfilled my intent].

Bodhisattvas fill the space like a dense forest of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, and hemp; throughout incalculable eons, they have accomplished the bodhisattva practices and gathered these virtues together to form a single noble and enlightened wisdom of a bodhisattva. Compared to the wisdom of a Tathāgata, this is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousand-billionfold, and even a hundred-trillionfold greater, beyond all analogy. This, O Son of the Buddha, is how a bodhisattva enters into such noble wisdom.

In the Tathāgata, the Most Perfectly Awakened One, the actions of body, speech, and mind are non-dual; the Bodhisattva does not abandon the power of the various samādhis, personally beholding all Buddhas, making offerings and serving them, and throughout each and every kalpa, the offerings made to these Buddhas are beyond measure or description.

With all offerings provided without deficiency, they enter into the transformative teachings of the Path; bowing in refuge to the Buddhas, they increase their practice within the established teachings, becoming peerless and without equal.
Regarding this inquiry, the Dharma-realm is immeasurable and limitless, even unto hundreds of thousands of millions of koṭis of kalpas.

It is like a son of the Buddha who is a master goldsmith, crafting a celestial jewel crown and fashioning a great necklace; he polishes a great precious gem for the Sovereign King of the Gods to wear upon his neck, such that it is peerless. No other celestial beings, nor any other exquisite jewel necklaces, can ever equal its magnificent adornment.
"So it is, so it is! Son of the Buddha!

If there is a bodhisattva who attains the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and by means of this bodhisattva’s pure cultivation of wisdom, becomes peerless and transcendent, thereby surpassing and perfecting the ninth stage; when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, the light of their path is majestic and they achieve all-encompassing sagacity. Their conduct is incomparable, and as such a sacred vessel, there are none who do not receive their salvation. Just as the light of the Great and Wondrous Heavenly King transcends the positions of all other born devas and illuminates the mental natures and actions of sentient beings, so too does the bodhisattva, having attained and established themselves in the tenth stage, the Stage of the Rain of Dharma, dwell in the light of noble wisdom that cannot be reached by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas."
Even reaching the ninth stage, one still cannot equal it.
Its establishment reaches all sagely wisdom (*prajñā*), guiding and benefiting sentient beings, and establishing them in the principles of the Way.

Furthermore, this Bodhisattva, by being able to enter such noble wisdom—the wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, which penetrates the three periods of time without end; the noble wisdom of the Dharma-realm that pervades all Buddha-worlds, illuminating all Buddha-lands and establishing them; fully knowing all phenomena and the lands of all sentient beings—constantly attains universal understanding through impartiality up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), so that all sentient beings may hear it.
These are the sons of the Buddha, the great bodhisattvas, known as the Ten Abodes of the Dharma-Rain Bodhisattva.

When a bodhisattva dwells in these, even if they were to become a great and wondrous deity or a celestial king, in expounding the various perfections of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, as well as the Dharma-realm that is inquired about, they would have no peer.

In all the deeds they cultivate—the principles of giving, affection, respect, and benefiting others, as well as the meaning of equal benefit—they never depart from mindfulness of all Buddhas, until they are fully endowed with the mindfulness of omniscience (*sarvajñā*). With the thought of how they might bring all sentient beings to the state of supreme honor and guide them toward universal wisdom, at the very moment they resolve their minds, they manifest such forms and diligently practice with vigor; in a single instant, they reach incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-lands, filling them with as many atoms as there are in those lands, while remaining in the meditative absorption of *samādhi*.

In ten incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-lands, one sees bodhisattvas filling those lands as numerous as the atoms of dust therein, all equal and without distinction. Surrounded by their retinues, they manifest according to their vows, through the power of the bodhisattvas, their extraordinary and vast aspirations, and their transformations and spiritual footprints; their meritorious virtues are beyond measure or description.

Their conduct is majestic and pure, characterized by profound faith and joyful delight; whatever they practice, whether it be their physical manifestations, the clarity of their divine vision, their voice, or their lineage—even throughout hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas—they perceive and understand them all with complete lucidity.

“Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas who enter the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and gradually perfect the gateway to the path of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). They are like the summit of the flowing four rivers from the great lake Anavatapta; riding upon the water-gate of the sūtras, they moisten and nourish the four regions, causing them to grow and flourish until they become inexhaustible, eventually entering the vast ocean. Just as the great ocean has no boundaries, so it is with the Bodhisattva: the roots of goodness of their vows, following the sequence of their resolute will, fulfill and transform sentient beings through the principles of the four debts of gratitude (*caturṇām ṛṇānām*); their merit is inexhaustible, progressing ever upward until they reach the boundless conduct of omniscience.”

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, these ten stages of the bodhisattva, which lead to the attainment of the Buddha-wisdom, are like the ten great mountain kings that stand firm because of the great earth.
What are the ten? First is called Snowy Mountains;
second is called Fragrant Incense.
The third is called Khadiraka;
the fourth is called Mount Īrṣyā;
the fifth is called Gṛhītakṣepa.
Sixth is Horse-Ear Mountain;
seventh is Blink-Holding;
eighth is Iron-Circumference.
Ninth is Splendid Intent;
tenth is the Great Iron Ring Mountains and Sumeru, King of Mountains.
As for the Snowy Mountains, they serve as a dwelling place for all medicinal herbs, providing countless and immeasurable medicinal plants to heal sentient beings.

In this way, the bodhisattva, dwelling in the Stage of Joy, establishes his karmic practices and fully comprehends all worldly activities, while transmitting and reciting the words of the sūtras and divine mantras.
The conventional arts established therein transform beings without limit.
As for the Mountain of Perfumed Incense, it produces all manner of fragrances and flows into the chambers of manifold scents in measureless quantities;

likewise, the Bodhisattva dwelling on the Stage Free from Defilement makes this stage his abode, and the fragrance of precepts and learning, which guards the prohibitive laws, is beyond limitation as he nurtures the meaning of the precepts.
That Mount Khadiraka is composed of pure and refined jewels, serving as a dwelling place where all manner of flowers grow; these flowers are limitless, universally receiving all blossoms.

In this same way, the Bodhisattva, abiding on the Stage of Radiance (*arcismatī-bhūmi*), acts as a dwelling for the multitude; remaining in the world, his meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and samādhi-attainments (*samāpatti*) are likewise limitless, enabling him to inquire into the appropriate application of all states of meditative concentration.

That mountain of jealousy and the city of pure jewels constitute the dwelling place of the five supernormal powers; it is the palace where infinite sages reside, consisting of various kinds of mountains.

In this same way, the Bodhisattva dwells upon the Ground of Radiance (Arciṣmatī), making it his abode; there he expounds and teaches the means of deliverance (dhyāna-pāramitā), which is called the path of the infinite, and inquires after all forms of wisdom.
He upholds Mount Kṣuṇa-rāja, a jewel of true purity, which serves as the dwelling place for spirits and those with supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*); there are infinite spirits of various species.

In this same way, the Bodhisattva, abiding in the stage of "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā bhūmi*), manifests all supernormal powers and extensively expounds infinite, boundless spiritual transformations.
Mount Horse-Ear (Aśvakarṇa), composed entirely of jewels, serves as a dwelling and produces all manner of fruits, yielding countless treasures;

likewise, when a bodhisattva dwells near the stage of the bodhisattva path where it is clearly visible, that very place becomes their abode, for they proclaim the means of deliverance so that the śrāvakas and others may attain boundless fruits according to what is appropriate for the time.
The Mount Kṣema-dhara King is the dwelling place of the great nāga deity; there are boundless nāgas of various kinds.
In this same way, the Bodhisattva dwells in the Ground of Profound Mystery (Gambhīra-bhūmi), which is his chamber. [The commentary] states:

"In all editions, the wording for the 'Ground of Profound Mystery' here is incomplete, and the analogies for the 'Unshakable Ground' (Acalā-bhūmi) are entirely missing. Please verify this by consulting alternative translations to understand what has been omitted."

In this way, the Bodhisattva dwells in the immovable stage of the Bodhisattva path, serving as a sovereign chamber for all Bodhisattvas; his conduct is peerless as he inquires into and receives the teachings from the infinite worlds of the ten directions, where all together offer him their instruction.
Mount Sumeru in the realm of the Asuras is composed of pure jewels and serves as the dwelling place for the great deities of the Asura hosts, numbering beyond calculation;

likewise, the Bodhisattva, abiding in the stage of "Excellent Intention" (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), takes the maturing of sentient beings as his dwelling. The Buddha-bodies he manifests are without limit, received from the ten directions, as he pursues ultimate wisdom and practice, inquiring into the beginningless origins and ends of sentient beings and their boundless, limitless karma of transmigration.
That King of Mountains, Sumeru, is composed entirely of various jewels and serves as the dwelling place for the devas with supernormal powers and for incalculable numbers of asuras;
likewise, the bodhisattva dwells upon the stages of the path of the Dharma-rain, manifesting the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the infinite bodies of all Buddhas.

Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, just as the ten mountains of jewels surround the great ocean, so too does the Bodhisattva abide in this tenth stage of universal and equal wisdom, honoring all the skillful ones like the great ocean; through these ten matters, they achieve perfection without peer.

What are these ten? First is gradual and complete fulfillment; second is not being mixed or confused with corpses; third is subduing the multitudes through various gateways; fourth is the activity of a single flavor; fifth is countless precious jewels; sixth is receiving profound and distant forms; seventh is being vast and boundless; eighth is receiving all great bodies; ninth is following the time of abiding without overstepping the original shore; and tenth is receiving all rain without ever feeling satiated.
When a bodhisattva practices these ten deeds in this manner, they are without peer.

What are the ten? They are: cultivating the stage of the path of joy; gradually fulfilling their vows; guiding and transforming the masses; the practice of the stage free from defilement; and not dwelling together with those who violate the precepts.
In the Land of Arising Radiance, one subdues the worldly practice of taking life.
In the Land of Resplendent Splendor, one possesses profound faith in the Buddha-way such that none can destroy it, constantly cultivating impartial conduct.
This ground of invincibility possesses skillful means and supernormal powers that are immeasurable; it transforms worldly beings according to their inclinations.

This ground of direct vision consists of profound and wondrous causes and conditions; it observes the subtle and mysterious state of sentient beings, understanding them with precise discernment, such that all practices become unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The Ground of Immovability enables one to exhort and guide others toward the infinite, pure, and majestic conduct of the Tathāgata. How excellent is the ground of the mind! It is a profound and wondrous gate of liberation.

Like a son of the Buddha, it is like a great moon-pearl that surpasses ten kinds of jewels; wherever it is placed, there is no place that is not brilliantly illuminated. A master of peerless skill, using skillful means, polishes it until it shines with radiance. It is strung together with the clarity of pure light, made eternally ultimate, and secured with cords of rare gems. Through thorough understanding and penetration, it is threaded and passed through to serve as a straight lapis lazuli crossbar. Placed atop a high banner, it emanates its brilliance, illuminating both the near and the far. Belonging to the sovereign, this treasure is protected for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they may receive its light; it is brought forth and presented before them.

When a bodhisattva thus gives rise to the mind of omniscience, they immediately attain supernatural powers and enter the ten kinds of noble lineage. With wisdom alone as their sufficient sustenance, they delight in dwelling in seclusion, clearly understanding the concentration of virtue and the gates of liberation through single-mindedness.
Through the correct reception of samādhi, they clearly understand and synthesize these matters of the True Dharma—the path of practice for the three purities.

Having well cultivated pure clarity and skillful means (*upāya*), they discern and fully comprehend the various categories of the twelve links of dependent origination. Through the wisdom of skillful means, they uphold the banner of the sages and attain mastery.

By manifesting radiant light and through the appropriateness of wisdom, he observes the conduct of sentient beings until they reach the stage of *anābhoga* (the effortless), thereby accomplishing the path to supreme, perfect enlightenment.

He establishes sentient beings so that they may dwell in the ten stages; only then is one called "All-Knowing. This constitutes the accumulation of the bodhisattva’s practice and the compendium of all meritorious and skillful dharma-gates.
"If there are sentient beings who lack the root of virtue, they will ultimately never hear of this great path of practice.
Moon-liberation then asked again:
"If one hears this sound and attains this meaning, what merit must have been accumulated in the past?"

He replied: "As for his merit and blessings, they were cultivated in former lives when he formerly practiced in accordance with all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Because his noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*) was unable to illuminate accordingly, his vision could not reach far; he did not practice great compassion (*mahāmaitrīkaruṇā*) toward all beings, and thus he wandered about in this manner, bestowing favors and providing universal protection."

By means of these conditions, one accumulates merit and attains the chapter on the Dharma-gates; its illumination is such as this, and by beholding present merits, one penetrates into the accumulation of merit.
Why is this so? It is because one has attained the understanding of this.

Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha who, being no more than ordinary bodhisattvas, are unable to hear this chapter on the Dharma-gate, nor do they faithfully believe, accept, uphold, or recite it; how much less could they practice it, cultivate it with diligent effort, or subdue their afflictions to achieve its realization?
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!
Only those of similar caliber who have entered into the meritorious virtues of omniscience can receive and uphold this.
If one should hear this chapter of the Dharma-gate, having heard it, they shall believe, contemplate and practice it, and cultivate it with diligent perseverance.

At that time, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, ten billion Buddha-lands in the ten directions—equal in number to the dust motes filling them—all the worlds of the Buddhas shook in six ways. Great thunderous sounds arose, and by the Buddha’s holy decree and for the sake of nourishing the Dharma teachings, celestial flowers rained down and famous incenses wafted forth.
The celestial adornments—the heavenly garments and jewels, the heavenly necklaces, banners, and streamers, and the various celestial musical instruments—resounded spontaneously without being struck.
Flutes, pipes, lutes, and harps produced sounds naturally that surpassed all other celestial objects.

The Sage of All-Knowledge, having attained proximity to the realm of the unconditioned, rained down sublime offerings throughout this world, across the four quarters, and even as far as the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; such was the case for the celestial palaces of the King of that heaven, and likewise for all the worlds of the heavens throughout the ten directions.

This teaching of the Dharma has spread everywhere without exception; by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms filling ten billion buddha-lands throughout the ten directions—worlds numbering in the tens of billions—have each come together from all quarters, pervading the ten directions, and each has uttered these words of praise:
"Excellent, excellent!"
O Son of the Buddha!

You have now raised the discourse on this essential dharma-text of the Bodhisattva Stages. We, too, all bear the same name, Vajragarbha, and have come from the world-realm Vajraśekhara to this land. Our Buddha’s name is Vajradhvaja; we have come from that Buddha’s presence, for all Buddhas likewise turn this essential dharma-text, the holy intent of the Buddhas.
The various assemblies are likewise so.

If these chapters and verses have such subtle and profound principles, and their forms and images are thus, then their meaning is also thus; the practice of benefiting others is no different and not distinct, nor does it rely upon anything else. We bear witness to this, having come to this assembly by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, just as we have arrived in this Buddha-land; so too it is in all the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.

In each and every buddha-field, throughout the four quarters, from the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven above down to the palaces of the Vaśavartin Heavenly Kings, with moon-bright pearls and jeweled treasury palaces—as numerous as the dust motes filling ten billion buddha-fields—bodhisattvas equal in number to these gathered together.

At that time, Vajragarbha surveyed the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, observed the assembly of the various divisions, and looked across the dharma-realm. He sighed with admiration for the arousal of the mind of omniscience, beheld the purity of the power of practice of the many bodhisattvas, and witnessed their reception of omniscience, their proclamation of the path of practice, their elimination of worldly defilements, their guidance and benefit through universal wisdom, and their manifestation of inconceivable transformations—the meritorious virtues of the deeds of all bodhisattvas.
Proclaiming this path in accordance with the holy intent of the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
"Tranquil and without delight, The mind is stilled, concentrated, and focused;
Equal as empty space, Level and upright as the vast firmament."
Having abandoned affliction, weariness, and defilement, they abide in the wisdom of the Path;
their hearing and practice are extraordinary, for these Bodhisattvas are most venerable.
With a thousandfold assembly of virtuous qualities, their mental conduct has persisted for billions of eons.
Making offerings up to the Great Sage, there have been hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;
through supreme mastery, they were honored with immeasurable reverence.
Out of compassion for the multitude of living beings, they gave rise to the Bodhisattva mind.
Diligence attends to the external path; patience nurtures gentleness and harmony.
A sense of shame and remorse are the preeminent head; meritorious achievement has wisdom as its supreme goal.
When the mind is free from defilement, the Buddha’s noble nature is luminous with wisdom.
Supreme power is eternally equal, inspiring the Bodhisattva mind.
All those who are the Benefactors of the Three Times provide the foremost and most excellent offerings;
their limits are like space, and all lands are pure.
Equally conforming to the meaning of the Buddha’s teachings, even unto all dharmas;
liberating and benefiting sentient beings, subduing them until reaching the site of enlightenment.
Attaining the ground of the Honored One, the resolve they have awakened is peerless.
Joyful and free from defilement, one eliminates all evils.
Practicing subtle and powerful influence, one thereby accomplishes pure and white dharmas;
upholding a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, one advances further into the supreme path.
Rich in the virtue of precepts, observances, and learning, With a compassionate heart pitying all sentient beings;
