Abandoning defilements and harboring no attachments, One then achieves a pure resolve.
Observing all worlds, The three fires burn with fierce intensity.
Third, his resolve is vast, transcending to benefit sentient beings.
Free from the afflictions of suffering and the sense of self, as well as diseases and wounds;
he brings peace to the three realms of suffering and constantly extinguishes all burning passions.
Longing for the Buddha’s meritorious achievements, he cultivates practice to perceive all flaws and impurities;
his wisdom shines forth vast and wide, surpassing all other lights.
With a mind and conduct that are equanimous and pure, he attains the noble wisdom of the Path.
Abiding well in this state, one makes offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas;
serving those supreme among humans with equal devotion, the mind is tranquil and all merits are perfected;
having subdued all multitudes, one transcends them to achieve a victory difficult to attain.
The Sage’s clarity is skillful means; the wisdom he cultivates is his intent.
His achievements are immeasurable, subduing others to benefit sentient beings.
He makes offerings to those of Ten Powers and transforms the masses through the Way.
Approaching the unarisen, one enters the sixth stage.
All sentient beings are difficult to comprehend; advancing universally, one turns back the world.
Because the body is used, there is no affliction; through realization and understanding, one knows existence and non-existence.
All dharmas are fundamentally pure and empty, arising from the twelve links of dependent origination;
by transforming base thoughts into the subtle and wondrous, one immediately attains entry into the seventh stage.
Through wisdom and skillful means, one achieves a clear and luminous mind.
The distant journey is difficult to surpass; the great resolve is difficult to illustrate.
It is inherently pure and tranquil, yet because the mind is sharp and the will is transformative, all sufferings are rendered equal, and one transcends them, remaining unshakable.
The merits and offenses created are manifold, while the wisdom of the sages is of innumerable kinds;
supreme among men, they are most excellent, established in profound stillness.
Having attained mastery over the ten natural laws, they traverse the realms of sentient beings.
For the sake of all living beings, he enters the path of virtuous precepts and intention.
Thus, at the very first subtle stage, he advances through all worlds;
he gathers and protects sentient beings equally, practicing to dissolve the dust and toil of defilements.
Those who revere these teachings of the Vinaya enter into the wealth of merit;
their conduct is like exquisite flowers, proclaiming my supreme wisdom.
Having received such practice, their past deeds are pure and bright.
Upon reaching the ninth stage, one attains merit and wisdom.
Through the power of the exhortations of all the Victors, one yearns for and delights in the supreme and correct path;
by virtue of the merit of proximity to wisdom, all attain the Way of the Buddha.
There are hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of unconditioned samādhis;
having attained vast and brilliant illumination, they dwell and move within a most great wisdom.
Only then do they achieve the universal wisdom of the stage of non-regression (avaivartika).
Its realm is vast and wide, and through samādhi it reaches inexhaustibility.
It is as if having attained the ultimate, one draws near to all wisdom;
there are infinite great lotuses, composed of various kinds of jewels.
His body is of infinite length, yet he sits in the midst;
the assembly of the Sons of the Most Victorious stand around him, gazing upon him.
His virtues are countless thousands, and his radiance is immeasurable billions.
He extinguishes all afflictions and manifold sufferings throughout the ten directions;
thereafter, the supreme leader shines with hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light.
Amidst the assembly of those honored among men, he transcends and enters the ten directions.
Abiding in the space above, they manifest a canopy of interlaced light;
there they receive the Buddha’s manifold practices and accord with him in making offerings.
There they behold all the Buddhas, who are supreme in their complete understanding of the Way.
The Buddha-son Avīkṣaṇa has attained the excellence of the supreme Dharma.
There is no Buddha-son who is not universally encompassed; he circulates everywhere to offer worship.
Such is Avīkṣaṇa, radiating forth the sublime light.
Between the brows of the Supreme among Men, he has perfected all-knowledge;
receiving a radiance surpassing all luminaries, he enters this crown-protrusion.
He proclaims immeasurable quiescence, shaking all worlds.
The manifold sufferings of the Avīci Hell were instantly extinguished at that moment.
It was as if they had returned to the path of all Buddhas, my own refuge;
it was like being before the most sovereign monarch, his most honored and supreme crown prince.
My accomplishment is likewise so, with all wisdom brought to ultimate completion;
thus proceeding toward attainment, the rain of Dharma falls upon the sublime site of enlightenment.
The Benevolent One dwells herein, his wise conduct immeasurable.
All sentient beings join in praise, establishing this awakening to attain Buddhahood;
In the realm of form and the formless realm, and that which is recited in the realm of desire;
Throughout the lands of all nations, it is extolled within the Dharma-realm.
The conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as the realm of the bodiless;
all are discerned through selection, and all praises are offered through the Dharma.
Thus, there is the addition of the infinite, wherein all actions are free from pride.
Establishing such practices, the subtle wisdom of all Buddhas—
the secrets of the Honored One among Men— penetrates countless eons;
like the number of hairs or grains of sand, it enters universally into all worlds.
Born among men as a human being, the Awakened One renounced the home;
He circumambulated the Iron Ring Mountains, having achieved his goal and manifested his presence.
All return to their destination, reaching the gate of tranquil liberation.
Whatever their aspirations may achieve, all shall enter the Way.
With vast resolve abiding herein, the Victorious Ones pour forth the rain of Dharma;
it circulates universally everywhere, gathering and sustaining the minds of all.
Raining upon all sentient beings, just as the wind sustains the water;
the Dharma-rain of the Buddhas is likewise gathered by all.
Abiding in the single Dharma, they cause it to be heard through their far-reaching voice.
Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, Countless sentient beings plant their seeds.
Hearing the World-Honored One’s teachings and upholding them, All become śrāvakas;
Yet those who practice at all times among the countless multitudes Are the bodhisattvas of vast learning.
Practicing wisdom to the limit of its power, he recalls his past fundamental deeds;
in a single moment, he pervades billions of Buddha-fields,
raining down drops of ambrosia to delight all beings and extinguish their afflictions.
The nature of what is created is benevolent and harmonious; it is the Dharma-rain of all Buddhas.
Abiding herein by means of the six supernormal powers, one transcends to the celestial palaces;
within the supreme realm among humans, one manifests throughout the ten directions.
Undergoing constant transformation and change throughout countless billions of kalpas, Brahmā penetrates all sentient beings, causing their minds to practice the Buddha-way.
Through his holy wisdom he establishes this; even within the span of a single step.
They immediately reach the ninth stage, where their dwelling is immovable.
With the merit and power of their dhāraṇīs and wisdom, how much less would they fear sentient beings?
Even the multitudes of all the three realms who have become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas [cannot move them].
The Most Victorious One stands upon this, yet manifests it everywhere;
unimpeded throughout the three realms, he possesses the wisdom that fully comprehends the dharma-realm.
He pervades all lands, leaving no sentient being or phenomenon untouched.
The meritorious achievements of all Buddhas likewise rely upon the Triple Gem;
the noble and realized ones dwell herein, reverently practicing and serving the Buddha;
throughout all lands of the ten directions, they traverse the entire Dharma-realm.
Making offerings before one’s eyes, reverently honoring all classes of followers;
accomplishing every merit and virtue, adorned like the celestial garments of the gods.
The sages dwell herein, illuminating the multitude with the light of wisdom.
They extinguish the darkness of all delusions and manifest the sun of the Dharma.
With supreme and sovereign brilliance, they eliminate the chaos of the world;
so it is with the sons of the Buddhas, whose radiance dispels the dust of affliction.
Abiding here throughout the three periods of time, he is the most honored one above all worlds;
having realized the Way, he is the supreme hero who proclaims the activities of the Three Vehicles.
In a single moment, he attains countless samādhis.
In all lands throughout the ten directions, one beholds Buddhas beyond measure.
Such is the case for these sons of the Buddha; I have briefly set forth the stages of the path, yet even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one could never exhaustively praise their virtues.
Such is the virtue of being free from defilement; their ground is the awakening to equality.
Their support is like a flower, or as Mount Sumeru rests upon the earth.
These foremost sons of the Buddhas behold their enemies without anger or resentment.
Like snow piled upon a mountain peak, yet serving as medicine for sentient beings within;
clear understanding of the precepts and learning is like the pervasive fragrance of famous incense;
it is just like a lotus flower in a pond, which arises and flourishes because of this.
The Jewel of the Path cannot be disturbed; one immediately attains the holy radiance.
Like a seer dwelling among the mountains, one finds joy and self-delight in that abode.
Through the wondrous fragrance of spirits and gods, one attains the five supernormal powers.
Discoursing on the six retributive fruits is like the precious jewel of the horse-ear;
The sevenfold supreme enlightenment is like the dragon grasping a auspicious response;
Attaining the eight masteries is like the great Iron Ring Mountains.
By entering the ninth dwelling, one attains the subtle and wondrous Supreme Vehicle;
the ten meritorious virtues of all Buddhas shine forth like Mount Sumeru.
Fully endowed with the foremost vows, one has long since spread the fragrance of precepts and prohibitions.
Practicing the third merit, one practices the fourth in this way;
the purity of the fifth, the profound subtlety of the sixth;
the seventh mind is unattached, and the eighth is said to be immeasurable.
Having received the ninth stage of the noble ones, their minds seek subtle wisdom;
as they act for the sake of sentient beings, they then enter into noble insight.
The ten-fold body of the Buddhas arises from the dhāraṇī of all dharmas.
Thus practicing the great ocean, the bodhisattva’s mind is free from anger.
Having attained the ten practices, it still relies on the original aspiration;
cultivating the twelve ultimate practices, one-pointed concentration is the third.
Having purified the fourth stage, one then illuminates the fifth;
in the sixth, the suffering of the lower realms is destroyed, and by means of that cause, one immediately reaches the seventh dwelling.
Holding the banner of correctness with mastery, the eighth stage becomes the Great Harmony.
The ninth is the stage of Receiving the Multitude of Practices, where the light of wisdom shines afar.
The tenth is the stage of Akaniṣṭha, which is understood as most preeminent;
its meritorious jewels are pure and harmonious, for such was his original practice.
One can destroy the lands of the ten directions and calculate them all;
with a single mind, one can perceive and universally understand the minds of all sentient beings.
One might even measure the entirety of empty space with a single hair.
"Even if one were to praise for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, one could not exhaust the Buddha’s virtues. Vajragarbha said:

"This is why it is called the Samādhi of Great Radiance. When the wisdom of the Way is fully perfected and the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) is attained, one then completes the Buddha-way, and all beings receive peace, just like the brightness of the sun which the world looks up to with reverence. All Buddhas of the ten directions are born from within this state; it is by means of it that they achieve success."
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Excellent, excellent, Vajragarbha!"
Alas! I praise and expound upon these matters of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which are what the various bodhisattvas (*bodhisattva*) ought to practice.

From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*) until reaching the stage of *avaivartika* (the stage of non-retrogression), it is like the new moon gradually waxing until it is full on the fifteenth day, shining alone among the multitude of stars. In this same way, the bodhisattva gradually perfects all practices: the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action; the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) and the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*); the six perfections (*ṣaṭ pāramitāḥ*) and great kindness and great compassion; and through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they bring themselves to the attainment of Buddhahood.

To nourish and moisten sentient beings is like planting a tree: it develops roots, stems, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit; when people consume them, their hunger and emptiness are removed.

It is thus with the Bodhisattva: from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until his own attainment of Buddhahood, there are none who do not receive his salvation and universally attain the Way.

Just as the hundred grains, grasses, trees, fruits, and various medicinal herbs all grow because of the earth, so it is with the Bodhisattva: by practicing these ten stages (*bhūmi*), he attains Buddhahood himself and delivers those throughout the ten directions.
Just as the great ocean produces a multitude of wondrous jewels and immeasurable treasures that benefit all under heaven, so too is this sutra:
it brings to fulfillment the ten stages of the bodhisattva path, thereby enabling one to attain Buddhahood.

His virtue surpasses empty space, like the sun and moon suddenly illuminating the four quarters; the world looks up to him with reverence. When a Bodhisattva practices this, he personally attains the Way of the Buddha; sentient beings receive his grace, being freed from the immeasurable hardships of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and all ascend to the Hall of the Way.
Just as a king of physicians treats the ailments of the multitude, none of which fail to be cured, so too is this sutra:
it eliminates the diseases of lust, anger, and delusion within the classes of sentient beings, leading them to the state of true correctness.

Just as a Wheel-Turning King transforms and instructs the four quarters so that none do not obey his commands, so too does the Bodhisattva, through the four immeasurables and the four ways of attracting beings, transform and instruct those who cling to a self and rely upon the four great elements, leading them to fearlessness. Thus, the four things need not be guarded against, and the maladies of the mind are forever eliminated.

Just as Mount Sumeru stands at the center of the four quarters, so too is this sutra the preeminent among all scriptures; its virtue and morality are vast and luminous, its resolve is impartial and correct, and it leads to the realization of the bodiless state, even unto the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path. It delivers all beings from the afflictions of birth, death, old age, and sickness throughout the beginning and end of existence, and it is that by which the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are born.

It is the deep ocean of all sutras and the palace of the Way and its Virtue; it is the treasury where the practices of all bodhisattvas are stored, the hall of the Way where they assemble, and the provisions of merit sought by all beings within the three realms.

Their lust, anger, and delusion suddenly vanish of their own accord, becoming like empty space which contains all forms and species; they are born and nurtured by it, and there is nothing that does not depend upon it. This sutra is likewise: it is the source from which the bodhisattvas, as well as the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, arise. Through skillful means and wisdom, it transforms and enlightens the assembly of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, causing them all to attain liberation. All the common people of the triple world receive its salvation; they are freed from the three sufferings and released from their bonds. They universally resolve to seek the Way, enter the profound treasury of Dharma, and through the inexhaustible Dharma-body, transform and enlighten the ten directions.

To fill the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with the seven treasures and offer them to the Buddhas of the ten directions is not as meritorious as receiving this [teaching], reciting and expounding it, and proclaiming it to one's fellow students, thereby repaying the kindness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

The ground of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions is the non-existence of the path of the sages; even space may be measured, and the number of drops in the oceans of the ten directions may be known, yet the virtue of one who studies this sutra is beyond limit.
When the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had thus expounded the Dharma, the Tathāgata expressed his approval.

All the bodhisattvas, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, Śakra, Brahmā, the four heavenly kings, the great and wondrous devas, and the Śuddhāvāsa devas—those dwelling in the sixth celestial palace of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, who move through their abodes like bright moon-jewel halls—had cultivated joy since first generating the mind of enlightenment. Progressing from the first stage to the second, from the third to the fourth, from the fifth and sixth to the seventh, and from the eighth and ninth to the tenth, they attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
All those in the assembly, having heard what the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had spoken, were without exception filled with joy.

The fifth fascicle of the *Anupūrvasamudgataparipṛcchā-sūtra*. On the twenty-first day of the eleventh month in the seventh year of the Yuankang era, the śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa, while at the Xisi Monastery in Chang’an, personally held the Sanskrit manuscript and transcribed it into the language of Jin with his own hand. May all beings throughout the ten directions receive this light, attain the formless state, and liberate sentient beings, so that all may joyfully share in their deliverance.

Now, to explain the Ten Abodes: Śakra and Brahmā are translated as "Jin" (Venerable) in Chinese; this is called the First Abode. In the language of India it is called *Muditā*, which in Chinese means "Joyful.
The Second Abode is named *Vimalā*, which in Chinese means "Free from Defilement."
The third dwelling is named Pṛthagjanābhilakṣita, translated in the Jin language as "Emerging Radiance" (Xìngguāng).
The fourth dwelling is named Arciṣmatī, translated in the Jin language as "Resplendent Brilliance" (Huīyào).
The fifth dwelling is named Sudurjayā, translated in the Jin language as "Difficult to Conquer" (Nánshèng).
The sixth dwelling is named Abhimukha, which in the Jin language means "Direct Vision.
The seventh dwelling is named Sudurjaya, which in the Jin language means "Profound Wonder.
The eighth dwelling is named Acala, which in the Jin language means "Unmoving."
The ninth dwelling is named Sādhumatī, translated in the Jin language as "Excellent Intention.
The tenth dwelling is named Dharmameghā, translated in the Jin language as "Dharma Rain."
